examples.professional: We're a week behind schedule on the data pipeline, so I'll move the dashboard review to next Thursday.
examples.analytical: A project that falls behind schedule is not necessarily failing, but its delay reveals gaps in the original estimate.

nuance.analogy: Being behind schedule is like a train running several minutes off its timetable: the route is still on track, but everything after it is delayed.
nuance.etymology: Schedule comes from Medieval Latin schedula, a small strip of paper, and behind comes from Old English behindan, meaning on the back side.
common_mistakes: Adding 'the' before schedule, as in 'behind the schedule,' which is not the standard phrase.
Using 'late' for a project, when 'behind schedule' is more precise for work and timelines.

conversation.text: Construction on the new office is three weeks behind schedule.
We're a little behind schedule because of the holiday.
If we're behind schedule, we need to tell the client now.

senses.definition: A system of beliefs; a set of beliefs with interrelations.
senses.example: Her research on decision-making drew on a belief system shaped by both economics and philosophy.

core.definition: A set of connected beliefs that together form a coherent worldview, ideology, or religion.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel in belief is a long ee, spelled ie, so it is not like the word beef with a different vowel. Stress falls on SIS in system, and the final -em is a reduced syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic and everyday use. It can sound dismissive when someone describes another person's views as just a belief system, implying they are rigid or unexamined.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in conversation, teaching, and writing about religion, politics, science, or personal values. It is a neutral way to describe the whole package of ideas someone holds. Saying 'That's just your belief system' can sound like a brush-off, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: A worldview is the broad overall picture of reality, while a belief system stresses the explicit set of beliefs and how they connect.
Ideology is usually political or social and often includes a program for action, while belief system is broader and covers religious, philosophical, or personal convictions.
Religion usually implies institutions, rituals, and community, while belief system names only the set of ideas, and can describe a non-religious view too.

examples.everyday: My sister's belief system is pretty different from mine, but we still get along great.
examples.professional: Our data team's belief system is that every dashboard number needs a traceable source before anyone presents it.
examples.analytical: Kuhn argued that a paradigm works like a belief system, shaping which anomalies scientists are willing to notice at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a city map: each belief is a street, and the belief system is the whole network that tells you how to get around.
nuance.etymology: Belief comes from Middle English bileve, and system comes from Greek systēma, a whole made of parts.
common_mistakes: Stressing belief as BE-lief; the stress is on SIS in system, with belief getting a lighter stress.
Writing believe system instead of belief system.

senses.definition: In a belligerent manner; with aggressive hostility.
senses.example: He answered the reporter belligerently, insisting the story was false and refusing further questions.

core.definition: In an aggressive, combative way, showing a readiness to fight or argue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIJ, and the other syllables are reduced to short 'uh' sounds. Many learners stress the middle syllable GER or say the -ent ending too clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes hostile or aggressive behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'belligerently' in news reports, formal writing and descriptions of people who are confrontational. In casual talk, people more often say 'aggressively', 'angrily' or 'like a jerk'. It is a strong word, so use it to describe clear hostility rather than ordinary disagreement.

distinctions.note: Aggressively is the common everyday word and can describe energetic, forceful behavior that is not necessarily hostile.
Truculently suggests defiant, rude and hard-to-handle behavior, while belligerently suggests readiness to fight or argue.

examples.everyday: He yelled belligerently at the waiter when his order took too long.
examples.professional: The client responded belligerently to our revised proposal and refused any compromise.
examples.analytical: Historians note that the diplomat belligerently rejected every peace offer, which hardened the conflict.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog that growls and bares its teeth before anyone even gets close.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bellum, war, and gerere, to wage.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'belligerantly', with an a in the ending.
Stressing the middle syllable, as in 'bel-li-GER-ent-ly'.
Using 'belligerently' for ordinary disagreement, which is too strong.

senses.definition: Synonym of berserker (“a Norse warrior who fought in a frenzy”).
senses.example: The saga describes a berserk who charged into battle howling and tearing at his shield.

senses.definition: Furiously, injuriously, or maniacally violent or out of control.
senses.example: After seeing his sister stabbed to death, he went berserk and attacked the killer like a wild animal.

senses.definition: Bizarre; weird.
senses.example: Their plan to paint the bus purple sounded berserk, but it actually worked.

senses.definition: To be or become berserk.
senses.example: When the printer jammed again, the whole office began to berserk.

senses.definition: To make berserk.
senses.example: The constant ringing of the phone would berserk anyone trying to finish a report.

core.definition: Out of control with anger or excitement, acting wildly or frenziedly; also used informally for something extremely intense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the 'er' in the first syllable is a reduced American r-colored vowel. Keep the final 'k' crisp, without adding a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing violent or uncontrolled anger; can be humorous or intensified in casual speech, as in 'going berserk' over a sale.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'go berserk' in casual talk to mean lose control, get very angry, or get very excited, such as 'the crowd went berserk.' A natural reply might be 'Calm down!' or 'Don't go berserk on me.' It is informal but common, and it works well in sports, shopping, and family settings.

distinctions.note: 'Furious' describes intense anger alone. 'Berserk' adds the idea of losing control and acting wildly.
'Ecstatic' describes great joy. 'Berserk' suggests a frenzied, out-of-control state, which can be positive or negative.

examples.everyday: When the Dodgers hit that home run, the whole bar went berserk and everyone was yelling.
examples.professional: The stock traders went berserk when the report came out, and the volume spiked for an hour.
examples.analytical: A berserk state of collective rage can erase individual judgment and turn a crowd into a single, reckless body.

nuance.analogy: Being berserk is like a kettle boiling over: the pressure builds until it spills everywhere and nobody can stop it.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse berserkr, 'bear-shirt,' a warrior who fought in frenzy, possibly wearing a bearskin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the berserk' as a noun for the state, which is wrong; use 'going berserk.'
Using 'berserk' as a formal word in writing where 'enraged' or 'frenzied' would fit better.
Pronouncing the second syllable with a short vowel instead of a clear 'ur' sound.

senses.definition: A person with a reputation of importance or power.
senses.example: They stopped traffic so some big shot and his entourage could have the whole road to themselves.

senses.definition: A rare and significant chance to achieve fame or success.
senses.example: her one big shot at the brass ring

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see big,‎ shot.

core.definition: An important, powerful, or influential person, often one who acts self-important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SHOT, which uses the cot-caught vowel, like 'hot' and 'not,' rather than the long oo of 'shoot.' Many learners say 'shoot' by mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe a respected leader, but it often sounds mocking when used about someone who acts self-important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use big shot in casual talk about executives, politicians, or local celebrities. Saying 'He thinks he's a big shot' is usually a criticism. In a more neutral way, you can say 'She's one of the big shots at the firm,' and a natural reply is 'Oh really? I didn't know that.'

distinctions.note: Bigwig is a close synonym that is also informal, but it often suggests someone with official status or a long record of influence.
VIP is a formal, neutral term for a very important person who gets special treatment, while big shot is informal and can be sarcastic.

examples.everyday: My neighbor acts like a big shot because he sells cars downtown.
examples.professional: The big shots from headquarters will join the review, so please prepare a short summary.
examples.analytical: The rhetoric of the big shot relies on status rather than argument, so its authority depends on the audience's deference.

nuance.analogy: Like a tall tree in a small forest, noticed by everyone because it stands above the rest.
nuance.etymology: Big plus shot, where shot here means a person of a particular kind; the phrase is American informal slang.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing shot as 'shoot,' with a long oo sound.
Using it as a formal title in writing; in formal documents say 'senior executive' or 'leader.'

senses.definition: Statements which are boastful or exaggerated.
Major topic of conversation; current gossip.
senses.example: The big talk around the office was whether the boss would retire next year.

core.definition: Boastful or exaggerated statements about what someone can do or has achieved, often without action to back them up.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TALK, which has the cot-caught vowel 'aw,' and the l is silent. Many learners say 'tak' with a short a, which is incorrect.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests bragging or empty promises.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say this in a dismissive way: 'That's just big talk' or 'Cut the big talk and show me the numbers.' It is informal and fine among friends or colleagues, but it can sound harsh if aimed at someone's face in a meeting. A natural reply is 'Okay, let's see the results first.'

distinctions.note: Bragging is the general act of boasting about achievements, while big talk focuses on grand claims about future plans or abilities.
Trash talk means insults or taunts, especially in sports or games, while big talk is boastful claims about oneself.

examples.everyday: Mike says he'll fix the car this weekend, but that's just big talk.
examples.professional: Cut the big talk in the planning meeting and give us a realistic delivery date with milestones.
examples.analytical: Big talk about transformative change often masks a lack of concrete mechanisms for achieving it.

nuance.analogy: Like a billboard promising a feast when the restaurant only serves crackers.
nuance.etymology: Talk comes from Middle English talken, to speak; the idiom 'big talk' is informal American English.
common_mistakes: Using big talk for a serious, important conversation; in American English it usually means boasting.
Pronouncing talk with a short a, as in 'tak.'

senses.definition: Someone who binges.
senses.example: As a serious binger, he finished three seasons before breakfast.

senses.definition: A session of drinking alcohol heavily.

core.definition: Someone who eats, drinks, or watches a lot in one long session, especially a series of TV episodes watched back to back.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Say the 'ng' as one sound, not 'n' plus 'g', and make the final syllable a quick, reduced 'er'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. Friends often use it jokingly about themselves, but it can imply a lack of self-control when used about someone else's drinking or eating.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'binger' most often for binge-watching TV, as in 'I'm a total binger.' For drinking or eating, it suggests a pattern rather than one event, so calling someone a binger can sound judgmental. A natural reply to 'I'm a binger' is a laugh and 'Same, I finished the whole season last weekend.'

distinctions.note: A glutton is a person who eats too much as a habit; the word is stronger and more negative than 'binger'.
A heavy drinker drinks a lot over time, while a binger drinks a large amount in one episode with periods of abstinence in between.

examples.everyday: I'm such a binger, so I watched all six seasons in one weekend.
examples.professional: Our data shows that bingers drive most of the weekend viewing on the platform.
examples.analytical: The word binger describes a pattern of behavior rather than a single lapse, which is why researchers care about it.

nuance.analogy: A binger is like a sprinter rather than a marathon runner: all the effort comes in short, intense bursts.
nuance.etymology: From the British dialect verb binge, meaning 'to soak,' later 'to drink to excess'.
common_mistakes: Using 'binger' for someone who only enjoys a show once in a while; it means a person who consumes a lot in one sitting.
Pronouncing the final 'er' as a full syllable, as in 'bin-jer'.

senses.definition: Synonym of life cycle.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see biological,‎ life.

core.definition: The full series of stages a living organism passes through, from its beginning to death and reproduction; usually called life cycle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAH in the first word and on LIFE in the second. In fast speech the phrase links smoothly, so 'biological life' sounds like 'bye-uh-LAH-jih-kuh-LIFE'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It sounds academic in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: This phrase is uncommon in American English. Biologists normally say 'life cycle' for the stages an organism goes through. 'Biological life' also appears in general discussions about living things on Earth, such as 'the biological life of the planet', so check the context before you use it. In everyday conversation, say 'life cycle' or 'living things' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Life cycle' is the standard American term for the stages of an organism's development; 'biological life' is a rarer, more abstract variant.
'Life' is general and philosophical, while 'biological life' refers only to living systems studied in science.

collocations: the biological life of a parasite

examples.everyday: Our high school biology teacher explained how a frog moves through its whole biological life, from egg to adult.
examples.professional: The grant proposal describes the biological life of the parasite in three stages, each with different drug sensitivities.
examples.analytical: Philosophers distinguish biological life, the process of an organism's living, from a biography, which is the narrative of a person's life.

nuance.analogy: The biological life of an organism is like a season of a year: a fixed sequence of stages that returns in a cycle.
nuance.etymology: Combines biological, from Greek bios 'life', and life, from Old English lif.
common_mistakes: Using 'biological life' in everyday speech where 'life cycle' is more natural.
Stressing 'life' too weakly; the phrase is usually spoken with LIFE strongly stressed.

senses.definition: To censor or cover up by writing over with black ink.
senses.example: The editor blacked out the classified names before the report was published.

senses.definition: To censor or cover up.
senses.example: The network blacked out the controversial scene for its late-night broadcast.

senses.definition: To lose consciousness; to suffer a blackout.
To cause (someone) to lose consciousness.
To obscure in darkness.
senses.example: A storm knocked out the power and blacked out the whole neighborhood.

senses.definition: To be in a state of blackout, as a building, a city, a ship.
senses.example: The countryside blacked out to avoid helping enemy aircraft.

core.definition: To lose consciousness or memory for a short time, often from illness, a hard blow, heat, or heavy drinking.

pronunciation.tip: As a verb, the main stress falls on OUT: black OUT. As a noun, blackout, the stress moves to BLACK. Say the diphthong ow clearly, as in out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, since it describes a sudden loss of control or a health scare; it can be casual when used about heavy drinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I blacked out for a second in everyday speech to describe fainting or losing track of time. In medical contexts, doctors and nurses usually say lost consciousness or fainted, and passed out is the most common everyday phrase. The verb also means to censor with black marks, but in writing that is more often redact.

distinctions.note: Pass out is the most common everyday phrase for falling unconscious, and it often means falling asleep from exhaustion or drinking.
Faint is more precise and medical, describing a brief loss of consciousness from low blood flow to the brain.
Redact is the formal term for blacking out text in a document, especially in legal or government writing.

examples.everyday: I stood up too fast and almost blacked out in the kitchen.
examples.professional: Our new intern blacked out during the safety training, so we called the nurse right away.
examples.analytical: Some people black out under extreme stress, and the cause is often a sudden drop in blood flow to the brain.

nuance.analogy: Like a computer that goes to sleep in the middle of a task: the screen goes dark, and when it returns, the work in between is gone.
nuance.etymology: From black (Old English blæc) plus out (Old English ut).
common_mistakes: Stressing BLACK in the verb; the verb stresses OUT, and only the noun blackout stresses BLACK.
Using black out for simply falling asleep; it refers to losing consciousness or memory, not normal sleep.

senses.definition: Ostentatious display, verbal or otherwise; publication; description; record.
senses.example: The wedding's blazon of gold leaf and fireworks was far more than the couple had planned.

senses.definition: A verbal or written description of a coat of arms.
senses.example: The heraldry student wrote out the blazon of the family's arms in precise, formal language.

senses.definition: A formalized language for describing a coat of arms.
senses.example: Learning blazon took me weeks, because its formal vocabulary for describing shields seemed like a foreign language.

senses.definition: A coat of arms or a banner depicting a coat of arms.
senses.example: The castle gate was draped with a blazon showing a silver lion on a red field.

senses.definition: To describe a coat of arms.
senses.example: Before the tournament, the herald had to blazon each knight's shield for the spectators.

senses.definition: To make widely or generally known, to proclaim.
senses.example: The mayor blazoned the city's new recycling program across every newspaper and radio station in the county.

senses.definition: To display conspicuously or publicly.
To shine; to be conspicuous.
To deck; to embellish; to adorn.
senses.example: The grand hall was blazoned with gold banners and fresh garlands for the royal visit.

core.definition: To display or announce something proudly and conspicuously so that everyone notices it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BLAY. The final -on is a reduced schwa, not ohn, and the z is voiced as in zone.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somewhat negative, because it suggests showy or ostentatious display.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blazon mainly in literary, journalistic or heraldic writing and it sounds stiff in everyday talk. In conversation people would more likely say flaunt, splash or plaster across. It is more common as a verb in headlines and descriptions than as a noun.

distinctions.note: Flaunt is informal and implies showing off something you should be modest about; blazon is more formal and often neutral.
Proclaim means to announce publicly; blazon adds the idea of visible display or decoration.
Emblazon means to decorate with a bold design or to display boldly; blazon can also mean announcing or describing.

examples.everyday: Her new car has the company logo blazoned on both doors.
examples.professional: The press release blazoned our quarterly results across the headlines, which gave the board the wrong impression.
examples.analytical: Medieval heralds used a precise technical language to blazon the arms of noble families.

nuance.analogy: Like a banner across a parade float: the message goes up so everyone can read it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French blason, meaning a shield or coat of arms; of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Confusing blazon with blaze, meaning a fire or a bright light.
Using blazon casually where show or display would be more natural.

blazon.etymology: From Middle English *blason*, *blasoun* (“shield”), from Old French *blason* (“shield”).

senses.definition: The condition or state of being blessed; holy.

core.definition: The state of being blessed: deep happiness and favor, especially the joy that comes from God's grace and holiness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ed is pronounced as a separate syllable (id), not as blest, which is the verb form and is used only in certain phrases.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names a deep and lasting joy or favor, often with religious meaning, and it carries a sense of spiritual peace.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use blessedness in everyday talk. You will hear it mainly in sermons, devotional writing, theology, and literary prose. In casual conversation, people say happiness, blessing, or being blessed. A natural everyday reply to someone saying they feel blessed is 'That's great, I'm glad to hear it.'

distinctions.note: Happiness is a feeling that depends on circumstances. Blessedness is a deeper state that many believers see as a gift from God, lasting beyond moods.
A blessing is a particular good thing or a prayer that asks for good. Blessedness is the state of being favored, not a single gift or words said over someone.

examples.everyday: After the long winter, we sat on the porch with lemonade and felt a quiet kind of blessedness.
examples.professional: In his keynote to the engineering team, the director spoke of blessedness as the reward of honest work.
examples.analytical: Augustine locates true blessedness not in created goods but in the soul's rest in God.

nuance.analogy: Blessedness is like a lamp lit from a source outside itself: it is received and shared, not manufactured.
nuance.etymology: From bless, from Old English blēdsian, probably from blōd 'blood', plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -ed as a separate blest sound at the end, which mixes the verb and adjective forms.
Using blessedness for ordinary happiness in casual speech, where it sounds stiff or overly religious.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind blessed in the Beatitudes is makarios, meaning happy, fortunate, and favored by God. The Hebrew equivalent in the Psalms is 'ashre, which means blessed or happy. Matthew 5:3-12 (RSV) opens the Sermon on the Mount with a series of blessings on the poor in spirit, the meek, and the merciful, showing that blessedness belongs to those who depend on God. Psalm 32:1-2 (RSV) describes the blessedness of the person whose transgression is forgiven, which Paul later quotes in Romans 4:7-8 to explain justification by faith. Psalm 1:1 (RSV) begins the Psalter by describing the blessed person who delights in God's law.

traditions.view: Blessedness is the beatitude that is the final end of human life, fulfilled in the beatific vision of God after purification. Catholic teaching also uses blessed as a title for those beatified on the way to canonization.

Blessedness is understood as theosis, the ongoing participation of the human person in the uncreated life and energies of God. It is pursued through prayer, sacraments, and ascetic life rather than defined mainly as a legal status.

Blessedness is grounded in God's favor, received through justification by faith and God's forgiveness. Lutheran writers emphasize the comfort of the gospel for sinners, while Reformed writers stress God's covenant and the glory of God as the purpose of blessedness.

senses.definition: Very bright (as if to cause blindness).
senses.example: The blinding noon sun made it impossible to read the trail map.

senses.definition: Making blind or as if blind; depriving of sight or of understanding.
senses.example: blinding tears; blinding snow

senses.definition: The act of causing blindness.
senses.example: Doctors investigated the blinding caused by a chemical splash at the factory.

senses.definition: A thin coat of sand or gravel used to fill holes in a new road surface.
senses.example: Workers spread a thin blinding of sand over the new road before the rain.

senses.definition: A thin sprinkling of sand or chippings laid on a newly tarred surface.
senses.example: The crew added a layer of blinding over the fresh tar to keep tires from sticking.

core.definition: So bright or intense that it temporarily prevents you from seeing clearly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the diphthong 'eye' sound in 'bl-eye' is long. Don't reduce the 'i' in the second syllable to a schwa; it stays a short 'ih' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to vivid. It describes intense light, pain or emotion, and can be used positively (a blinding smile) or negatively (a blinding headache).
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly for light, such as 'the blinding sun on the highway', and for sudden overwhelming feelings, such as 'a blinding headache.' It is also common in the phrase 'blinding speed' or 'blinding talent.' The figurative sense of 'making someone unable to see the truth' is more formal, as in 'blinding ambition.'

distinctions.note: Dazzling suggests beauty or impressiveness, while blinding suggests a harsh, overwhelming brightness that stops you from seeing.
Blind means unable to see at all, while blinding describes something so bright or intense that it causes temporary loss of sight.

examples.everyday: I had to squint because the sun was blinding on the drive home.
examples.professional: The monitor's glare was blinding, so we moved the dashboard to a darker screen.
examples.analytical: Her argument was blinding in its clarity, yet it obscured the ethical assumptions beneath it.

nuance.analogy: Like walking out of a dark movie theater into the midday sun: for a moment, you can see nothing.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'blind,' from Old English 'blind,' meaning without sight.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'blinding' with 'blinded' (the past participle, as in 'I was blinded by the light').
Using 'blinding' only for the sense of 'blind'; it usually means 'extremely bright or intense,' not total lack of sight.

senses.definition: An uneven patch of color or discoloration.
An irregularly shaped area.
senses.example: A purple blotch spread across the canvas where the paint had pooled.

senses.definition: Imperfection; blemish on one’s reputation, stain.
senses.example: The leaked memo left a blotch on the company's reputation.

senses.definition: Any of various crop diseases that cause the plant to form spots.
senses.example: Farmers noticed a blotch disease spreading through the potato fields this season.

senses.definition: A bright or dark spot on old film caused by dirt and loss of the gelatin covering the film, due to age and poor film quality.
senses.example: Scratches and a dark blotch on the old film made the scene hard to watch.

senses.definition: A dark spot on the skin; a pustule.
senses.example: The dermatologist said the red blotch on his cheek was a harmless pustule.

senses.definition: Blotting paper.
senses.example: She pressed a sheet of blotch against the wet ink on the letter.

senses.definition: To mark with blotches.
senses.example: Allergies had blotched her neck and chest with red patches all afternoon.

senses.definition: To develop blotches, to become blotchy.
senses.example: His face blotches whenever he gets angry or embarrassed in front of people.

core.definition: An irregular patch of discoloration on skin or a surface, or a stain or flaw in something.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, with the vowel 'ah' as in 'father' in General American, which merges with 'aw' in words like 'caught'. End with a sharp 'ch' sound, like 'watch'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes an unattractive mark, usually on skin, fabric, paper or a surface, and can be used figuratively for a blemish on someone's reputation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blotch for red or dark patches on skin, such as after crying, in a rash, or from sun exposure. It can also describe ink or paint stains on paper. In a figurative sense, a blotch on one's record is a stain on reputation, and this is more formal than everyday speech.

distinctions.note: A spot is usually small and round, while a blotch is larger and irregularly shaped.
A stain comes from a substance that soaks in and is often hard to remove, while a blotch is simply an uneven patch of color, whatever causes it.
A blemish is an imperfection in a surface or in someone's appearance or character, and it is a broader term than blotch.

examples.everyday: She gets red blotches on her neck whenever she is nervous.
examples.professional: The scan showed a faint blotch on the image, so the technician reran the test.
examples.analytical: The author treats the scandal as a blotch on the senator's reputation that no later achievement can fully erase.

nuance.analogy: A blotch is like a drop of coffee spreading unevenly across a white tablecloth.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; probably a 16th-century alteration of blot.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel as in 'blow' (/bloʊ/) instead of the 'ah' vowel.
Confusing blotch (a patch) with blotter (blotting paper or a police log).

senses.definition: A bluish green color.
senses.example: blue green:

senses.definition: An ecocapitalist; a person concerned with ecocapitalism.
senses.example: The conference panel was full of blue greens who believed profit and conservation could coexist.

senses.definition: A blue-green alga.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the pond sample was crowded with blue greens drifting in long chains.

senses.definition: Of a bluish green color.
Synonym of ecocapitalist; Pertaining to ecocapitalism.
senses.example: The blue green movement pushed the city council to fund wetland restoration and solar panels.

core.definition: Describing a color between blue and green, like teal or turquoise; in software, a deployment strategy with two identical production environments.

pronunciation.tip: Usually written as blue-green with a hyphen; stress the first word, BLOO, when the compound is an adjective or noun for the color. Pronounce green with a clear r and long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a descriptive color term. In technical contexts, blue-green deployment is a neutral, precise term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'blue-green' for teal-like colors, often for paint, clothing, or the ocean. In software engineering, blue-green deployment means running two production environments and switching traffic between them. The ecocapitalist and blue-green algae senses are rare, so use the color or software sense in everyday and work conversation.

distinctions.note: Teal is a specific dark blue-green color. Blue-green is a broader, more general description of the color range.
Turquoise is a bright, light blue-green, often associated with jewelry or tropical water. Blue-green is less specific.

examples.everyday: I'd like to paint the bathroom a soft blue-green, like the ocean in the morning.
examples.professional: We'll use a blue-green deployment so we can roll back to the old environment if the release fails.
examples.analytical: The author describes the sea in blue-green tones, a color that carries both the sky's calm and the earth's life.

nuance.analogy: Like the color of a swimming pool with light reflecting off the water, or a tropical lagoon.
nuance.etymology: From blue and green, two basic color words combined in a compound; blue-green deployment came from software practice in the 2010s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing green with a short e sound instead of a long ee.
Using blue-green for a deep navy color; it is clearly between blue and green.
Confusing blue-green deployment with blue and green teams in sports; the software term is specific.

senses.definition: A person who blusters.

core.definition: A person who speaks or acts loudly and aggressively, often with empty threats or boasts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the last two syllables are weak, each with an r-colored vowel, not 'air'.

nuance.connotation: Clearly negative; it calls someone noisy and empty rather than strong.
nuance.usage_note: This word is rare in everyday American speech; Americans more often say blowhard, windbag or bully. You might see it in a newspaper column or book review describing a loud politician or executive. Calling someone a blusterer is an insult, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Blowhard is informal American slang for someone who brags loudly; blusterer is more formal and focuses on noisy, empty threats.
A bully uses force or intimidation over people; a blusterer mainly makes noise without necessarily harming anyone.
A windbag talks at length without substance; a blusterer talks loudly and aggressively, often with threats or boasts.

examples.professional: In the review, the blusterer from finance kept demanding deadlines without showing a single number.
examples.analytical: Plato's dialogues often expose the blusterer whose confidence outruns his argument.

nuance.analogy: A blusterer is like a loud speaker with a weak battery: plenty of noise, little power behind it.
nuance.etymology: From bluster (verb), of uncertain origin, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using blusterer for someone who is only loud or cheerful, not boastful or threatening.
Confusing blusterer with blusher, which means cheek makeup or a person who blushes.

senses.definition: A tool used for drilling.
A knife fit for a stabbing.
A person who bores or drills; a person employed to drill bore holes.
A tedious person, who bores others; a bore.
An insect or insect larva that bores into wood.
One of the many types of mollusc that bore into soft rock.
A cyclostome, such as a hagfish, which bores into injured, dead, or decaying sea creatures to feed on their flesh.
The penetrating root of a parasitic plant.

core.definition: A tool or machine for drilling holes; also an insect whose larvae tunnel into wood or plants.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the final -er is a weak, rhotic syllable. It sounds the same as 'boar', a male pig, so context decides the meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'borer' mainly in entomology, forestry, carpentry and manufacturing. For an ordinary hand tool, people say 'drill'. In forestry reports, 'emerald ash borer' is a familiar insect name, and it is a pest of trees, not something you find in a kitchen.

distinctions.note: 'Drill' is the everyday word for the tool and is common in home and hardware talk; 'borer' is more technical and used mainly in forestry and entomology.
An 'auger' is a spiral-bit tool for boring holes in wood; a 'borer' can be a machine or an insect, so context decides.

examples.everyday: The arborist said the emerald ash borer had killed most of the trees on our street.
examples.professional: The shop uses a hand borer for small pilot holes, but the CNC machine handles the production run.
examples.analytical: The entomologist argued that the borer's larval tunnels, not drought alone, explained the decline of the trees.

nuance.analogy: Like a tiny drill that works from inside the wood, leaving holes you can't see until the tree is weak.
nuance.etymology: From bore (verb) plus the suffix -er, one who or that which bores.
common_mistakes: Saying 'borer' for an ordinary hand drill in everyday talk; 'drill' is more natural.
Pronouncing the final -er too strongly, like 'air'; keep it short and rhotic: BOR-er.

senses.definition: Having a quantity or amount that is generous or plentiful; ample.
senses.example: They enjoyed a wet summer and a bountiful harvest.

core.definition: Existing or given in large amounts; plentiful and generous.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BOUN. The middle syllable is a reduced 'tih', and the final -ful is often a syllabic 'l', so it sounds like 'fuhl' with no separate 'oo' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests warmth and generosity, not just quantity, so it is pleasant to hear in most contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bountiful in everyday speech and writing for harvests, meals, gifts, or benefits, as in a bountiful Thanksgiving table. Plentiful is the neutral synonym; bountiful adds a feeling of generosity. It is common in news, cooking, and religious contexts.

distinctions.note: Plentiful only says there is a lot; bountiful adds a sense of generosity or abundance that feels given freely.
Abundant is more neutral and often technical, as in abundant data; bountiful suggests warmth and generous giving.

examples.everyday: Grandma's kitchen was always bountiful at Thanksgiving, and nobody went home hungry.
examples.professional: Our cloud vendor has a bountiful supply of credits, so we can run the experiments this quarter.
examples.analytical: Psalm 104 presents creation as a bountiful provision, sustaining every living thing.

nuance.analogy: A bountiful harvest is like a pantry that never runs low.
nuance.etymology: From bounty, from Old French bonté, goodness, plus -ful, meaning full of.
common_mistakes: Using bountiful and bounteous interchangeably in speech; bountiful is far more common.
Stressing the second syllable as 'boun-TI-ful' instead of BOUN-ti-ful.

senses.definition: Any of many closely related thorny plants in the genus Rubus including the blackberry and likely not including the raspberry proper.
senses.example: Wild blackberry bushes grew along the fence, and their bramble tangled everything in the back field.

senses.definition: Any thorny shrub.
A cocktail of gin, lemon juice, and blackberry liqueur.
senses.example: The bartender shook a bramble with gin, lemon juice, and crème de mûre over crushed ice.

senses.definition: A collection of mutually touching connected subgraphs, where two subgraphs touch if they share a vertex or each includes one endpoint of an edge.
senses.example: The graph theorist showed that every pair of subgraphs in the bramble touched each other.

senses.definition: To pick or collect blackberries from brambles.
senses.example: Every August we bramble along the creek, filling buckets with berries for my grandmother's pies.

core.definition: A thorny shrub, especially a blackberry or raspberry-type plant, with prickly stems that tangle and scratch.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BRAM. The final -ble is a syllabic l with no full vowel, so it sounds like 'buhl' with the l heard clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, suggesting a tangled, thorny place.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech people more often say blackberry bushes or briar patch, and bramble is mostly used in nature writing, poetry and older language. In a conversation about a hedge or a hiking trail, saying 'the brambles' is natural and not wrong. Americans may also use it for a cocktail, but that is a specialized use.

distinctions.note: Briar is a broader word for any thorny plant, often wild rose, while bramble refers to the Rubus genus like blackberries.
A thicket is a dense area of shrubs or small trees, while a bramble is an individual thorny plant or tangle of them.

examples.everyday: Watch your legs in those brambles, they scratch like crazy.
examples.professional: The crew cleared the brambles along the fence line before planting the new hedge.
examples.analytical: In Jotham's fable, the bramble is an unworthy king who accepts the throne the better trees refuse, which makes it a sharp satire of power.

nuance.analogy: A bramble is like a barbed-wire fence that grew on its own, catching anything that brushes against it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bræmbel, from bremel, 'bramble', related to broom.
common_mistakes: Using bramble for any shrub; in American English it refers to thorny plants of the Rubus type.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: In Judges 9:14–15 the trees ask the bramble to reign over them, and the bramble answers with a warning, which is part of Jotham's fable. In Luke 6:44, the Revised Standard Version says that figs are not gathered from thorns, nor grapes picked from a bramble bush, to illustrate that a tree is known by its fruit. The Greek word in Luke 6:44 is batos, 'bramble bush'; the Hebrew word in Judges 9 is atad.

bramble.etymology: From Middle English *brembel*, from Old English *bræmbel*, from earlier *brǣmel*, *brēmel*, from dialectal **brāmil*, diminutive of **brām*.

senses.definition: The number of choices available at each step of a search; it determines how fast the search space grows.
senses.example: A chess engine's branching factor grows quickly, so deeper searches become expensive very fast.

core.definition: In search or planning, the number of choices available at each step. It determines how quickly the search tree grows.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'fac' in 'factor,' and 'branching' has its own stress on 'bran.' The t in 'factor' is often soft or flapped in American speech, so it sounds close to 'FAK-der.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical measure, and a high value simply means the problem is harder to search.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in artificial intelligence, computer science, and game theory courses, and in discussions of planning algorithms. It almost never appears in everyday conversation. Use it precisely: it refers to options per step, not the total number of possible states.

distinctions.note: Search depth is how many levels deep the search goes, while the branching factor is how wide each level is.
Search space is the total set of possible states, while the branching factor is only the number of options at each step.

collocations: branching factor of the game tree

examples.everyday: My son's chess app explained that the branching factor explodes after a few moves, which is why computers have to be clever.
examples.professional: Once we added the new action types, the planner's branching factor jumped, so we started pruning unlikely options early.
examples.analytical: A problem's branching factor, more than its raw size, determines whether exhaustive search remains computationally tractable.

nuance.analogy: It is like a maze where every junction has more doors than the last one: the number of possible paths grows fast.
nuance.etymology: Branch comes from Late Latin branca; factor comes from Latin factor, 'doer, maker,' from facere, 'to do.'
common_mistakes: Calling it 'branch factor' without 'ing,' which sounds unnatural to American technical readers.
Treating it as the total number of states, when it only counts the options available at one step.

conversation.text: Go has a much larger branching factor than chess, which made brute-force search impractical.
Reducing the branching factor by pruning unlikely actions made the planner usable in real time.

senses.definition: A human child.
senses.example: a spoiled brat

senses.definition: A child who is regarded as mischievous, unruly, spoiled, or selfish.
senses.example: a spoiled brat

senses.definition: The qualities possessed by a confident and assertive woman.
senses.example: Her brat energy on stage, loud and unapologetic, made the whole crowd cheer.

senses.definition: A child (at any age) of an active member of the military or the diplomatic service.
senses.example: an army brat

senses.definition: A submissive partner who is disobedient and unruly.
senses.example: In their scene, she played the brat while he set firm rules for the evening.

senses.definition: An immature, spoiled and/or selfish person.
senses.example: My little cousin is a brat who screams whenever he doesn't get dessert.

senses.definition: A turbot or flatfish.
senses.example: The fishmonger said the brat was fresh that morning from the North Sea.

senses.definition: A rough cloak or ragged garment.
senses.example: A ragged brat hung over the old sailor's shoulders against the sea wind.

senses.definition: Bratwurst.
senses.example: We grilled brats and corn at the backyard party on Saturday afternoon.

senses.definition: A thin bed of coal mixed with pyrites or carbonate of lime.
senses.example: Miners hit a thin brat of coal mixed with pyrites while digging the lower shaft.

senses.definition: To act in a bratty manner as the submissive.
senses.example: Tonight she wants to brat a little, so he's ready with the playful consequences.

senses.definition: (rare) Characteristic of a confident and assertive woman.
senses.example: Her brat attitude in the meeting made everyone notice her confidence.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A child, usually one who behaves badly, is spoiled, rude or demanding, and who is annoying to adults.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short a as in 'cat.' Keep the final t crisp and clear, not a soft flap, and use the American r before the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative, though parents may use it playfully about their own children; calling someone else's child a brat is insulting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use brat mostly for children who act spoiled or defiant, and they say it critically or jokingly. Saying it about someone else's child in front of the parents can cause offense. For adults, brat is informal and insulting. A parent might tease their own kid, 'You little brat,' but not a stranger.

distinctions.note: Kid is neutral; brat adds a judgment that the child is badly behaved or spoiled.
Spoiled child describes the cause, meaning a child indulged by parents; brat is a blunt label for the behavior.

examples.everyday: Those kids at the next table are total brats, and their parents are ignoring them.
examples.professional: The junior analyst gets a little brat-like when reviews point out errors, so the manager plans a one-on-one talk.
examples.analytical: Commentators often label rebellious young people as brats, a dismissive term that lets adults avoid examining their own role.

nuance.analogy: A brat is like an untrained puppy: energetic and demanding, and nobody has set clear limits.
common_mistakes: Calling a stranger's child a brat in front of the parents, which is rude.
Using brat as a neutral word for child; it always carries a negative judgment.

senses.definition: One who buckles something.
senses.example: As the team's designated buckler, Maria checked every strap before the climb.

senses.definition: A kind of shield, of various shapes and sizes, held in the hand or worn on the arm (usually the left), for protecting the front of the body. In the sword and buckler play of the Middle Ages in England, the buckler was a small shield, used not to cover the body but to stop or parry blows.
senses.example: The knight raised his buckler to deflect the sword strike.

senses.definition: One of the large, bony, external plates found on many ganoid fishes.
senses.example: The paleontologist identified the fossil fish by its thick bony buckler.

senses.definition: The anterior segment of the shell of a trilobite.
senses.example: The anterior buckler of the trilobite showed clear ridges under the microscope.

senses.definition: A block of wood or plate of iron made to fit a hawse hole, or the circular opening in a half-port, to prevent water from entering when the vessel pitches.
senses.example: The sailor fitted a wooden buckler over the hawse hole before the storm.

core.definition: A small, round shield held in the hand and used to block blows, common in older or biblical contexts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'BUK,' and make the final syllable a weak, reduced 'ler' with an American r. Do not pronounce it like 'book-ler' with a long oo sound.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests protection and defense, and is often used in religious or poetic language.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'buckler' in everyday conversation. You will meet it in older translations of the Bible, in fantasy novels, in historical fiction, and at Renaissance fairs or in museums. In modern speech, people say 'shield' for almost any defensive plate.

distinctions.note: A shield is the general word for a defensive plate; a buckler is a smaller, hand-held version that was often used for quick parrying.
A buckle is a metal clasp used to fasten belts or straps; a buckler is a shield, though the two words look and sound alike.

examples.everyday: The kids at the Renaissance fair were battling each other with wooden swords and bucklers.
examples.professional: The museum curator labeled the Tudor buckler for the new armor exhibit and explained how it was used in close combat.
examples.analytical: Psalm 91:4 pictures God's faithfulness as a buckler, a shield that guards the one who trusts in him.

nuance.analogy: A buckler is like a frying pan used as a shield: small, held in one hand, and meant to deflect quick blows.
nuance.etymology: From Old French bocler, from boucle meaning boss of a shield, from Latin buccula meaning small cheek or boss.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'buckler' with 'buckle' because the words look similar.
Pronouncing the first vowel as in 'book' instead of 'buck.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew words behind buckler include magen (shield, a general term for defense) and tsinnah (a large shield covering the whole body). Psalm 35:2 (RSV) calls on God to take hold of shield and buckler and rise to help the psalmist. Psalm 91:4 (RSV) describes God's faithfulness as a shield and buckler for the one who trusts him. Proverbs 2:7 (RSV) says that God is a buckler to those who walk in integrity.

buckler.etymology: From Middle English *bukler*, *bokler*, *bokeler*, *bokeleer*, from Old French *bocler*, *boucler*, *bucler*, from Vulgar Latin **bucculārius* (“bossed”), from Latin *buccula* (“boss”).

senses.definition: A person who is intentionally physically or emotionally cruel to others, especially to those whom they perceive as being vulnerable or of less power or privilege.
senses.example: A playground bully pushed a girl off the swing.

senses.definition: A noisy, blustering, tyrannical person, more insolent than courageous; one who is threatening and quarrelsome.
senses.example: The loudmouth bully in our office shouted at anyone who questioned his decisions.

senses.definition: A hired thug.
senses.example: The mob boss sent a bully to collect the unpaid debts from the shop owners.

senses.definition: A sex worker's minder.
senses.example: Police said the bully had been taking most of the women's earnings from the brothel.

senses.definition: Bully beef.
senses.example: For the camping trip, we packed canned bully beef, crackers, and dried fruit.

senses.definition: The small scrum in the Eton College field game.
senses.example: At Eton, the boys lined up in a bully before the ball was kicked back into play.

senses.definition: Any of various small freshwater or brackishwater fish of the family Eleotridae; sleeper gobies. A common bully, Gobiomorphus cotidianus.
senses.example: While snorkeling in the stream, we spotted a common bully hiding beneath a flat rock.

senses.definition: A standoff between two players from the opposing teams, who repeatedly hit each other's hockey sticks and then attempt to acquire the ball, as a method of resuming the game in certain circumstances.
senses.example: After the whistle, the referee dropped the puck and the players held a bully at center ice.

senses.definition: A miner's hammer.
senses.example: The old miner swung his bully against the rock until the seam finally cracked open.

senses.definition: To intimidate (someone) as a bully.
senses.example: You shouldn't bully people for being weak.

senses.definition: To act aggressively towards.
senses.example: The older boys bullied the younger kids on the playground every single day.

senses.definition: Well done; often sarcastic in modern use.
senses.example: Bully, she's finally asked for that promotion!

senses.definition: Very good.
senses.example: a bully horse

core.definition: A person who repeatedly hurts, threatens, or intimidates someone weaker or less powerful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, use the short oo vowel of 'full', and end with a clear ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes cruel or abusive behavior toward others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bully mostly for children, coworkers, and public figures who intimidate people. As a verb, it takes an object: to bully someone. The adjective 'very good' and the interjection 'Bully!' are old-fashioned and mostly appear in literature or as jokes.

distinctions.note: Harassment is often legally defined and tied to sexual or discriminatory conduct; bullying is repeated abuse of power, not always illegal.
A troublemaker causes problems but may not target someone weaker; a bully specifically intimidates the vulnerable.
A tyrant rules through absolute power; a bully intimidates individuals in more personal settings.

examples.everyday: The coach made sure the bully stopped picking on the younger kids.
examples.professional: A manager who humiliates staff in meetings is a bully, and HR must treat that as misconduct.
examples.analytical: Calling a supervisor a bully names a pattern of abuse rather than a harsh style, which is why the term matters.

nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; early uses meant sweetheart or fine fellow, and the negative sense developed later.
common_mistakes: Saying 'bully to someone'; the verb takes a direct object, as in 'bully someone'.
Misspelling the -ing form as 'bullieng'; the form is bullying, with a y.

bully.etymology: From 1530, as a term of endearment, probably a diminutive (*y*) of Dutch *boel* (“lover; brother”), from Middle Dutch *boel*, *boele* (“brother; lover”), from **buolo*, from Proto-Germanic **bōlô* (compare, (whence *Buhle* (“lover”)), *Bōlla*, diminutive…

senses.definition: To grow or expand.
senses.example: Gradually, the town burgeoned into a thriving city.

senses.definition: To swell to the point of bursting.
senses.example: Mosquito populations burgeon after the spring rains, filling every backyard pond.

core.definition: To grow or expand quickly and vigorously, especially a business, population, or interest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BUR, and the final syllable is a weak 'un'. The g is pronounced like the j in 'judge', so say 'BUR-jun', not 'BOOR-gee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests healthy, rapid growth and energy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use burgeon in business writing, news, and descriptive prose, as in 'a burgeoning market.' In casual speech, people more often say 'booming' or 'taking off'. It is polite and descriptive, and works well in meetings or reports.

distinctions.note: Flourish means to thrive healthily over time. Burgeon emphasizes rapid expansion and swelling.
Mushroom means to grow suddenly and quickly. Burgeon suggests a more sustained, vigorous growth.
Blossom describes flowers opening, and figuratively a development into fullness. Burgeon focuses on growth in size or number.

examples.everyday: The farmers market has really burgeoned since they opened the new parking lot.
examples.professional: Demand for our data platform has burgeoned, so we need to double the support team by Q3.
examples.analytical: In the Renaissance, trade and learning burgeoned together, reshaping European cities and universities.

nuance.analogy: Like a spring bud that pushes outward until it swells and opens.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French burjon, meaning a bud or sprout.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'bourgeois', which is a different word with a different sound
Using burgeon with a direct object, as in 'burgeon the market', which is not standard usage

burgeon.etymology: From Middle English *burjon,burjoun* (“shoot, bud”), from Anglo-Norman *burjun*, *burgeon*, *burgon*, from Old **burjō* (“sprout, offshoot, descendant”), from Proto-Germanic **burjô* (“sprout, descendant, offshoot”), from Proto-Germanic **burjaną* (“to…

senses.definition: A motor vehicle for transporting large numbers of people along roads.
senses.example: I'm on the bus.

senses.definition: A coach, a bus used for long travels.
senses.example: The school bus carried us to the stadium for the state championship game.

senses.definition: An electrical conductor or interface serving as a common connection for two or more circuits or components.
senses.example: The engineers routed the data over a shared bus connecting all the chips.

senses.definition: Part of a MIRV missile, having on-board motors used to deliver the warhead to a target.
senses.example: The warhead separated from the bus, which then maneuvered toward multiple targets.

senses.definition: An ambulance.
senses.example: The paramedics loaded him onto the bus and raced to the emergency room.

senses.definition: A network topology with each computer connected to a single cable.
senses.example: Our office network used a bus topology, so one broken cable took everything down.

senses.definition: An aeroplane.
senses.example: Grandpa swore the old bus could still outfly any jet in the sky.

senses.definition: To transport via a motor bus.
senses.example: The district buses students to the schools across town each morning.

senses.definition: To transport students to school, often to a more distant school for the purposes of achieving racial integration.
senses.example: The court ordered the district to bus children across town to integrate its schools.

senses.definition: To travel by bus.
senses.example: We bused to the concert and walked the last mile through the crowd.

senses.definition: To clear meal remains from.
senses.example: He bussed tables as the restaurant emptied out.

senses.definition: To work at clearing the remains of meals from tables or counters; to work as a busboy.
senses.example: He’s been bussing for minimum wage.

core.definition: A large motor vehicle that carries many passengers along a fixed route, usually in a city or between towns.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short u, as in 'but' and 'cup', not the 'aw' of 'boss' or the 'oh' of 'bowl'. Make the final s clear, because learners often add an extra vowel and say 'buh-suh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word for everyday transportation, and it can sound slightly lower-class or unfashionable to some Americans, but that is rarely an issue.
nuance.usage_note: This is the everyday American word for city or school transit vehicles, and everyone uses it. People say 'take the bus' or 'catch the bus', and they say 'by bus' with no article. A long-distance bus is often called a coach or Greyhound, but bus is also widely understood.

distinctions.note: Coach is used for intercity or tour buses with comfortable seating. Bus is the general everyday word for local transit.
A streetcar runs on rails in the street. Bus is used for vehicles that run on roads without tracks.
A subway is an underground train system. Bus refers to road vehicles, so the two are not interchangeable.

examples.everyday: I usually take the bus to work because parking downtown is terrible.
examples.professional: The company provides a shuttle bus from the parking lot to the main office during peak hours.
examples.analytical: Public transit scholars often compare the bus with the rail system to explain differences in urban mobility.

nuance.analogy: A bus is like a shared taxi that follows a fixed path and carries many people at once.
nuance.etymology: Short for omnibus, from Latin omnibus, for all. The word was first used in this shortened form in the mid-1800s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'go by the bus' or 'take bus' without the article in the wrong place. The usual forms are 'take the bus' and 'go by bus'.
Pronouncing it with an 'aw' vowel like 'boss' instead of the short u of 'but'.

conversation.text: I take the bus to work every day.
The bus was late again, so I walked.
Does this bus stop near the library?

senses.definition: To work very hard, to put in a great amount of effort.

core.definition: To work very hard and put in a great deal of effort, often for a long time or to meet a deadline.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress is on ASS, with a short a like the vowel in 'cat.' The word one's reduces to 'wunz,' and the t in bust is aspirated before the unstressed word.

nuance.connotation: Positive about the effort, but the language is crude, so it is best kept to casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: This is crude slang, common in casual American speech among friends and coworkers who know each other well. In speech, people say 'my,' 'your,' or 'his' rather than 'one's,' as in 'I busted my ass all week.' Avoid it at work, in front of children, and in formal settings; 'work my butt off' or 'bust my butt' are milder alternatives. A natural reply is 'It shows, and I appreciate it.'

distinctions.note: Work hard is neutral and suitable for any setting, while bust one's ass is crude and informal.
Bust one's butt is a milder, more common version that is more acceptable in mixed company.
Grind is informal and suggests repetitive, exhausting work, but it is less crude.

collocations: bust my ass for the promotion
bust your ass on this project
bust ass to finish the report
bust my ass to get the job done

examples.everyday: I busted my ass all week to get the garage cleaned out, so I'm exhausted.
examples.professional: Thanks for busting your butt on the migration, Sam; I know it was a lot of work for one sprint.
examples.analytical: Cultural narratives that praise people who bust their asses for employers rarely ask who benefits from the exhaustion.

nuance.analogy: Busting your ass is like pushing a car up a hill with your whole body, not just your hands.
nuance.etymology: Bust (to break, wear out) plus ass (buttocks); an informal idiom whose exact origin is undocumented.
common_mistakes: Using bust one's ass in formal or professional writing, where work hard or work very hard is appropriate.
Saying one's in speech; native speakers say my, your, or his in the idiom.

inflections: busted one's ass, bust one's ass

senses.definition: A high cover providing shelter, such as a cloth supported above an object, particularly over a bed.
senses.example: We rested under a white canopy draped over the bed to keep out mosquitoes.

senses.definition: The portion of a plant community (e.g. forest, scrub, or crop) formed by plant crowns.
senses.example: The soybean canopy closed by July, shading out most weeds in the field.

senses.definition: The zone of the highest foliage and branches of a forest.
senses.example: Howler monkeys spend most of their lives high in the forest canopy.

senses.definition: In an airplane, the transparent cockpit cover.
senses.example: The pilot slid the canopy shut before the aircraft taxied toward the runway.

senses.definition: In a parachute, the cloth that fills with air and thus limits the falling speed.
senses.example: After the parachute canopy opened, the jumper drifted gently toward the field below.

senses.definition: Any overhanging or projecting roof structure, typically over entrances or doors.
senses.example: We waited under the hotel's canopy while the doorman hailed a taxi in the rain.

senses.definition: To cover with or as if with a canopy.
senses.example: Ancient oaks canopy the trail, so the path stays cool even in July.

senses.definition: To go through the canopy of a forest on a zipline.
senses.example: Our guide promised we would canopy through the treetops on the zipline near the waterfall.

core.definition: A cover hung or raised above something, such as a bed, a doorway, or a platform, or the upper layer of leaves and branches in a forest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle to a schwa, so it is KAN-uh-pee. The dictionary's dotted form is simplified in American speech, and the final y sounds like 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest shelter, luxury, or natural beauty depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use canopy for a fabric cover over a bed, an entrance awning, or the treetops in a forest. A store entrance canopy is common in American retail and gas stations. As a verb, to canopy means to cover like a canopy, and the zipline sense is common in tourism and adventure travel.

distinctions.note: An awning is usually a fixed, sloping cover attached to a building; a canopy is often freestanding or more decorative.
A roof is a permanent structure; a canopy is a lighter cover that is often open at the sides.

examples.everyday: We ate lunch under the big canopy of an oak tree behind the house.
examples.professional: The hotel's entrance canopy needs to be inspected before the conference.
examples.analytical: Isaiah 4:5 describes a canopy over the glory of Zion, which in its context evokes protection and divine presence.

nuance.analogy: A canopy is like an umbrella held up high, sheltering what lies beneath it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English canape, from Medieval Latin conopeum, from Greek konōpeion, 'mosquito net'.
common_mistakes: Saying KAY-no-pee with a long first vowel.
Using canopy for any roof, when the word suggests a lighter, open cover.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible the canopy is a cover over a bridal or ritual space, linked to the Hebrew huppah. Isaiah 4:5 describes God's glory as a canopy over Zion, a picture of shelter and presence. The image echoes the wedding canopy and the protection of God's people.

canopy.etymology: From Middle English *canapy*, *canepie*, *canapee*, *canape*, *canope*, from Old French *conopé*, Medieval Latin *canapeum*, *canopeum*, from Latin *cōnōpēum* (“mosquito net, canopy”), from Ancient Greek *κωνωπεῖον* (“mosquito net”), from Ancient Greek…

senses.definition: Melodious.
Resonant.

core.definition: Melodious and resonant, having a pleasing, musical sound, often used of voices or birdsong.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, which has an 'or' vowel like in 'north.' The r is pronounced in American speech, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Positive and poetic, suggesting beauty of sound. It is rarely used in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use canorous in conversation; it appears mainly in poetry, literary criticism, or descriptive writing about music or nature. In everyday speech, people say 'melodious,' 'musical,' or 'beautiful.' If you use it, it sounds elegant, and a reply might be 'That's a lovely word for it.'

distinctions.note: Melodious is common and everyday; canorous is more literary and emphasizes resonant, ringing sound.
Sonorous describes deep, full, impressive sound; canorous stresses musical, singing quality.

examples.professional: The presenter's canorous narration made the product video memorable, though it was a little too poetic for the audience.
examples.analytical: The poet's canorous diction relies on sound patterns that echo the rhythm of the liturgy.

nuance.analogy: Like a bell that rings clearly and keeps humming after it is struck.
nuance.etymology: From Latin canorus, melodious, from canor, a melodious sound, from canere, to sing.
common_mistakes: Confusing canorous with canopy or canorous with canorous-sounding words; it means melodious, not 'covered.'
Dropping the r in the pronunciation, which changes the word's sound in American English.

senses.definition: American and Oxford British English standard spelling of capitalization.
senses.example: The journal's style sheet prefers capitalization over the British capitalisation spelling.

core.definition: The use of capital letters in writing, or the total market value of a company's outstanding shares.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on ZAY, and the 'ize' sound becomes a quick 'uh-ZAY.' The first syllable has a secondary stress, and the t is a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical or grammatical term without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use capitalization in grammar and writing, such as 'Check the capitalization in your title,' and in finance, such as 'market capitalization.' Its spelling uses -ization, the standard American form, while British writers often use -isation. Note that the item's gloss only covers spelling; in finance and grammar the word has specific meanings. A natural reply to 'The capitalization is wrong' is 'Thanks, I'll fix it.'

distinctions.note: Capitalization refers to capital letters or market value, while capitalism is an economic system.
Capitalization is the noun for the process, while capitalize is the verb, as in 'capitalize the first letter.'

examples.everyday: Can you check the capitalization on the sign? It says 'open daily' instead of 'Open Daily.'
examples.professional: The company's market capitalization rose above two billion dollars after the earnings call.
examples.analytical: The style guide's rules for capitalization in headings reveal a commitment to consistency, even where grammar alone would permit variation.

nuance.analogy: Capitalization is like a sign on the door: the capital letter tells the reader where something important begins.
nuance.etymology: From capitalize, from capital, from Latin capitalis 'of the head,' with the suffix -ization for the process.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling capitalisation in American writing.
Confusing capitalization with capitalism, which is an economic system.

senses.definition: Containing carbon dioxide gas under pressure, especially pertaining to beverages, as natural mineral water or man-made drinks.
senses.example: Soda pop, lemon soda and soda water are carbonated drinks. Champagne and beer are naturally carbonated through fermentation.

senses.definition: Containing calcium carbonate, often as a result of mineral carbonation.
senses.example: The carbonated rock layers in the cave were dissolved by slightly acidic groundwater.

core.definition: Containing bubbles of carbon dioxide gas under pressure, like soda or sparkling water.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHR. The ending '-ed' after a 't' is pronounced 'id', so the word has four syllables, with the last one a short 'id' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a feature of a drink, and people may prefer or avoid carbonated drinks for taste or health reasons.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'carbonated' mostly for drinks and on labels, as in 'carbonated water' or 'a carbonated soft drink.' In casual talk people say 'fizzy' or 'bubbly.' On menus, 'sparkling' is more common than 'carbonated' for water.

distinctions.note: Fizzy is informal and casual, while carbonated is the precise word used on labels and in product descriptions.
Sparkling is common on menus for water, while carbonated is used on labels and in technical contexts.

examples.everyday: I prefer still water, but my brother only drinks carbonated stuff.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants to launch a lightly carbonated version of the drink next summer.
examples.analytical: Carbonated beverages can change how we perceive flavor, because dissolved carbon dioxide adds a slight acidity.

nuance.analogy: A carbonated drink is like a bottle of soda held under pressure: the bubbles wait inside until you open the cap.
nuance.etymology: From carbonate, with the suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Saying 'KAR-bun-ated' with an extra syllable that is not there; the word has the same structure as 'carbonate' plus '-ed'.
Using 'carbonated' for any bubbly thing; it refers to dissolved carbon dioxide.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or resembling a carbuncle.

core.definition: Relating to a carbuncle, a deep, painful skin infection made of a cluster of connected boils; also resembling a red gem.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BUNG, and the u is a short 'uh' sound as in 'bung'. The final -ar is an r-colored reduced vowel, so the word ends in 'ler'. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or drop the n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral medical description, but it can sound grim.
nuance.usage_note: This is mainly a medical or literary adjective and is rarely used in conversation. Americans would say 'a bad boil' or 'an abscess' in everyday speech, while a doctor might write 'carbuncle' in a clinical note. Use it in writing when describing a cluster of infected boils or a gem-like red glow.

distinctions.note: Furuncular relates to a single boil, while carbuncular refers to the larger, deeper cluster of connected boils that is more serious.

examples.professional: The clinic note describes a carbuncular lesion on the lower back that will need incision and drainage.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers used carbuncular imagery for the glow of a red gemstone, a metaphor that linked the jewel to a festering sore.

nuance.analogy: Like several boils gathered together under one swollen patch of skin.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin carbunculus, meaning small coal or ember, which gave English carbuncle for both a boil and a red gem.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as carbunkular or carbonular; the root is carbuncle, spelled with -unc-.
Using it for an ordinary pimple; a carbuncle is a deep, serious infection.

senses.definition: A thing which is closely associated with or related to another thing.
senses.example: Anxiety and insomnia are cater-cousins, so treating one often helps the other.

core.definition: A close friend who is not a blood relative but is regarded as so close that he or she is almost like a cousin.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable is stressed, and the -er is a reduced r sound. Cousin is pronounced KUZ-uhn, not KOO-zin, and the ou sounds like 'uh', not like 'out'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm, but old-fashioned. It sounds whimsical in modern speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use cater-cousin today, and it is mostly found in older British or literary writing. In everyday American English, say best friend, close friend or my bestie. The word may be understood, but using it today will sound quaint or deliberately playful.

distinctions.note: Best friend is the normal American term, while cater-cousin is archaic and carries a sense of an intimate bond with no family tie.
A kinsman is a blood relative, while a cater-cousin is a friend who is treated as if related.

examples.everyday: Ruth isn't my cousin, but she's my cater-cousin, the friend I have known since we were kids.
examples.professional: Our former project lead became a cater-cousin to the team over the years, more a friend than a boss.
examples.analytical: The novel calls the narrator's loyal companion his cater-cousin, a term signaling a bond stronger than ordinary friendship.

nuance.analogy: Like a relative you chose rather than one you were born with, a cater-cousin is family by affection.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; the cater element may come from Old French quatre, meaning four, but this is disputed.
common_mistakes: Assuming it means a literal cousin, when it refers to a non-blood friend.
Using it in modern American speech where best friend is normal.

senses.definition: A language model that predicts each token only from the tokens before it; used for text generation.
senses.example: Our team fine-tuned a causal language model to generate product descriptions from short bullet lists.

core.definition: A language model that predicts each token only from the tokens before it, generating text one token at a time.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MAH in model. Language ends with a soft j sound, like gwuhj, not gwaj or gwayj.

nuance.connotation: Neutral technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers use this term for GPT-style models that generate text from left to right. In meetings people often shorten it to causal LM or call it a decoder-only model. It contrasts with masked language models, which use context from both sides, so calling a model causal signals how it generates text.

distinctions.note: A masked language model predicts hidden tokens using context from both sides, while a causal language model uses only the earlier tokens.
Causal here refers to the generation order and attention mask, not to cause and effect in the world.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the chatbot uses a causal language model, so it writes one word at a time.
examples.professional: We'll fine-tune the causal language model on our support tickets before the Thursday review.
examples.analytical: A causal language model factorizes the joint probability of a sequence into conditional probabilities, each conditioned only on the preceding tokens.

nuance.analogy: Like a storyteller who writes each sentence without peeking at the ending.
common_mistakes: Assuming causal means the model captures cause and effect in the world; in this term it means the model only looks at earlier tokens.
Saying LANG-gwage; the word is pronounced LANG-gwidj.

conversation.text: A causal language model only attends to earlier tokens, which is what makes left-to-right generation possible.
The causal language model uses a triangular attention mask so no position can see future tokens.
All baselines are decoder-only causal language models trained with the same tokenizer.

senses.definition: A person who cavils; a faultfinder, quibbler or nitpicker.

core.definition: A person who cavils, meaning someone who raises petty objections and finds fault over trivial matters.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -er is a reduced American r-colored vowel, not a full 'ee' sound. Many learners confuse this word with 'caviar' and stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a caviler criticizes them for nitpicking and for focusing on small faults instead of the main issue.
nuance.usage_note: This is a bookish word that Americans more often meet in reviews, essays and formal criticism than in casual talk. In everyday speech, Americans say 'nitpicker' or 'nit-picker' for the same kind of person. The verb 'cavil at' is more common than the noun, as in 'cavil at every detail'.

distinctions.note: Nitpicker is informal and common in everyday American speech, while caviler is formal and literary, with a more deliberate and argumentative tone.
A critic offers a reasoned evaluation of a work, while a caviler raises trivial or technical objections without engaging the main point.

collocations: a habitual caviler in committee meetings

examples.everyday: My brother is a caviler who complains about every small detail of our vacation plans.
