pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KAH, the second syllable. The '-ol-' is reduced to 'uh', and the '-ogy' part of the root becomes 'uh-jist' in this word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a scientist is respected, but calling an activist an ecologist can sound loose or political.
nuance.usage_note: Americans normally use 'ecologist' for a trained scientist who studies ecosystems, often in universities, government agencies or consulting firms. Many Americans also use it loosely for an environmental activist, though that is less precise. When you mean a campaigner, 'environmentalist' is the clearer choice.

distinctions.note: An environmentalist advocates for protecting nature and may have no scientific training, while an ecologist studies ecosystems, usually with a research degree.
Biologists study all living things, from cells to organisms, while ecologists focus on organisms within their environments.

examples.everyday: My cousin is an ecologist, so she spent the summer counting frogs in the wetlands.
examples.professional: Our ecologist recommended delaying construction until after the bird nesting season.
examples.analytical: The ecologist's model treats the forest as a network of interactions rather than a collection of separate species.

nuance.analogy: Like a doctor for a whole ecosystem, checking how each part is connected to the others.
nuance.etymology: From ecology plus the suffix -ist, meaning a person who studies or practices a field.
common_mistakes: Using 'ecologist' for anyone who cares about nature, which is loose usage in technical contexts.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'EE-kol-uh-jist' instead of KAH.

senses.definition: In an economical manner; not wastefully; not extravagantly.
From the perspective of economics or an economy.
According to divine economy.
senses.example: The pastor argued that God had acted economically, using each prophet exactly as needed for salvation history.

core.definition: In a way that saves money or resources; without waste. Also: in terms of economics or the economy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on NAH, and the final syllable is "klee", not "klay". The middle syllables are weak and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests efficiency and sensible use of resources, and it can also be a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people say something is run economically when it uses little money, fuel, or space. In professional and academic speech, it often means "from an economic point of view," as in "economically viable." Listeners will understand from context which sense you mean.

distinctions.note: Efficiently focuses on getting the most output from the least effort or time; economically focuses more on cost and money.

examples.everyday: We can't afford a new couch, so we're shopping economically this month.
examples.professional: The new model runs economically on a single GPU, so we can cut our cloud bill.
examples.analytical: Economically speaking, the policy shifts wealth from renters to property owners.

nuance.analogy: Acting economically is like packing a suitcase carefully so that every item has a purpose and nothing is wasted.
nuance.etymology: From economical plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using economically to mean "economically" when you mean "economic" in front of a noun, as in "economically growth" instead of "economic growth".
Forgetting the stress is on NAH, which shifts the vowel quality.

senses.definition: Nervous, apprehensive.
senses.example: Before the job interview, I felt edgy and kept checking my watch.

senses.definition: Creatively challenging; cutting edge; leading edge.
senses.example: The gallery's edgy new exhibit features sculptures made from recycled circuit boards.

senses.definition: On the edge between acceptable and offensive; pushing the boundaries of good taste; risqué.
senses.example: The comedian's edgy jokes about politics and religion made some of the audience gasp.

senses.definition: Having some of the forms, such as drapery or the like, too sharply defined.
senses.example: The sculptor's edgy folds of marble cloth looked too stiff for the gentle figure.

senses.definition: Sharp; having prominent edges.
senses.example: The edgy broken glass along the windowsill cut my hand when I reached for the latch.

senses.definition: Cool by virtue of being tough, dark, or badass.
senses.example: He wore a black leather jacket and thought he looked edgy on his motorcycle.

senses.definition: Exhibiting behavior that is disconcerting or alarming, sometimes in an effort to impress or to troll others.
senses.example: Her edgy comments on the forum were meant to provoke everyone and get attention.

senses.definition: (dated) Irritable.
senses.example: an edgy temper
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Bold and unconventional, pushing boundaries, often with a slightly provocative or risky quality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EDGE, the first syllable. The final y is a clear ee sound, so say EJ-ee, not EJ-ay.

nuance.connotation: Often positive, describing creative or fashionable boldness. It can be negative when it means too provocative or tasteless.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use edgy in conversation about movies, fashion, comedy, advertising and restaurants. It is informal and usually positive, though it can mean risqué or in poor taste. Someone who is nervous may be described as on edge, not edgy.

distinctions.note: Nervous means anxious or apprehensive; edgy describes a style or work that pushes limits, though in British and older usage it can mean tense.
Avant-garde is more formal and art-focused; edgy is casual and used for ordinary products, shows and jokes.

examples.everyday: That comedian's jokes are a little edgy, so I would not bring your grandmother.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants an edgy campaign, but legal wants to avoid anything that could offend customers.
examples.analytical: Critics praise the film's edgy style, although its shock value sometimes replaces genuine moral complexity.

nuance.analogy: An edgy design is like a bold, unexpected seasoning on a familiar dish: some people love it, and others find it too strong.
nuance.etymology: From edge, meaning a sharp border or limit, with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using edgy to mean nervous or on edge; Americans say on edge or nervous for that.
Pronouncing the final y as ay; it is a clear ee sound.

senses.definition: To encourage or coax (a person) to do something, especially something foolhardy or reckless.
senses.example: My friends kept egging me on to jump off the dock into the freezing lake.

core.definition: To encourage or urge someone to do something, often something risky or foolish, usually by repeated prompting.

pronunciation.tip: The stress lands on 'on', which is the particle, so say 'egg-ON' with the second word stronger. Link the two words so it sounds like 'eh-gon' with a quick, soft transition.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, because it suggests pushing someone toward a bad decision. It can be neutral when the encouragement is light, such as 'egging on the team'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrasal verb in casual conversation, often about friends or siblings who dare each other to do something silly. It needs an object, as in 'egged him on' or 'egged me on'. A natural reply might be 'Don't let them egg you on' or 'Yeah, I shouldn't have let them egg me on.'

distinctions.note: Urge is neutral or formal and can be positive; egg on is informal and usually suggests someone is pushing another person into trouble.
Encourage is positive and everyday; egg on implies that the encouragement leads to recklessness or a bad choice.

examples.everyday: My cousin kept egging me on to jump off the dock, so I finally did.
examples.professional: Please don't let the sales team egg each other on into promising features we haven't tested.
examples.analytical: Certain media outlets egg on public outrage because controversy drives engagement and advertising revenue.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach yelling from the sidelines, pushing a player to take a risk the player might otherwise avoid.
nuance.etymology: From the verb egg, to incite, from Old Norse eggja, to urge on, combined with the particle on.
common_mistakes: Omitting the object, as in 'He egged on' with no person named; use 'egged someone on'.
Using 'egg on' for ordinary encouragement in a positive situation without considering that it often carries a negative sense.

egg-on.etymology: * From Middle English *eggen* (“to incite; urge on; instigate”), from Old Norse *eggja* (“to incite”), from *egg* (“edge”).

core.definition: A king of Moab in the Bible who oppressed Israel until the judge Ehud assassinated him, and also a town in Judah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EG. The final syllable is a short 'un' sound in American English, and the 'o' is the cot vowel, pronounced 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a biblical name and place name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Eglon mainly in Bible study, sermons, or historical discussions of the Book of Judges. People often use it when retelling the story of Ehud. It is not a word used in everyday conversation.

examples.everyday: In Sunday school, we learned about Ehud and King Eglon, the Moabite king who got into trouble with Israel.
examples.professional: In the sermon, the pastor used Eglon's story to illustrate how God raised Ehud to deliver his people.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Eglon in Judges 3 uses satire and bodily detail to depict the collapse of a foreign ruler's power.

nuance.analogy: Eglon is like a villain in a famous story whose name is remembered because of how he fell.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'lon' with a long o.
Confusing Eglon with Eglah, the wife of David in 2 Samuel 3:5.
nuance.biblical_note: Eglon is the king of Moab in Judges 3. The Hebrew name is ʿEglôn, and the meaning is uncertain. The most important passage is Judges 3:12-30. Moab, with Ammon and Amalek, oppressed Israel for eighteen years, and Eglon ruled over them. Ehud, a left-handed Benjaminite, brought tribute to Eglon, then returned alone and killed him in his roof chamber, which lets the story show God's deliverance through an unlikely hero. Joshua 10:3-5 and 10:34-37 also mention Eglon as a town in the southern hill country of Judah that Joshua defeated.

senses.definition: To make joyful or proud.
senses.example: The good news about her test scores elated the entire family.

senses.definition: To lift up; raise; elevate.
senses.example: Ancient builders elated the heavy stones into position using wooden rollers.

senses.definition: Elated; exultant.
senses.example: She was elated when she heard that her application had been accepted.

core.definition: To fill someone with great joy or pride, making them feel happy and excited.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LAYT. In the past tense, elated, the t becomes a quick flap that sounds like 'ih-LAY-ded.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes happiness or pride that feels sudden and intense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the adjective elated in everyday speech, as in 'I was elated.' The verb is more formal or literary, as in 'The news elated the team,' and it can sound stylish or old-fashioned. For casual talk, say 'That made me so happy' or 'I was thrilled.'

distinctions.note: Delight is warmer and more everyday, while elate suggests a sudden lift of spirits, often with pride.
Exhilarate emphasizes physical energy and excitement, while elate focuses on joy or pride.

examples.everyday: Hearing that you passed the bar exam really elated me, and I called everyone I knew.
examples.professional: The announcement of the new contract elated the sales team and changed the mood of the whole week.
examples.analytical: The poem elates its reader less through argument than through an almost physical lift of rhythm and imagery.

nuance.analogy: Like a balloon lifted by warm air: the spirit rises and carries the person upward.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elatus, past participle of efferre 'to carry out or raise up.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am elate' instead of 'I am elated.'
Using elate as an adjective, when the adjective form is elated.

elate.etymology: From Middle English *elat*, *elate*, from Latin *ēlātus* (“exalted, lofty”), perfect passive participle of *efferō* (“bring forth or out; raise; exalt”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: A point in time which is nearly too late; the last minute.
senses.example: We finally submitted the grant application at the eleventh hour, just minutes before the portal closed.

core.definition: The last possible moment, just before something would be too late, usually to avoid failure or disaster.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on OW in 'hour', which is pronounced like 'our' with a silent h. In 'eleventh', avoid adding an extra syllable, so say 'unth' as one quick unit.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it often suggests last-minute rescue, urgency or relief, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'at the eleventh hour' for something done just before a deadline, and it often appears in news and business writing. A natural reply after a rescue is 'Just in time!' or 'Phew, that was close.' Writers may write '11th hour' in headlines, but 'eleventh hour' is more formal.

distinctions.note: Last minute is neutral and general, while eleventh hour usually suggests a late rescue or a change made just before a deadline.
A deadline is the time limit itself, while eleventh hour describes an action taken right before that limit.

examples.everyday: My sister showed up at the eleventh hour with the cake, just before the party started.
examples.professional: Legal sent eleventh-hour changes to the contract, so we had to reschedule the signing.
examples.analytical: Many interpreters read the parable of the workers in the vineyard as showing that grace can come at the eleventh hour.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who crosses the finish line just before the clock stops, the eleventh hour is the last chance before it is too late.
nuance.etymology: The phrase comes from the idea of the eleventh of the twelve hours in the working day, as in the parable of the vineyard workers in Matthew 20.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the last eleventh hour', which is redundant; 'at the eleventh hour' is enough.
Pronouncing 'eleventh' with an extra syllable, as in 'eleven-th'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Greek of Matthew 20, the word for hour is hōra, meaning a period of time or a fixed hour of the day, and the parable counts the workday in twelve hours. Matthew 20:1-16 describes a landowner who hires workers at different hours and pays them all the same wage. Matthew 20:6 and 20:9 mention the workers hired about the eleventh hour, the last hour of the day, to show that the landowner's generosity and the kingdom's grace can reach people late.

eleventh-hour.etymology: From a parable in the Bible of workmen hired at the eleventh hour, known as the Parable of the Workers of the Eleventh Hour or the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard:

senses.definition: Characteristic of an elf; elfin, elven.
senses.example: She had a mischievous, elfish grin that made the children suspect she knew their secrets.

senses.definition: Mischievous.

core.definition: Resembling an elf; playful, mischievous or slyly humorous in a small, otherworldly way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EL. The final -ish is a short 'ish' sound, not 'eesh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, with a mischievous edge; it can describe a playful grin or charm, but it can also suggest someone is a bit sly.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly see 'elfish' in fiction, poetry, or descriptions of someone's grin or humor, and it is uncommon in everyday American speech. For small, delicate features, Americans more often say 'elfin' or 'elf-like'. Calling a friend 'elfish' is a warm, slightly literary compliment.

distinctions.note: Elfin usually describes small, delicate, slender beauty, while elfish emphasizes mischief or playful charm.
Elven refers to elves as a people in fantasy literature, while elfish describes a quality or manner.

examples.everyday: Her elfish grin told me she already had a prank planned for the office party.
examples.professional: Our new intern has an elfish sense of humor that keeps the team's stand-ups light.
examples.analytical: The poet's elfish irony hides a serious critique of the village's moral hypocrisy.

nuance.analogy: Like a kid who smirks after hiding your keys, elfish describes a playful look that hints at mischief.
nuance.etymology: From elf and the suffix -ish, from Old English ælf.
common_mistakes: Using elfish for small physical size; say elfin for delicate features.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable instead of EL.

senses.definition: The act of elucubrating.
senses.example: His late-night elucubration produced a dense essay that nobody in the department could finish.

core.definition: Laborious writing or study, often done late at night by lamplight; also a pretentious or overwrought literary product.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on BRAY. The 'cu' is 'kyoo', with a clear y sound, and do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Often mildly negative or mocking; implies pretentious or overwrought work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word; it appears in older essays, satire and some academic writing, often humorously. Calling someone's work an elucubration suggests it was labored or pompous. In everyday speech, say late-night writing, all-nighter or grind.

distinctions.note: Elaboration means adding detail to something and is neutral and common; elucubration suggests laborious writing or study, often at night, with a mocking tone.
Meditation suggests quiet reflection; elucubration implies strained or heavy effort, often with pretension.

examples.everyday: My dad jokes that his tax planning is pure elucubration at the kitchen table.
examples.professional: The memo reads like elucubration, so please shorten it and state the recommendation in the first paragraph.
examples.analytical: Much of his later work is elucubration, dense with allusions that signal learning more than they clarify the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle burned down to a stub while the writer chases one more idea.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elucubrare, to work by lamplight, from e- (out) and lucubrare (to work by lamplight).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with elucidation, which means explanation; elucubration means laborious work or pretentious writing.
Using it as a compliment; the word usually carries a hint of mockery.

elucubration.etymology: From the past participle of Latin *elucubrare* (“compose by lamplight”).

senses.definition: A final product, especially one resulting from a series of stages or processes.

core.definition: The final result of a series of stages or processes, ready to be sold, used or delivered, as opposed to the intermediate steps.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PRAH in 'product' because this is the noun form, while the verb 'produce' is stressed on the second syllable. The final 't' is light and almost unreleased in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a result without judging its quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'end product' in manufacturing, software, engineering, science and business reports, and in everyday talk about the result of a process, such as a recipe. It is slightly more formal than 'finished product' and is often used when describing stages of a process. In a casual setting, 'the final result' or 'what you end up with' may be more natural.

distinctions.note: A by-product is an unintended secondary result of a process, while an end product is the intended final output.
Finished product means something complete and ready for sale; end product stresses the final stage of a sequence of steps.
Output is a general term for what a system produces, while end product usually refers to the last step of a defined process.

collocations: the end product of a process

examples.everyday: The bakery's end product was a tray of perfect cinnamon rolls, even though my kitchen looked like a disaster.
examples.professional: The end product of this sprint is a deployable model with an API and documentation for the team.
examples.analytical: In Aristotelian terms the end product is the telos of the process, though many modern accounts reduce it to mere output.

nuance.analogy: Like the finished loaf that comes out of the oven after flour, water and yeast have gone through every step.
nuance.etymology: Product comes from Latin productum, 'something brought forth'; end comes from Old English ende.
common_mistakes: Confusing end product with by-product, which is an unintended extra result.
Stressing the second syllable of the noun, saying 'pro-DUCT' instead of PRAH-dukt.
Using 'end product' for a single item that has no stages behind it, where 'product' or 'item' is more natural.

senses.definition: In an enduring manner or fashion; so as to endure or last.
senses.example: The painter's works were enduringly popular.

core.definition: In a way that lasts a long time, or so as to continue through time without fading.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the 'DOOR' syllable. The final syllable is 'lee' and should be unstressed and short, not 'lay'.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'enduringly' in speech; it appears mainly in writing, reviews, essays or literary prose. In everyday talk, say 'for a long time' or 'still' instead. You will sometimes see it with words like 'popular' or 'influential' in praise of a book, film or artist.

distinctions.note: Permanently means forever with no change at all; enduringly suggests lasting a long time and surviving challenges.
Lastingly is also rare, and both are less common than 'lastingly' or 'for good'; enduringly carries a stronger sense of surviving through time.

examples.everyday: That old song still sounds enduringly good, even after all these years.
examples.professional: The design principles remain enduringly useful, so we decided not to change them in the new release.
examples.analytical: The essay shows how the novel remains enduringly relevant to questions of justice and memory.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone that keeps its shape while the river flows past, something enduringly good stays the same as time moves on.
nuance.etymology: From 'enduring' (from 'endure') plus the adverb suffix '-ly.'
common_mistakes: Using 'enduringly' in casual speech where 'for a long time' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'enduringly' as 'endlessly' (which means without end and can sound negative).

senses.definition: Someone who is hostile to, feels hatred towards, opposes the interests of, or intends injury to someone else.
senses.example: under enemy duress

senses.definition: A hostile force or nation; a fighting member of such a force or nation.
senses.example: Rally together against a common enemy.

senses.definition: Something harmful or threatening to another.
senses.example: Sleep deprivation is the enemy of good decisions, especially during exams.

senses.definition: Of, by, relating to, or belonging to an enemy.
senses.example: The building was destroyed by enemy bombing.

senses.definition: A non-player character that tries to harm the player.
senses.example: The boss fight in level three requires you to defeat ten enemies before the gate opens.

senses.definition: To make an enemy of.
senses.example: Her blunt memo on budget cuts quickly enemied several senior managers.

core.definition: A person who hates you or wants to harm you, or who opposes your side in a conflict or war.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'EN-uh-mee' rather than 'eh-NEH-mee' or 'EN-ah-mee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'enemy' for people who really oppose or hate you, or for opposing nations and armies. For mild disagreement, say 'rival' or 'opponent' instead; calling a coworker your 'enemy' sounds dramatic. 'Frenemy' is a playful American term for someone who is partly a friend and partly a rival. The verb sense 'to make an enemy of' is rare, so use 'make an enemy of someone' instead.

distinctions.note: An opponent is the person you compete against in a game, debate or election, and it does not require hatred; an enemy is a more personal or hostile opposition.
A rival competes with you for the same goal, often with respect; an enemy is more hostile and may want to harm you.
Adversary is more formal and often used for legal or military opposition; enemy is more emotional and common in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about him; he's not your enemy, he's just grumpy before lunch.
examples.professional: Our biggest enemy right now is the schedule, so let's cut the nonessential meetings this week.
examples.analytical: Augustine distinguishes between a personal enemy and an enemy of justice, and the distinction shapes his ethics of forgiveness.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire that burns down a house, an enemy is something that works against your interests on purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'enemi,' from Old French 'enemi,' from Latin 'inimicus' 'unfriendly,' from 'in-' 'not' and 'amicus' 'friend.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable, as in 'eh-NEM-ee.'
Using 'enemy' for mild disagreement, which sounds too strong in American workplaces.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, 'enemy' translates the Hebrew 'oyeb' (אוֹיֵב, one who is hostile or hates) and the Greek 'echthros' (ἐχθρός, hostile, one who hates). Matthew 5:43-44 records Jesus' command to love one's enemies and pray for those who persecute you. Romans 12:20 says that if your enemy is hungry, you should feed him, and 1 Corinthians 15:26 calls death the last enemy to be destroyed.

enemy.etymology: From Middle English *enemy*, *enemye*, *enmy*, borrowed from Old French *enemi*, *anemi*, from Latin *inimīcus*, from *in-* (“not”) + *amīcus* (“friend”).

senses.definition: Preoccupied with something to the exclusion of everything else.
senses.example: The children were engrossed by the story.

senses.definition: Finalized, written in large letters.
senses.example: The clerk carefully prepared the engrossed copy of the bill for the governor's signature.

core.definition: Completely absorbed in something, so that you pay attention to nothing else.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on GROHST, the single main syllable, and the -ed is silent, so the word ends in a clear 'st'. Keep the first vowel short and light, not 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests deep focus, though it can imply that others were ignored.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'engrossed' mainly in writing and formal speech, as in 'She was engrossed in her novel.' In casual talk, 'absorbed' or 'really into' is more natural, as in 'I'm really into this show.' The legal sense, a document written out in final form, is technical and rare outside law.

distinctions.note: Absorbed is more common and conversational; engrossed sounds more formal and stresses total attention.
Distracted means your attention is pulled away; engrossed means your attention is completely held.

examples.everyday: I didn't hear you come in; I was completely engrossed in my book.
examples.professional: The team was so engrossed in debugging that nobody noticed the lunch order had arrived.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's readers often become so engrossed in the inner drama of the pseudonymous voice that they lose track of the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a swimmer who hears nothing but the water, the engrossed person is fully submerged in one thing.
nuance.etymology: From engross, from Anglo-French en gros, in large writing, from gros, large.
common_mistakes: Saying 'engrossed of' or 'engrossed by'; the standard pattern is 'engrossed in'.
Confusing 'engrossed' with 'engaged'; engaged means involved or committed, while engrossed means fully absorbed.

senses.definition: Placed in a trance.
senses.example: The medium remained entranced for an hour, murmuring words no one in the room understood.

senses.definition: Held at attention, as if by magic.
senses.example: The children were entranced by the magician's card tricks and did not blink.

core.definition: Completely fascinated or delighted, so that you cannot stop paying attention to something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, TRANST, and the -ed ending is a 't' sound after the 'ns' cluster. Avoid adding an extra vowel between n and s.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes intense attention or delight, often with admiration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entranced for people who are captivated by a show, a speaker, a story or a child's sight of something new. It is more intense than interested and more everyday than rapt. The word can also describe someone in a literal trance, but that use is rare.

distinctions.note: Fascinated is milder and more common in everyday speech. Entranced suggests total absorption.
Hypnotized implies being put into a trance by hypnosis or a repetitive effect. Entranced can describe purely emotional absorption.
Captivated is close in meaning and fairly formal. Entranced sounds more vivid and can describe a sleepy-eyed stare.

examples.everyday: The kids sat entranced in front of the aquarium for almost an hour.
examples.professional: The audience was entranced by the demo, so we ran it twice more.
examples.analytical: Readers are entranced by Dickens's prose, yet his social critique is often overlooked.

nuance.analogy: Being entranced is like being under a spell: your attention is held so completely that nothing else seems to exist.
nuance.etymology: From en- plus trance, from Old French transe, 'fear, passage from life to death'.
common_mistakes: Saying entranced with, when Americans more often say entranced by.
Pronouncing the word with a full extra vowel after the n.

core.definition: An ancient place name in Judah, another name for Bethlehem, near where Rachel died and was buried.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EF, the first syllable. The final 'th' is unvoiced, as in 'math', and the middle syllable is quick and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a biblical place name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use Ephrath in daily talk; it appears in Bible study, usually with Bethlehem. Ephrathah is a closely related form. In church, a friendly reply is 'It's an older name for Bethlehem.'

distinctions.note: Ephrathah is a closely related form, used with Bethlehem in Micah 5:2; both refer to the same region.

examples.everyday: Our pastor said Ephrath is the older name for Bethlehem, and I had never heard that before.
examples.professional: In the historical geography slide, we list Ephrath as a village name that later became Bethlehem.
examples.analytical: Genesis places Rachel's burial on the way to Ephrath, linking the matriarch to the town later associated with David and Jesus.

nuance.analogy: Like an old town name on a map that was later replaced by a city's modern name.
common_mistakes: Confusing Ephrath with Ephesus or Ephraim.
Stressing the second syllable; say EF-ruhth.
nuance.biblical_note: Ephrath, or Ephrathah, is an old name linked with Bethlehem. Genesis 35:16-19 records Rachel's death and burial on the way to Ephrath, identified as Bethlehem. Ruth 4:11 wishes prosperity for Ruth and Boaz in Ephrathah and renown in Bethlehem, and Micah 5:2 speaks of the ruler to come from Bethlehem Ephrathah.

senses.definition: To consider or assert as equal or equivalent (to or with).
To make equal or equivalent.
To set as equal.
A statement in assembly language that defines a symbol having a particular value.
senses.example: The assembler resolves the label through an equate that sets MAX_BUFFER to 256.

core.definition: To treat or regard two things as equal, similar, or equivalent, often when they are not actually the same.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, "KWAYT," which rhymes with "wait." The first syllable is a quick, reduced "ih," so do not stress it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, though it can sound like a criticism when someone equates two things that should not be equated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use equate often in arguments, news, and essays, as in "Don't equate being quiet with being unfriendly." It is also common in everyday disagreements, where it signals that someone has made an unfair comparison. Pair it with "with" or "to" to name the second thing.

distinctions.note: Compare means to look at similarities and differences; equate means to treat two things as equal or equivalent.
Identify with means to feel close to someone or something; equate means to assume two things are the same in value or meaning.

examples.everyday: Please don't equate my being late with not caring about the party.
examples.professional: We shouldn't equate a high number of users with a high number of paying customers.
examples.analytical: The argument equates moral worth with productivity, a move that many ethicists find deeply problematic.

nuance.analogy: To equate two things is like putting two different coins on a scale and declaring them equal because they weigh about the same.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aequare, "to make equal," from aequus, "equal."
common_mistakes: Using equate without an object, as in "they equate" instead of "they equate it with something."
Using "equate to" without "with" in formal writing, where "equate with" is more standard.

equate.etymology: From Middle English *equaten*, from Latin *aequātus*, perfect passive participle of *aequō*, see *-ate*.

senses.definition: The state of being in error; fallibility.
Holding the view that the Pope is not infallible.
senses.example: Historians traced how errancy spread among reformers who questioned papal authority in the sixteenth century.

core.definition: Fallibility, the state of being capable of error, especially in theology regarding popes or Scripture.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ERR. The middle syllable is a reduced vowel, so don't say 'AIR-ran-see', and the ending is '-see', not '-ci'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It names a fact of fallibility, but when applied to doctrine or people it can sound accusatory.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use errancy mainly in theology, philosophy, and formal writing, where it means the condition of being capable of error, especially in doctrine. In theological debates it is often paired with inerrancy, as its opposite. In everyday speech, people say mistakes or being wrong. Using errancy in casual talk sounds stiff or pedantic.

distinctions.note: Error is the everyday word for a mistake; errancy is an abstract state of being capable of error, used mainly in theology and philosophy.
Fallibility is the general capacity to be wrong; errancy names that condition in a more specific doctrinal sense, often in debates about Scripture or papal authority.
Errantry means wandering in search of adventure; errancy means being in error, so the spellings look close but the meanings are unrelated.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study got heated when someone raised the question of errancy in the Gospels.
examples.professional: For our seminar on doctrine, I'm asking students to define errancy before we compare Catholic and Protestant views.
examples.analytical: Modern accounts of errancy often distinguish between factual error in peripheral details and error in matters of faith and practice.

nuance.analogy: Errancy is like a map drawn by careful hands: useful and reliable, yet still capable of a wrong line.
nuance.etymology: From err, from Latin errare, 'to wander, to stray', with the suffix -ancy.
common_mistakes: Confusing errancy with errantry, which means wandering in search of adventure.
Using errancy in everyday speech for ordinary mistakes; say 'mistakes' or 'errors' instead.

traditions.view: The Pope is infallible when he defines doctrine ex cathedra on faith or morals, a teaching defined at the First Vatican Council in 1870. Catholics therefore deny that such definitions can be in error, though they accept that other papal statements can be mistaken.

Orthodoxy does not accept papal infallibility. It holds that truth is preserved by the whole Church, especially through ecumenical councils and the consensus of the faithful, which it considers protected from error.

Protestants reject papal infallibility and generally affirm Scripture as the final authority. Lutherans, Reformed, Anglicans, and Baptists differ on whether Scripture is inerrant or infallible only in matters of faith and salvation.

senses.definition: Straying from the proper course or standard, or outside established limits.
Roving around; wandering.
senses.example: The errant dog wandered through the neighborhood for hours before its owner found it.

senses.definition: Prone to erring or making errors; misbehaving.
senses.example: We ran down the street in pursuit of the errant dog.

senses.definition: A knight-errant.
senses.example: The old storybook described a brave errant who rode across the kingdom seeking adventure.

core.definition: Straying from the proper course or standard, or behaving in a way that breaks accepted rules or expectations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the second to a schwa, so it sounds like 'unt'. Keep the r clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly disapproving, suggesting someone or something has strayed from what is right or expected.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use errant mainly in writing, news, and literature, where it describes a wayward child, a misdirected ball, or a missile that goes off course. In everyday speech it sounds stiff, so people usually say wayward, off course, or wild instead. Errant is common in sports reporting, as in 'an errant pass.'

distinctions.note: Erroneous describes information or beliefs that are factually wrong, while errant describes behavior or movement that has strayed from its proper course.
Wayward is more common in everyday speech and suggests stubborn or willful misbehavior, whereas errant is more formal and suggests simply straying off course.

examples.everyday: My dog ran off after an errant squirrel and I spent twenty minutes finding him.
examples.professional: The quarterback's errant pass went straight to the defense, so we need better timing in practice.
examples.analytical: The novel depicts the errant knight as a figure who wanders beyond the boundaries of social order.

nuance.analogy: An errant arrow is like one that misses the target because the archer's aim has drifted away from the bullseye.
nuance.etymology: From Old French errant, meaning wandering, from errer, to wander, ultimately from Latin iter, a journey.
common_mistakes: Confusing errant with erroneous; a wrong fact is erroneous, but an errant ball is off course.
Using errant for a person who is simply mistaken rather than straying from proper behavior.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'eh' instead of AIR.

errant.etymology: From Middle English *erraunt*, from Anglo-Norman *erraunt*, from Old French *errant*, the present participle of *errer* (“to walk; to wander; to travel, voyage”), and then:

senses.definition: Formerly; in the past.
Respected, honorable.

core.definition: Former; previous; having been a particular thing in the past, such as a former friend, partner or colleague.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r sound in 'ur'. The 'st' cluster is clear, and the final syllable is a full 'wile', not 'wel' or 'wall'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, with a slightly old-fashioned or literary flavor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'erstwhile' in casual speech; it appears more in newspapers, essays, novels and formal writing. Most Americans would say 'former' or 'old' in everyday talk. If you use it, it may sound a little stylish or humorous, so it works well in a wedding toast or in writing.

distinctions.note: Former is the everyday, neutral word; erstwhile sounds more literary and is often used with a touch of irony.
Ex- is informal and used mostly for romantic partners or people with a job title; erstwhile is more formal.

examples.everyday: I ran into my erstwhile college roommate at the grocery store yesterday.
examples.professional: Our erstwhile vendor has been replaced by a new cloud provider.
examples.analytical: The essay traces the erstwhile alliance between the two parties and the reasons it fell apart.

nuance.analogy: Like an old photograph of someone you used to know well: they were a major part of your life once, but now they are only a memory.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English erst, 'formerly', and while, 'time'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'erstwhile' as 'ER-st-while' with the first vowel as in 'air'; the first vowel is the rhotic 'ur'.
Using it in casual speech where 'former' is more natural.

senses.definition: Having been in existence for a long time and therefore recognized and generally accepted.
senses.example: The bakery is well established, with customers who have shopped there for decades.

senses.definition: Having been successful for a long time and therefore recognized and generally respected.
senses.example: She is an established lawyer whose opinions carry real weight in court.

senses.definition: Of a religion, church etc.: formally recognized by a state as being official within that area.
senses.example: The Church of England was the established church of the English state.

senses.definition: Of any social or economic entity: part of the establishment (“groups with socioeconomic power”).
senses.example: Critics say the established media ignores voices from working-class communities.

senses.definition: (Model, procedure, disease) Explicitly defined, described or recognized as a reference.
senses.example: The established protocol requires two independent reviewers before any dataset is published.

core.definition: Long existing and widely recognized and accepted, such as an established company, rule or practice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress STAB, and end with lisht, using a short i and a final t sound. Don't pronounce it as lish-ed, which adds an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests reliability and credibility, though when applied to rules or customs it can imply resistance to change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use established for businesses, restaurants and professionals with a good reputation, as in 'an established law firm'. It also describes practices or facts that are widely accepted, such as 'an established procedure'. A casual reply to a compliment about a well-known place is 'Yeah, they've been here forever.'

distinctions.note: Famous means widely known, while established means it has existed long enough to be trusted and respected.
Traditional emphasizes customs passed down over time, while established emphasizes that something is recognized and stable.

examples.everyday: We went to that established Italian place downtown because it has been around since the 1970s.
examples.professional: The team is following an established procedure, so we don't need a new approval process.
examples.analytical: The essay challenges the established view that democracy requires a stable middle class.

nuance.analogy: An established reputation is like an old oak tree: it has deep roots, so people trust it in a storm.
nuance.etymology: From the past participle of establish, from Old French establir, from Latin stabilire ('to make firm').
common_mistakes: Using the adjective as a noun for a place, as in 'the established'; the noun is establishment.
Misspelling it as 'establised' with only one i; spell it establish-ed with the i before the sh sound.

core.definition: A person from Ethiopia, or relating to Ethiopia or its people, language or culture; in the Bible, a person from the region called Ethiopia or Cush.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on OH, and the final syllable is a reduced 'un' rather than a full 'ahn'. Keep the middle 'pee' clear and do not add an extra syllable between 'th' and 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a standard descriptive term for people and things from Ethiopia.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Ethiopian' as a noun for people and as an adjective, as in 'Ethiopian food' or 'an Ethiopian restaurant'. In Scripture it refers to the people of the ancient region, and the Ethiopian eunuch in Acts is the best-known example.

distinctions.note: Ethiopic refers specifically to the ancient Ge'ez script or liturgical language, not to people or nationality.
African is a broad continental term, while Ethiopian names a specific nationality or cultural identity.

examples.everyday: Let's try that Ethiopian place downtown, the injera there is amazing.
examples.professional: The Ethiopian team lead will present the regional data on Thursday's call.
examples.analytical: The Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8 is a significant figure because he is a foreigner who reads Isaiah and receives baptism, not an Israelite.

nuance.analogy: Like 'Norwegian' for a person from Norway, the word names both the people and the things that belong to them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Aethiopicus, from Greek Aithiopia, meaning 'land of burnt-faced people'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun for a person with the adjective; say 'an Ethiopian person' or 'Ethiopian food', not 'Ethiopians food'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'ahn', as in French.
nuance.biblical_note: The term renders the Hebrew Kushi or the Greek Aithiops, meaning a person from the region of Cush or Ethiopia. The best-known example is Acts 8:26-40, where Philip explains Isaiah to an Ethiopian eunuch and baptizes him. Jeremiah 13:23 uses the term in a proverb about a person's skin being unchangeable.

senses.definition: In a euphoric manner.

core.definition: In a way that feels extremely happy, excited or elated, often with energy and a sense of celebration.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FOR, the second syllable. In careful speech the -ically ending is pronounced 'ik-lee', so avoid adding an extra 'al' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes joyful, excited behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use euphorically in casual or journalistic writing to describe excited crowds, fans or people who have good news. It is a bit more intense than 'happily', and it can sound exaggerated if the feeling is only mild. Natural everyday alternatives include 'over the moon' or 'ecstatically'.

distinctions.note: Ecstatically is stronger and more physical, while euphorically emphasizes a general sense of joy and high spirits.
Happily is neutral and everyday, while euphorically suggests a much more intense, almost giddy happiness.

examples.everyday: When the baby finally slept through the night, we both shouted euphorically in the kitchen.
examples.professional: When the launch went live, the team cheered euphorically, although the monitoring dashboards still needed attention.
examples.analytical: Markets sometimes respond euphorically to new technologies, then correct sharply once expectations meet reality.

nuance.analogy: Like a bottle of soda shaken up, where the joy bubbles over all at once.
nuance.etymology: From euphoric, from Greek euphoria, 'well-bearing', plus the adverb suffix -ally.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word with extra syllables, such as 'yoo-FOR-ik-al-ly'.
Using euphorically to mean only 'happily', when it implies a stronger level of excitement.

senses.definition: To have a given result; to turn out (well, badly etc.); to result in.
senses.example: If the negotiations stall, the strike could eventuate in a complete shutdown of the plant.

senses.definition: To happen as a result; to come about.

core.definition: To result in a particular outcome, often used with in; to end up or happen as a consequence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VEN. The final syllable rhymes with late, so the word ends with a clear ayt sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a cause-and-effect chain and can be used for good or bad results.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use eventuate in casual speech. It appears in formal writing, policy discussion, and academic analysis, where people want to describe what a situation led to. In everyday talk, say end up, result, or lead to instead.

distinctions.note: Result is the everyday word, while eventuate is more formal and often describes the process that gets to the outcome.
Occur simply means happen, while eventuate emphasizes a final result after a sequence of events.

examples.everyday: The argument with my brother started small but eventuated in a loud fight at dinner.
examples.professional: The pilot program could eventuate in a full rollout if the metrics hold through the spring.
examples.analytical: Small institutional compromises can eventuate in deep structural transformations that no single actor intended.

nuance.analogy: Eventuate is like a river that gathers small streams until it finally flows into the sea.
nuance.etymology: From Latin eventus, outcome, with the verb-forming suffix -ate.
common_mistakes: Using eventuate without in when a result follows, as in it eventuated failure; say it eventuated in failure.
Using it in casual speech, where end up or lead to sounds more natural.

eventuate.etymology: American English, from *ēventus* + *-ate*, perhaps modeled after *actuate*.

senses.definition: Someone who eviscerates, whether physically or metaphorically.
senses.example: The critic was a brutal eviscerator of lazy arguments, leaving every weak claim in shreds.

senses.definition: A device for eviscerating something.
senses.example: The butcher used a stainless steel eviscerator to clean the fish quickly on the cutting board.

core.definition: A person or thing that thoroughly tears apart an argument, text, plan or reputation, leaving it weakened.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on VIS, with a lighter secondary stress on -RAY-, and the final -er is a reduced 'ur' in American speech. Learners often stress the -RAY- syllable too heavily.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes someone or something that harshly destroys another's work or argument, so it sounds forceful and sometimes unkind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eviscerator rarely, mostly for a sharp critic, debater or reviewer, and it is more common in writing than in speech. The word is often used figuratively, but it can also refer to a tool in medicine or industry. In casual talk, people would say 'a brutal critic' or 'a ruthless reviewer', which are more natural.

distinctions.note: A critic may be fair and balanced, while an eviscerator is someone whose criticism is especially harsh and destructive.
A demolisher tears down something whole, while an eviscerator exposes and removes its inner substance, which is a more surgical image.

examples.everyday: My sister is a total eviscerator in debates, so I never try to argue with her after dinner.
examples.professional: Our lead reviewer is an eviscerator of weak design docs, which is why the team's proposals are so solid by the time they reach us.
examples.analytical: In this essay, Hume becomes an eviscerator of the design argument, dismantling its inductive premises one by one.

nuance.analogy: An eviscerator is like a skilled surgeon who removes what is rotten from the inside, leaving the structure exposed and no longer working.
nuance.etymology: From eviscerate, from Latin eviscerare 'to disembowel', with the agent suffix -or.
common_mistakes: Confusing eviscerator with eviscerate, which is the verb and not the person or tool.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as putting the main stress on -RAY-; the main stress falls on VIS.
Using eviscerator only for physical violence when it is more often used for harsh critics or debaters.

senses.definition: That exacerbates.
senses.example: Lack of sleep was an exacerbating factor in his recent headaches and mood swings.

core.definition: Making a problem, illness or situation worse or more severe.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ZAS, the first syllable of the root, and give bay a secondary stress. The x is pronounced /ɡz/, so the first syllable sounds like ig, not eks.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always describes something getting worse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exacerbating in news reports, medicine, policy and business writing to describe problems that get worse because of something else. In casual speech people more often say making it worse or that makes it worse. Do not use it to mean annoying a person; for that, say aggravating.

distinctions.note: Aggravating is informal for annoying in everyday speech, while exacerbating is formal and describes things getting worse.
Worsening is a plain, general word for getting worse, while exacerbating adds the idea that something already bad is being intensified.

examples.everyday: Ugh, this humidity is exacerbating my allergies again.
examples.professional: The sudden traffic spike is exacerbating the latency problems in our API, so we need to scale the servers.
examples.analytical: Rather than resolving the conflict, the policy had exacerbating effects that deepened inequality over time.

nuance.analogy: Like pouring gasoline on a fire that is already burning: the fire was there already, but the gasoline makes it much worse.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exacerbare, to make bitter or irritate, from ex- (intensive) and acerbus, bitter or harsh.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ex- as eks; the correct sound is ig-.
Using exacerbating to mean annoying a person, which sounds unnatural; use aggravating instead.

senses.definition: The act of exasperating or the state of being exasperated; irritation; keen or bitter anger.
senses.example: To my exasperation, the printer jammed again just before the deadline.

senses.definition: Increase of violence or malignity; aggravation; exacerbation.
senses.example: The new policy caused an exasperation of the conflict between the two rival gangs.

core.definition: A feeling of strong irritation or frustration when your patience has been used up.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on AY, the syllable before -shun. The reduced middle syllable sounds like 'er', and the initial sound is 'ig', not 'ek'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a strong feeling of frustration that has built up over time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exasperation when describing a clear emotional state, such as 'to her exasperation' or 'in exasperation.' In casual speech people often say 'I'm so frustrated' instead. The word fits writing, news reports, and formal narration well.

distinctions.note: Frustration is the everyday word for being blocked; exasperation is stronger and suggests being pushed past patience.
Anger is a general feeling of displeasure; exasperation is specifically irritation from repeated provocation.

examples.everyday: To my exasperation, the store was out of the milk I needed again.
examples.professional: The team's exasperation with the vendor's delays is understandable, but we need a clear escalation path.
examples.analytical: His exasperation with the crowd reveals a deeper frustration with the failure of moral persuasion.

nuance.analogy: Exasperation is like a pot left on high heat: the frustration keeps building until something finally boils over.
nuance.etymology: From exasperate, from Latin exasperare 'to make rough or harsh', from asper 'rough'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'ek' rather than 'ig'.
Using exasperation for minor inconvenience; it suggests real, cumulative frustration.

senses.definition: Deserving honor, respect and admiration.
senses.example: Her exemplary service during the flood earned her the city's highest civic honor.

senses.definition: Of such high quality that it should serve as an example to be imitated; ideal, perfect.
senses.example: Her behavior was always exemplary.

senses.definition: Serving as a warning; monitory.
senses.example: exemplary justice, exemplary punishment, exemplary damages

senses.definition: Providing an example or illustration.
senses.example: The textbook included exemplary problems that showed each proof step by step.

core.definition: Outstanding and deserving to be copied, or serving as a warning when used of punishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on zem, the second syllable. The middle syllable is weak, so 'pluh' is quick, and the final syllable is a clear 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive when praising work or behavior, and negative when describing punishment meant as a warning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exemplary in workplace reviews, evaluations, award letters and formal praise, such as 'exemplary service'. In casual talk they often say great or outstanding. The phrase exemplary damages is a legal term meaning punitive damages.

distinctions.note: Excellent is everyday and general, while exemplary implies high quality that others should imitate.
Model as an adjective means ideal, while exemplary stresses the quality of the behavior or work itself.

examples.everyday: The waiter was exemplary tonight, so we left a big tip.
examples.professional: Her code review was exemplary, and the team agreed to use it as a template.
examples.analytical: The court imposed exemplary damages to deter future misconduct, not only to compensate the victim.

nuance.analogy: Like a gold-standard report card that other students copy.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exemplaris, serving as a model, from exemplum, example.
common_mistakes: Using exemplary for mild praise; it signals high admiration.
Confusing it with exemplar, the noun that names the model person or thing.

exemplary.etymology: From Middle English *exemplarie*, from Latin *exemplāris* (“exemplary; a copy, facsimile”), from *exemplum* (“an example; a sample; a copy or transcript”).

senses.definition: Capable of being extended.

core.definition: Able to be extended or expanded, such as a system, format, or design that can gain new features or capacity without being rebuilt.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, STEN, and the last two syllables are reduced to a quick schwa and l. Non-native speakers often stress the final syllable or pronounce the middle as a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, usually a positive quality in design: it signals flexibility and room to grow.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in software, markup languages, and product design, as in 'an extensible framework.' In everyday speech people say 'expandable' or 'can be added to' instead. It is not used for physical objects like rubber bands, where 'stretchable' or 'elastic' is the natural choice.

distinctions.note: Expandable usually means something physically gets bigger, like a folding table or expandable file folder, while extensible often means a system is designed to accept new parts or features.
Scalable focuses on handling more load or users efficiently, while extensible focuses on adding new functions or extensions to the existing design.

examples.everyday: My new backpack has an extensible strap that adjusts to my height.
examples.professional: We chose an extensible design so new data modules can be added without rewriting the core service.
examples.analytical: A formal system is extensible when new axioms can be added without invalidating the theorems already proven.

nuance.analogy: Think of a power strip: it is extensible because you can plug in more devices without replacing the whole strip.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extendere, to stretch out.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in ik-sten-SI-bul.
Confusing it with 'extensive,' which means wide in scope or covering a lot of ground, as in 'extensive research.'

senses.definition: A gradual disappearance or fading away.

core.definition: A gradual disappearance of sound, light or an image, especially at the end of a song, film or scene.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, the stress falls on 'FADE' and the second part is weaker. This is different from the phrasal verb 'fade OUT,' where the stress moves to 'out.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a transition or gradual end.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fadeout mainly in music, film and audio discussions, as in 'the song ends with a long fadeout.' It is written as one word or with a hyphen (fade-out) in some writing. In everyday talk, people usually say 'it faded out' rather than using the noun.

distinctions.note: A fade-in is the opposite transition, where something gradually appears; a fadeout is where it gradually disappears.
A blackout is a sudden loss of light or power, or of consciousness; a fadeout is gradual.
Decline describes a steady decrease over time in a general sense; fadeout usually refers to sound, light or images.

examples.everyday: The song ends with a long fadeout, so you can never tell exactly when it's over.
examples.professional: Use a short fadeout in the video so the transition to the sponsor card feels smooth.
examples.analytical: The novel's ending is a fadeout that leaves the central conflict unresolved and the reader uncertain.

nuance.analogy: A fadeout is like a dimmer switch slowly turned down until the room is dark.
nuance.etymology: A compound formed from fade out, the phrasal verb.
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on 'out' when using the noun, which sounds like the phrasal verb.
Writing it as two separate words in formal writing when the dictionary standard is one word.

senses.definition: Something said or reported; gossip, rumor.
One's reputation.
The state of being famous or well-known and spoken of, especially for something positive.
To make (someone or something) famous.

core.definition: The state of being widely known and admired, especially for something positive, such as talent or achievement.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the diphthong 'ay' as in 'pay'. Keep the final m closed and don't add a schwa, as in 'FAY-muh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses. It can carry a negative shade in phrases like 'fleeting fame', and 'notoriety' is the word for fame for bad reasons.
nuance.usage_note: Americans talk about fame in entertainment, sports, business and politics, often with the phrase 'rise to fame' or 'fame and fortune'. In casual talk, 'famous' is more common than 'fame', so 'she became famous' sounds more natural than 'she became a fame'. For a bad reputation, Americans say 'notoriety' rather than 'fame'.

distinctions.note: A celebrity is a person who is famous; fame is the state or condition of being known to many.
Reputation is what people generally think of you and can be good or bad; fame is specifically being widely known.
Notoriety is fame for something bad or shameful, while fame is usually positive.

examples.everyday: My cousin got a little bit of fame after her video went viral, but she says she's still the same person.
examples.professional: The company's brand gained fame in the market after the product launch, which doubled our web traffic.
examples.analytical: Fame, in Hume's sense, is a social judgment that depends on the opinion of others, not on the merit of the person judged.

nuance.analogy: Fame is like a spotlight: it lights you up for everyone to see, and it also shows every detail.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fama, report, rumor or reputation, from fari, to speak.
common_mistakes: Using 'fame' as an adjective; the adjective is 'famous', so say 'a famous singer', not 'a fame singer'.
Using 'in fame' instead of 'famous for' or 'with fame'; the natural preposition is 'famous for' for the reason someone is known.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea of fame is closest to the Hebrew shem, meaning name, reputation or renown. In Genesis 11 the builders of Babel want to make a name for themselves, which the text presents as human pride seeking its own renown. Ecclesiastes 7:1 says that a good name is better than precious ointment, suggesting that a good reputation outweighs outward glory. Proverbs 22:1 says that a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, making reputation a matter of moral character rather than public attention.

fame.etymology: From Middle English *fame*, from Old French *fame* (“celebrity, renown”), itself borrowed from Latin *fāma* (“talk, rumor, report, reputation”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰéh₂-meh₂*, from **bʰeh₂-* (“to speak, say, tell”).

senses.definition: Able to be fathomed.
senses.example: The mystery was finally fathomable after years of research.

core.definition: Able to be understood, measured, or fully comprehended by the human mind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FATH, and the th is voiced as in 'the'. The middle syllables are weak, so say 'uh-muh-bul' quickly and do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is usually used in negative or limiting phrases, and the negative form unfathomable is far more common.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use fathomable on its own in everyday speech. They more often say unfathomable, or phrases like hard to imagine, hard to understand, or hard to believe. Fathomable appears mostly in writing, or in phrases such as hardly fathomable or not easily fathomable.

distinctions.note: Unfathomable is the common, everyday form meaning impossible to understand or measure; fathomable is the less common positive form, usually found in negative sentences.
Comprehensible means understandable in general, while fathomable suggests reaching the deep bottom of something complex or mysterious.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the price of that wedding is hardly fathomable to me.
examples.professional: Some of these edge cases are barely fathomable until we look at the logs, so let's review them together.
examples.analytical: For Kant, some aspects of the noumenal world are not fathomable by human reason, which limits what we can claim to know.

nuance.analogy: Like the ocean floor: you can know its depth only if your line can reach the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From fathom plus -able; fathom comes from Old English fæðm, meaning outstretched arms or an embrace, later a unit of depth.
common_mistakes: Using fathomable to mean easy to understand, when it means capable of being fully understood; English speakers often reverse the meaning.
Stressing the second syllable, as in fa-THOM-a-ble; the stress belongs on the first syllable.

senses.definition: Fake or artificial.
Singular of fauces.
senses.example: The throat's narrow faux connects the mouth to the pharynx and is lined with mucous membrane.

core.definition: Fake or artificial, made to imitate something real, such as leather, fur, or wood.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long o, like 'go' or 'oh.' The x is silent, so do not say 'fox.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral, usually describing imitation materials or items, but it can sound pretentious when used for things that are not imitations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'faux' in shopping and fashion for imitation materials such as faux leather, faux fur, or faux marble. It usually signals an imitation that is openly admitted, not a deliberate fraud. The noun 'faux,' singular of 'fauces,' is an anatomical term for the throat and is rarely used; in everyday speech, 'faux' is an adjective.

distinctions.note: Fake often implies deception or fraud, while faux is usually an openly acknowledged imitation.
Artificial is broader and can describe anything made rather than natural, while faux specifically imitates a natural material or look.
Synthetic describes a material made by chemistry, while faux describes what the product is trying to look like.

examples.everyday: I bought a faux leather jacket because it was cheaper and easier to clean.
examples.professional: The brochure shows faux wood flooring, but the sample we received is laminate, so we need to correct the spec.
examples.analytical: The writer's faux humility conceals a claim to authority that the rest of the essay never admits.

nuance.analogy: Faux is like a poster of a sunset: from across the room it looks like the real thing, but up close you can tell it is an imitation.
nuance.etymology: From French faux, meaning false, from Latin falsus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'fox' because of the spelling.
Using faux for things that are real or deliberately natural, which can sound odd or pretentious.

senses.definition: Able to ferment or be fermented.
Any substance that can be fermented.
senses.example: Sugars are the most fermentable components of the wort, so yeast consumes them first.

core.definition: Able to be broken down by yeast or bacteria into alcohol, acid or gas, especially said of sugars and starches.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MEN, and the final -able is a reduced syllable ending in a syllabic l, so say 'bul', not 'bil' or 'bay-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise, descriptive technical word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in brewing, baking, food science, biofuel and agriculture, for example when discussing which sugars a yeast can use. In everyday talk people say 'can be fermented' or 'will ferment'. The noun use, 'a fermentable', is rare and usually appears in brewing or science writing.

distinctions.note: Fermented describes something already changed by microbes, while fermentable describes something capable of being changed.
Digestible means easy for the body to break down, whereas fermentable refers specifically to microbial breakdown, in a vat or in the gut.

examples.everyday: The sugar in this apple juice is fermentable, so it will turn into hard cider if you leave it in a jar.
examples.professional: We need to measure how much of the feedstock is fermentable before we scale up the brewing run.
examples.analytical: Whether a carbohydrate is fermentable depends less on its chemistry alone than on which enzymes the microbe can produce.

nuance.analogy: Like kindling, sugar is fermentable only when the right spark, here yeast, arrives to set it off.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fermentare, to cause to ferment, from fermentum, leaven, ultimately from fervere, to boil.
common_mistakes: Confusing fermentable (able to be fermented) with fermented (already fermented); say 'the fermentable sugars' when they have not changed yet.
Stressing the wrong syllable: fur-MEN-tuh-bul, not fur-men-TAY-bul.

senses.definition: The condition of being ferocious.

core.definition: The quality of being fierce or violent, especially the intensity of an attack, storm, or strong emotion.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, RAH. Americans pronounce the first vowel as a reduced schwa and the o in the stressed syllable as the 'ah' vowel of cot, so it does not sound like 'row'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It emphasizes danger, violence or intense force.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ferocity' in news, writing or formal talk about battles, storms, attacks, or intense emotion. In everyday talk they usually say 'intensity' or describe the fierce behavior directly. It sounds stiff if used for minor things.

distinctions.note: Intensity is neutral and can describe any strength, while ferocity suggests violence and danger.
Fierceness is more common in everyday English and less formal; ferocity sounds more literary and serious.

examples.everyday: I was surprised by the ferocity of the wind when we got out of the car.
examples.professional: The team underestimated the ferocity of the competition during the product launch.
examples.analytical: The historian explains the ferocity of the riots as a result of economic despair and political betrayal.

nuance.analogy: Ferocity is like a fire that spreads fast and cannot be calmed easily.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ferocitas, from ferox, 'fierce'.
common_mistakes: Using 'ferocity' for everyday small things, which sounds too dramatic.
Confusing the stress; the stress is on the middle syllable RAH, not the first.

ferocity.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *férocité*, from Latin *ferocitas*, from *ferox* (“fierce”), from *ferus* (“wild, savage, fierce”).

senses.definition: The condition of something that festers.
senses.example: The festering of the old wound worried the doctor more than the initial injury.

core.definition: The process of a wound, grudge or problem becoming infected, rotten or more bitter over time instead of being resolved.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak "-ter" where the r is pronounced, so it is not "FES-tuh-ring" with a hard t. The final "-ing" is short, not "-eeng."

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always describes something unhealthy that is getting worse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use festering for physical wounds and for emotional or social problems, such as a festering grudge at work. Most people use it as an adjective or in phrases like "let it fester." It sounds vivid, so it fits conversation, writing and speeches, but it is strong language for minor annoyances.

distinctions.note: Infection is a medical term for germs entering a body. Festering describes a wound or problem that stays unhealthy and gets worse over time.
Rot is a general word for decay. Festering is more specific, suggesting pus, irritation or bitterness that builds up under the surface.

examples.everyday: If you don't talk to your brother soon, that argument will just keep festering.
examples.professional: Unresolved bugs in the billing module have been festering for six months, and the backlog keeps growing.
examples.analytical: Resentment festering beneath a surface of civility corrodes a community long before anyone names the conflict.

nuance.analogy: Like a splinter left in the skin: ignored, it gets worse until it demands attention.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English festren, from Old English fǣstrian, meaning to fester.
common_mistakes: Using "festering" for ordinary minor problems, which sounds dramatic
Pronouncing the middle syllable as "tuh" and dropping the r sound
Confusing it with "festival" because of the similar opening

senses.definition: Invented, as opposed to real.
senses.example: Romeo and Juliet are fictional characters.

senses.definition: Containing invented elements.
senses.example: The Simpsons is a fictional television show.

senses.definition: Occurring in fiction.
senses.example: The detective in the novel is entirely fictional, though the author based him on a real investigator.

senses.definition: Concerning fiction (as a genre or medium): having to do with fiction; specific to fiction.
senses.example: fictional and nonfictional conventions

core.definition: Invented or imagined, not real; describing characters, events, or places created in a story or book.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -tion ending is pronounced as SHUN, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel plus l, so say it as FIK-shuhn-l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes something invented, and it can be a neutral or positive term in literature and film.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fictional for characters, places, and events in books, films, and shows, and also for invented people in examples or case studies. In news, Americans often use fictitious when something is made up to deceive, so avoid fictional for lies. Saying the character is fictional is a common, natural way to answer a question about someone who seems real.

distinctions.note: Fictional describes made-up stories or characters, usually neutrally; fictitious often implies a deliberate false invention, as in a fictitious name.
Imaginary means existing only in the mind; fictional applies specifically to works of fiction.

examples.everyday: Is Sherlock Holmes a real person, or is he fictional? I think he is fictional, but people still visit his museum in London.
examples.professional: For the usability test, we used a fictional customer profile so no real user data appeared in the slides.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguishes history from poetry partly because the poet's fictional events can reveal what is universal in human action.

nuance.analogy: A fictional world is like a model railroad: detailed and convincing, built entirely by the imagination of its maker.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fictio, from fingere, to shape or invent, through fiction and the suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using fictional to describe a lie; for deliberate falsehoods, use fictitious or made up.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as FIK-shuh-NAL, which shifts the stress incorrectly.

senses.definition: Capable of being fixed, repairable.
senses.example: The mechanic said the leaking radiator was fixable, so we avoided buying a new car.

senses.definition: Attachable.
senses.example: The word has no fixable meaning.

core.definition: Able to be repaired, corrected, or solved.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FIX. The last two syllables are reduced: the middle is a weak 'uh' and the ending is a syllabic 'l,' so it sounds like 'bul,' not 'bel' or 'bl.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting that a problem is not hopeless.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fixable in everyday talk about cars, appliances, relationships, and software bugs, as in 'It's fixable, don't worry.' In technical writing, repairable or correctable may sound more precise. Use it when you want to reassure someone that a problem can be solved.

distinctions.note: Repairable is more formal and is used mainly for physical objects or machines; fixable is more casual and can refer to problems in general.
Curable is used for diseases or medical conditions; fixable is a general word for any problem that can be solved.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about the dent in the bumper; it's fixable and the body shop can do it cheaply.
examples.professional: The team agreed the outage was fixable within a sprint, so no rollback is needed.
examples.analytical: Whether a moral failure is fixable or simply a permanent feature of human nature is a classic question in theological anthropology.

nuance.analogy: Like a loose screw: the machine still works, and a few turns of a screwdriver put it right.
nuance.etymology: From fix (from Latin fixus, 'fastened') plus the adjective suffix -able, 'capable of being.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on the first: FIX-uh-bul.
Using fixable for a person who cannot change; it describes problems or objects, not people.

senses.definition: To fall asleep from exhaustion or intoxication; to lie down.
To flake or be flaky: to prove unreliable; to abandon or desert someone.
senses.example: John said he could drive me to the airport, but then he flaked out on me, and I had to call a cab at the last minute.

senses.definition: To crack up or break down; to have a mental episode; to behave eccentrically.
senses.example: After three sleepless nights of finals, Jenna started to flake out during her oral exam.

core.definition: To fall asleep or collapse from exhaustion, or to lie down to rest after a long, tiring day.

pronunciation.tip: The particle 'out' carries the main stress, while 'flake' gets a lighter stress. The t in 'out' is strongly aspirated because it is stressed, so don't reduce it to a d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing tiredness; negative when used as 'flake out on someone', meaning to cancel or fail to show up.
