nuance.etymology: From 'maintain' plus '-ance', from Old French 'maintenir', to keep in hand.
common_mistakes: Using 'maintenance' as a countable noun, as in 'a maintenance' for each task; it is usually uncountable.
Using 'maintenance' for one-time fixes instead of repeated upkeep.

maintenance.etymology: From Middle English *mayntenaunce*, from Old French *maintenance*, from *maintenir*, from Latin.

conversation.text: I put in a maintenance request for the broken window.
Call maintenance if the hot water goes out again.
The car needs regular maintenance, like oil changes.

senses.definition: Any of the five longer prophetic books in the Old Testament: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, or Daniel.

core.definition: In the Christian Old Testament, the four longer prophetic books: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are stressed on their first syllable, MAY and PRAH. Say the flapped t in prophets like a soft d, and do not add a vowel between p and h.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a standard label in Bible study and church settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in Bible classes, church, seminary and reference works. Major means longer or more extensive here, not more important than the Minor Prophets. Lamentations is sometimes placed with the Major Prophets, and Baruch appears in some Catholic lists, so the grouping depends partly on the Bible edition.

distinctions.note: The Minor Prophets are twelve shorter books, from Hosea to Malachi; the name refers to length, not rank.
Prophets alone is a general term; Major Prophets is the specific Christian grouping of four long books.

collocations: the Book of Isaiah among the Major Prophets
the order of the Major Prophets

examples.everyday: Our Bible study is working through the Major Prophets this semester, starting with Isaiah.
examples.professional: In my seminar syllabus, the Major Prophets come before the Minor Prophets, so students read Isaiah through Daniel first.
examples.analytical: The Christian ordering of the Major Prophets, placing Daniel among them, reflects a canon arrangement that differs from the Hebrew Bible, where Daniel is in the Writings.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of encyclopedia volumes sorted by page count, the Major Prophets are grouped by length rather than importance.
nuance.etymology: Major is from Latin major, greater; prophet is from Greek prophētēs, one who speaks for God.
common_mistakes: Thinking Major means more important, when it refers to the longer books.
Assuming the Hebrew Bible groups Daniel among the prophets; in the Hebrew canon Daniel is among the Writings.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible the prophets are called nevi'im (prophets), and the Former Prophets and Latter Prophets are its divisions. The Christian grouping of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel as Major Prophets follows the length of the books. Key passages: Isaiah 7:14 announces a sign of a virgin bearing a son called Immanuel; Ezekiel 37 describes a vision of dry bones brought to life; Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises a new covenant written on the heart. Daniel 7:13 describes one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven.

senses.definition: To cause a disturbance.
To upset the status quo.
senses.example: Her proposal to cut the budget will make waves, but someone has to challenge the status quo.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see make,‎ wave.

core.definition: To cause trouble or disturbance by challenging the normal way things are done, often in a group or at work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WAVES, with the long 'ay' diphthong and a clear final z sound. Do not add an extra vowel before the z, and keep MAKE lighter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. 'Don't make waves' suggests avoiding conflict, while 'made waves' can be positive when someone challenges a bad system.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for workplace or group situations, usually when someone speaks up in a way that disturbs the calm. 'Don't make waves' is a common piece of advice. A natural reply is 'Yeah, but someone had to say something.'

distinctions.note: 'Rock the boat' is almost identical in meaning but slightly more informal and often refers to disturbing a stable situation.
'Speak up' is neutral and simply means to voice an opinion; 'make waves' suggests the opinion causes disruption.
'Stir up trouble' is more negative and suggests deliberately causing problems, while 'make waves' can be unintentional or admirable.

collocations: make waves with a new policy

examples.everyday: My sister doesn't want to make waves, so she never complains about the rent, even when it goes up.
examples.professional: The new analyst made waves by questioning the quarterly forecast in front of the whole leadership team.
examples.analytical: Galileo made waves in the seventeenth century, and his challenge reached beyond astronomy into the authority of the Church's reading of Scripture.

nuance.analogy: Like dropping a stone into a still pond: one small action sends ripples outward across the whole surface.
nuance.etymology: The idiom comes from the image of disturbing the calm surface of water.
common_mistakes: Adding 'the' and saying 'make the waves' instead of 'make waves.'
Using 'cause waves' in place of 'make waves,' which sounds unnatural to most Americans.

make-waves.etymology: Derived from disruptions caused by waves in water.

senses.definition: Belonging to the sex which typically produces sperm, or to the gender which is typically associated with it.
senses.example: male writers

senses.definition: Characteristic of this sex/gender.
senses.example: stereotypically male interests

senses.definition: Tending to lead to or regulate the development of sexual characteristics typical of this sex.
senses.example: the male chromosome

senses.definition: Masculine; of the masculine grammatical gender.
senses.example: In Spanish, the noun libro is male, so it takes the article el.

senses.definition: Having the F factor; able to impart DNA into another bacterium which does not have the F factor (a female).
senses.example: In the lab, the male strain carries the F factor and transfers plasmid DNA.

senses.definition: Of instruments, tools, or connectors: designed to fit into or penetrate a female counterpart, as in a connector, pipe fitting or laboratory glassware.
senses.example: Make sure the fitting is male so it slides into the female pipe thread.

senses.definition: One of the male (masculine) sex or gender.
senses.example: Among the participants, the number of males outnumbered females two to one.

senses.definition: A human member of the masculine sex or gender.
senses.example: The survey asked each male whether he had visited a doctor this year.

senses.definition: An animal of the sex that has testes.
senses.example: The male lion guarded the pride while the females hunted nearby.

senses.definition: A plant of the masculine sex.
senses.example: In the orchard, every male is cut down, since only females bear fruit.

senses.definition: A bacterium which has the F factor.
senses.example: Researchers mixed the male with a female strain to observe conjugation.

senses.definition: A male connector, pipe fitting, etc.
senses.example: Use the male on the cable to plug into the back of the amplifier.

core.definition: Belonging to the sex that produces sperm, or to the gender typically associated with it, as opposed to female.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long a and a final l. Do not add a schwa, and do not confuse it with 'meal'; male and mail are homophones in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in biology and on forms; for people it can sound clinical, so 'man' or 'men' is usually warmer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use male for animals, plants, and surveys, such as 'male and female students' on a form or 'a male cardinal' in birdwatching. For people, 'man' or 'boy' is more natural in conversation, and 'male nurse' sounds dated. The noun 'a male' is used mostly for animals or in technical contexts, not for everyday descriptions of men.

distinctions.note: Male describes biological sex; masculine describes traits, styles, or cultural expectations usually linked with men.
Man is the everyday word for an adult male person; male is more formal or technical, so use man in most conversation.
Manly describes admirable masculine qualities such as courage and strength, and it can sound old-fashioned or judgmental.

examples.everyday: The vet said the male kitten needs to be neutered next month.
examples.professional: Please label the field as male or female on the intake form, or choose 'prefer not to say.'
examples.analytical: Biologists distinguish sex, which is tied to reproductive anatomy, from gender, which is a social category, though the two are often conflated.

nuance.analogy: Male is like a sex-category label on a form; masculine is like the reputation people build around it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French masle, from Latin masculus, a diminutive of mas 'male'.
common_mistakes: Calling a man 'a male' in everyday conversation; it sounds clinical, so say 'a man' instead.
Confusing male with masculine: 'male behavior' suggests biology, while 'masculine behavior' refers to social traits.

male.etymology: From Middle English *male*, borrowed from Old French *malle*, *masle* (Modern French *mâle*), from Latin *masculus* (“masculine, a male”), diminutive of *mās* (“male, masculine”).

senses.definition: Unable to fully realize one's ambitions; would-be.
senses.example: an artist manque

core.definition: Having failed to achieve one's ambition in a particular field, used after the noun to describe a would-be professional.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the final syllable, KAY. The first vowel is nasal, so let air pass through your nose, and do not add a hard n sound after it.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or teasing. It suggests someone who has not reached a goal and may be frustrated or pretentious about it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use manque mainly in literary criticism, journalism, and wry commentary, almost always after the noun, as in 'a painter manque'. It can sound snobbish or unkind if said about a friend. The everyday American alternatives are would-be or, informally, wannabe.

distinctions.note: Would-be is plain and common, while manque is literary and suggests a talent that never fully developed, often with some bitterness.
Failed is harsh and final, but manque implies that the ambition is still visible in the person's life or work.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a jazz pianist manque; he plays every weekend but never got a record deal.
examples.professional: Our product manager is an engineer manque, so she still rewrites the code instead of writing the spec.
examples.analytical: Her criticism reads like the work of a novelist manque, attentive to structure but unable to escape the books she never wrote.

nuance.analogy: A career manque is like an unfinished sketch: the outline of the ambition is clear, but the full picture was never painted.
nuance.etymology: From French manqué, past participle of manquer 'to miss, lack, or fail'.
common_mistakes: Placing manque before the noun; the usual order is after, as in 'a poet manque'.
Pronouncing it as MAN-kwee or MAN-kway; the final syllable carries the stress.

senses.definition: The additional utility to a consumer from an additional unit of an economic good.

core.definition: In economics, the extra satisfaction a consumer gets from using or buying one more unit of a good or service.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on TIL in utility, and the first word has a secondary stress. The final -ty is a light tee, not the long ee of TEE-nuh-tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is an economics term and rarely used in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use marginal utility in economics classes, policy discussions, and business strategy. The concept explains why each extra slice of pizza is worth less to you than the one before. Outside economics, people usually say the value of one more or the benefit of an extra unit.

distinctions.note: Total utility is the full satisfaction from all units consumed, while marginal utility is the change from one more unit.
Marginal cost is the extra expense of producing one more unit, while marginal utility is the extra satisfaction to the buyer.

examples.everyday: After my third slice of pizza, I could feel the marginal utility dropping fast.
examples.professional: Our pricing model assumes diminishing marginal utility, so the discount should go down as customers buy more.
examples.analytical: The principle of diminishing marginal utility helps explain why people spread their spending across many goods.

nuance.analogy: Marginal utility is like the last bite of a big meal: it still tastes good, but each new bite gives you a little less.
common_mistakes: Confusing marginal utility with marginal cost.
Saying marginal utilities as a plural when the concept is singular.
Using it as a synonym for usefulness in everyday speech.

senses.definition: Exhibiting the Markov property, in which the conditional probability distribution of future states of the process, given the present state and all past states, depends only upon the present state and not on any past states.
senses.example: The weather model is Markovian, so tomorrow's forecast depends only on today's conditions.

core.definition: Describing a process whose next state depends only on its current state, not on the states that came before it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, KOH, in the name of the Russian mathematician Andrei Markov. Say the final syllable as a light 'un', and do not add an extra syllable between 'vi' and 'an'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in mathematics, statistics, data science, machine learning, and economics. You will hear it in lectures, papers, and technical meetings, but almost never in casual talk. In conversation people usually say 'memoryless' or explain the idea in plain words.

distinctions.note: Markovian is the standard term for a process with the Markov property, while memoryless is a broader everyday description that is often used for the exponential distribution in probability.
Stochastic means random or involving probability in general, while Markovian is a narrower property about how the future depends only on the present.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in statistics says tomorrow's weather forecast is basically Markovian, since it depends mostly on today's conditions.
examples.professional: We modeled user navigation as a Markovian process, so the next page a visitor sees depends only on the page they are on now.
examples.analytical: A Markovian assumption makes the model tractable, but it discards the memory that real human decisions often carry, and the error this introduces must be checked.

nuance.analogy: A Markovian walker is like someone playing a board game who decides each move by looking only at the square they are standing on, not at the path that led them there.
nuance.etymology: Named after the Russian mathematician Andrei Markov (1856-1922), who introduced the idea around 1906.
common_mistakes: Putting stress on the first syllable, as in MAR-koh-vee-un; the stress belongs on KOH.
Using Markovian for any random process; it refers specifically to the memoryless property of the present state.

markovian.etymology: From *Markov* + *ian*, named for the Russian mathematician Andrey Markov.

senses.definition: The quality of being martial or warlike.

core.definition: The quality of being martial, meaning warlike, military, or having a fighting spirit in manner or bearing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r: MAHR, not MAH. The 'tial' ending reduces to 'shuhl' and the final '-ness' is a weak 'nuhs'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it describes a warlike quality, which writers may praise or criticize depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word that appears mainly in literary, historical or journalistic description of a person's bearing or a nation's spirit. Americans usually say 'military bearing' or 'militaristic' in everyday talk. In conversation the word would sound stilted, so save it for writing.

distinctions.note: Militaristic describes a policy or society that glorifies war; martialness describes a quality of manner or spirit.
Military is the everyday adjective for armed forces; martial is more formal and suggests a warlike spirit rather than organization.
Marshal is pronounced the same but means to arrange or to lead; it never describes warlike qualities.

examples.everyday: The coach's whole martialness came out when he barked orders at the kids.
examples.professional: The consultant's martialness in planning meetings made the whole team feel under siege.
examples.analytical: Critics read the novel's martialness as an uncritical celebration of the nation's wars.

nuance.analogy: Like the rigid stance of a drill sergeant, where posture itself carries the spirit of battle.
nuance.etymology: From Latin martialis, 'of Mars', the Roman god of war, with the English suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'marshal' in speech, since both are pronounced MAHR-shuhl.
Using it for literal armed forces; say 'military' instead.

senses.definition: The action of rubbing, kneading or hitting someone's body, to help the person relax, prepare for muscular action (as in contact sports) or to relieve aches.
senses.example: Having a massage can have many beneficial effects.

senses.definition: The action of rubbing or kneading anything.
senses.example: The baker gave the dough one final massage.

senses.definition: To rub and knead (someone's body or body part), to perform a massage on (somebody).
senses.example: My neck doesn't hurt as much as it did last night since my wife massaged me after I got back from the concert.

senses.definition: To rub or knead anything.
senses.example: Massage the kale to soften it before making the salad.

senses.definition: To manipulate (data, a document etc.) to make it more presentable or more convenient to work with.
senses.example: Before the meeting, the analyst massaged the sales figures into a neater spreadsheet.

senses.definition: To falsify (data or accounts).
senses.example: The auditors discovered that the managers had massaged the quarterly accounts to hide losses.

core.definition: The action of rubbing and kneading someone's body to relax muscles or ease aches; to give someone this treatment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final sound is the voiced zh of 'measure', not j or sh. Reduce the first vowel to a soft uh.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests relaxation and care. It is also used neutrally in sports and medical settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use massage for spa treatments, sports recovery and physical therapy. Massage therapist is the standard professional term, while masseuse sounds dated and is being replaced. In casual talk, I need a massage is natural, and a good reply is That sounds great.

distinctions.note: A rub is a quick, informal stroke; a massage is a deliberate, systematic treatment of the muscles.
Physical therapy is a clinical rehabilitation plan; massage is usually for relaxation or soreness and is often done without a medical goal.
A rubdown is a short, casual massage, often after exercise, and is less technical than a full massage.

examples.everyday: I'm getting a massage after work because my back is killing me.
examples.professional: Our wellness benefit covers one massage per quarter, so you can book through the portal.
examples.analytical: Studies of massage often measure perceived relief rather than physiological change, which limits what they can claim.

nuance.analogy: Like kneading dough, massage works the muscle until it softens.
nuance.etymology: From French massage, from masser 'to knead, handle', probably from Arabic mass 'to touch'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final sound as j (MAS-ij) or sh; it is a zh sound, as in garage.
Saying make a massage; Americans say get a massage or give someone a massage.

massage.etymology: From French *massage*, from *masser* (“to massage”) (borrowed around the end of the 18th century from Arabic *مَسَّ* (“feel, touch”), or from Portuguese *amassar*) + *-age*.

senses.definition: Mediocre; lackluster; unexceptional; uninspiring.
Apathetic; unenthusiastic.
senses.example: Her review of the new phone was meh, saying only that it was fine.

senses.definition: Expressing indifference or lack of enthusiasm.
senses.example: “What do you want for dinner?” — “Meh. I’m not really hungry.”

senses.definition: A bleating sound, as that of a sheep or goat.
senses.example: The goat in the barn went meh, meh, meh all morning long.

senses.definition: A judgment marked by indifference; lack of impression.
senses.example: The committee's response was a shrug and a meh, which disappointed the founders.

senses.definition: Final question particle expressing skepticism.
senses.example: Really meh?

core.definition: Mediocre or unexciting; not especially good, and not worth much enthusiasm.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'e' like the vowel in 'bed' and do not add a long 'ay' sound. Say it quickly with a shrug in your voice.

nuance.connotation: Negative or dismissive, but mild. It expresses a shrug rather than anger, though it can sound rude if said about someone's work to their face.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use meh mainly in casual speech and texts to show that something is just average or that they do not care much. It is informal and playful, so avoid it in job interviews, customer complaints and formal writing. A friend might ask, 'How was the movie?' and you can answer, 'Meh.'

distinctions.note: So-so is neutral and suggests something is acceptable but average, while meh is more dismissive and suggests you are unimpressed.
Blah describes something dull or boring, often in a mood, while meh is a casual verdict on quality or interest.

examples.everyday: How was the new pizza place? Honestly, it was kind of meh.
examples.professional: The first prototype was meh, so we rebuilt the interface before the demo.
examples.analytical: The critic's meh reaction reveals less about the novel than about the expectations the genre had created.

nuance.analogy: Meh is like a half-hearted shrug in word form: it says 'it's fine, I guess' without the effort of a real opinion.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of a shrug or bored sound; its exact origin is unclear.
common_mistakes: Writing meh in formal reports or emails, where it sounds unprofessional.
Pronouncing it as 'may', which makes it sound like a different word.

meh.etymology: Popularized by the American television show The Simpsons; first used on the show in the episode titled "Sideshow Bob Roberts" (1994).

senses.definition: The property of being melodious.
senses.example: The melodiousness of the cellist's playing filled the small concert hall with warmth.

core.definition: The quality of having a pleasing, tuneful, and sweet sound, especially in voices or music.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LOH. The '-ious' reduces to 'ee-us', and the final '-ness' is a short, reduced 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a sound that is sweet and pleasant to hear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'melodiousness' for the sound quality of voices, birdsong, music, or a poem. In casual talk, people more often say 'a pleasant sound' or 'a beautiful voice', so 'melodiousness' sounds a bit formal or literary.

distinctions.note: Tunefulness refers to singing or playing accurately in tune. Melodiousness refers to the pleasing sweetness of the sound itself.
Sweetness is a general quality of pleasantness in taste, tone, or manner. Melodiousness is specific to musical or vocal sound.
Harmony means several notes or voices sounding together. Melodiousness describes how pleasant a sound is, even from one voice.

examples.everyday: I could listen to the melodiousness of her laugh all afternoon.
examples.professional: We tested the new alert sound for melodiousness, but users wanted it clearer, not prettier.
examples.analytical: Critics often praised the melodiousness of Tennyson's verse, though later readers questioned whether sound alone sustains a poem.

nuance.analogy: Like a bell ringing clearly across a quiet valley.
nuance.etymology: From 'melodious' plus the suffix '-ness'; 'melodious' comes from Late Latin melodiosus.
common_mistakes: Writing 'melodiosity', which is not the standard English noun.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'MEL-odiousness'.
Pronouncing the '-ious' ending with a full 'oh' sound, as in 'mel-oh-DEE-oh-us'.

senses.definition: To form an Internet meme out of something.

core.definition: To turn something, such as a photo, quote, or video, into an internet meme, often by adding a caption or altering it for humor.

pronunciation.tip: Meme is pronounced meem, with a long ee, not mem. Stress the first syllable, and end with a clear fy sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. It can sound mocking when used about a serious person or event.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word online and in casual conversation, mostly among younger people and in social media circles. It is usually passive or used with a dog, a photo, or a video as the object, such as 'that clip got memeified overnight'. In formal writing, say 'turned into a meme' instead.

distinctions.note: Go viral describes something spreading rapidly, while memeify means specifically remaking it as a meme with captions or edits.
Meme is the thing itself, while memeify is the act of creating one from something else.

examples.everyday: My sister memeified my dog's photo with a caption about Monday mornings, and now the whole group chat uses it.
examples.professional: Marketing wants to memeify the product demo, so we need a clip that works as a six-second loop.
examples.analytical: To memeify a serious argument is to strip it of context and reduce it to a repeatable joke, which changes what it means.

nuance.analogy: Memeifying something is like putting a sticky note on a painting: the original stays the same, but everyone reads the note first.
nuance.etymology: From meme, coined by Richard Dawkins in 1976 from Greek mimēma, 'something imitated', plus the verb suffix -ify.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing meme with a short e, as in mem, rather than the long ee of meem.
Using memeify in formal writing, where turned into a meme is more appropriate.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being memorable.

core.definition: The quality of being easy to remember or worth remembering, often used for slogans, products, experiences, and stories.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the BIL syllable, as in memorable. The final -ity sounds like 'ih-tee', and the middle syllables are quick and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing something that sticks in people's minds, and neutral in research or marketing contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use memorability in marketing, advertising, user research, and design reviews, as in 'the memorability of the logo.' In casual talk people usually say 'catchy' or 'hard to forget' instead. The word is useful in meetings when discussing what makes a message stick.

distinctions.note: Memory is the mental faculty or a stored recollection, while memorability is a property of an item that makes it easy to remember.
Recall is the act of retrieving information, while memorability describes how likely something is to be recalled later.
Catchiness is informal and mostly used for tunes, slogans, or phrases, while memorability is a more general and more analytical term.

examples.everyday: That jingle has high memorability, because I've been humming it all day.
examples.professional: User testing showed that the new logo has better memorability than the old one, so we're keeping the redesign.
examples.analytical: The memorability of a story depends less on its factual content than on vivid images and emotional stakes.

nuance.analogy: Memorability is like a name tag with bright letters: people read it once and still remember it later.
nuance.etymology: From memorable, from Latin memorabilis, plus the English suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Using memorability to mean memory, as in 'I have good memorability'; say 'I have a good memory'.
Stressing the wrong syllable: the main stress is on BIL, not on the first syllable.

senses.definition: A nervous breakdown.
senses.example: After months of work pressure, he suffered a mental breakdown and took a leave of absence.

core.definition: A period of severe emotional collapse when someone can no longer cope with stress, often requiring rest or treatment.

pronunciation.tip: Mental is light and unstressed, while the compound noun breakdown gets the main stress on BRAYK. Keep the t in mental clear and don't make the first word heavy.

nuance.connotation: Negative or serious: it describes a real crisis but is often used loosely as hyperbole.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say mental breakdown or nervous breakdown when someone has a severe crisis, such as after prolonged stress, grief or trauma. In casual talk people overstate it, as in 'I'm having a mental breakdown over this spreadsheet.' For a real situation, say you're really struggling or talk to a doctor or counselor. A natural reply is 'That sounds so hard; do you want to talk about it?'

distinctions.note: Burnout describes exhaustion and cynicism caused by long-term work stress; mental breakdown is a more acute crisis.
A panic attack is a sudden, intense episode of fear with physical symptoms that passes within minutes; a breakdown is a longer period of collapse.

collocations: on the verge of a mental breakdown

examples.everyday: After months of caring for her dad, she had a mental breakdown and needed a few weeks off.
examples.professional: HR said that if an employee has a mental breakdown at work, the manager should contact the wellness program right away.
examples.analytical: The term mental breakdown is clinically vague, which is why psychiatrists tend to use more specific diagnoses such as major depressive episode.

nuance.analogy: A mental breakdown is like a bridge that has been overloaded for too long: it finally gives way under the weight.
nuance.etymology: Mental from Latin mens 'mind'; breakdown from the verb break down, meaning to collapse or stop working.
common_mistakes: Using it casually for minor stress; Americans may hear that as exaggeration.
Giving mental and breakdown equal stress; the compound's main stress belongs on BRAYK.

senses.definition: A hospital facility specialized to treat patients with serious mental disorders.

core.definition: A hospital for people with serious mental illnesses, where patients may stay for treatment, observation or long-term care.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HAH in hospital and keep mental light. The second syllable of hospital is reduced, so say 'spih-tul' rather than 'spy-tal', with a very weak final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or stigmatizing today; it suggests old institutions and can sound outdated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans still use mental hospital in history, news reports and some everyday speech, but many now prefer psychiatric hospital, behavioral health hospital or inpatient facility to reduce stigma. The older word asylum now sounds archaic, though it appears in historical discussions. Use a modern term in professional settings.

distinctions.note: Psychiatric hospital is the clinical term in most current medical settings; mental hospital sounds older and more informal.
Rehab is short for rehabilitation facility, usually for addiction; a mental hospital treats a wider range of psychiatric conditions.

examples.everyday: My grandfather spent a few months in a mental hospital after his depression got much worse.
examples.professional: The health system closed its old mental hospital and moved those patients into community programs.
examples.analytical: Goffman's study of the mental hospital as a total institution showed how daily routines can strip patients of their sense of self.

nuance.analogy: A mental hospital is like a large old house built for one purpose and now being rebuilt into smaller homes.
nuance.etymology: Mental from Latin mens 'mind'; hospital from Latin hospitalis 'relating to a guest', from hospes 'host or guest'.
common_mistakes: Using it for an ordinary hospital visit for a mood problem; the term refers to facilities for serious mental illness.
Saying mental hospital in a professional setting where psychiatric hospital is now preferred.

senses.definition: Reeking, oppressing, having the nature of miasma.
senses.example: The swamp air hung over the town, thick and miasmatic, after weeks of summer rain.

core.definition: Of or relating to a miasma, a foul or poisonous vapor once thought to spread disease.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MAT, the third syllable, while miasma itself stresses the second syllable (my-AZ-muh). Keep the first vowel as a diphthong, like my.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something foul, heavy or unhealthy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word today, and it appears mainly in historical writing about miasma theory or in literary descriptions of heavy, foul air. In everyday speech, people say foul-smelling, stifling or musty. The miasma theory of disease was replaced by germ theory in the later nineteenth century.

distinctions.note: Malodorous simply means bad-smelling, while miasmatic suggests a poisonous or oppressive vapor.
Noxious means harmful or poisonous in general; miasmatic adds the sense of a hanging, foul vapor.

examples.everyday: The old basement had a damp, miasmatic smell that made me want to leave right away.
examples.professional: The historical report explains the miasmatic theory that guided city planners before germ theory took hold.
examples.analytical: The novelist describes the city as a miasmatic atmosphere where moral corruption seems to hang in the air like the rot of a swamp.

nuance.analogy: A miasmatic room is like a sealed car on a hot day, where the air is heavy, sour and hard to breathe.
nuance.etymology: From Greek miasma (pollution, stain), from miainein (to stain or pollute).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in my-AZ-muh-tik; the stress falls on the MAT syllable.
Using miasma, the noun, where the adjective is needed, as in a miasma smell.

senses.definition: Someone who mimes during a performance of a song.

core.definition: A performer who acts out or mimes a song or speech, moving the lips or body to a recording.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the final '-er' be a light, reduced sound. Keep the vowel as in 'mime', not as in 'mimic'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since it can imply that the performer is not really singing or playing live.
nuance.usage_note: 'Mimer' is rare in American English. Most Americans say 'lip-syncer' or 'a performer lip-syncing' for a singer who moves to a recording, and they use 'mime artist' for a performer of wordless theater. You may see 'mimer' in dictionaries or in older writing, so recognize it but use the American alternatives in speech.

distinctions.note: A mime artist is a performer of wordless theater, while a mimer, in this sense, acts out a song or speech.
Lip-syncer is the common American term for a performer who moves to a recording.
A mimic imitates someone's voice or manner, while a mimer acts out a song or speech in performance.

examples.everyday: The guitarist was really just a mimer, so nobody was playing live.
examples.professional: The festival booked a mimer for the closing act, but the audience was disappointed when the track cut out.
examples.analytical: A mimer's performance raises questions about authenticity, since the audience hears a voice that is not the performer's own.

nuance.analogy: A mimer is like a puppet: the movements look live, but the voice comes from somewhere else.
nuance.etymology: From mime (verb), with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'MIM-er' with a short 'i', which sounds like 'mimic'.
Using 'mimer' for a silent stage performer, when Americans say 'mime artist'.

senses.definition: An act or ability to simulate or effect the appearance, characteristics, or behavior of someone or something else.
senses.example: They say that mimicry is the sincerest form of flattery, but I still think I'm being mocked when he acts just like me.

core.definition: The act or skill of imitating someone's voice, behavior or appearance, often to entertain, mock or deceive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MIM. The last syllable is a clear 'ree', and the middle syllable is short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on whether it is used for play, deception or biology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mimicry' for comedians' impressions, animal camouflage, and the copying of voices or accents. In biology it refers to a species that resembles another for protection. In everyday talk, 'impressions' is often more natural for entertainment, and 'copying' for ordinary behavior.

distinctions.note: Imitation is a general copy; mimicry often implies a close, skillful copy that may be playful or deceptive.
An impression is a comic imitation of a famous person; mimicry is the broader ability or act of imitating.

examples.everyday: Her mimicry of our old boss is so good that everyone at the party was laughing.
examples.professional: The vendor's demo showed impressive mimicry of our accent-based voice commands, but we still need to test it with real customers.
examples.analytical: Some scholars argue that religious ritual involves a kind of mimicry of divine action, yet this mimicry becomes meaningful only when it expresses real participation.

nuance.analogy: Mimicry is like a skilled chameleon matching its surroundings: the copy looks so close that it can fool the eye.
nuance.etymology: From mimic, from Latin mimicus, from Greek mimikos.
common_mistakes: Using 'mimicry' as a verb; the verb is 'mimic' and the noun is 'mimicry'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'kree' with a hard 'k'; it is 'ree'.

senses.definition: In a state of misery: very sad, ill, or poor.
Very bad (at something); unskilled, incompetent; hopeless.
senses.example: He's good at some sports, like tennis, but he's just miserable at football.

senses.definition: Of the weather, extremely unpleasant due to being cold, wet, overcast, etc.
senses.example: The miserable weather kept us indoors all weekend, with cold rain and gray skies.

senses.definition: Wretched; worthless; mean; contemptible.
senses.example: a miserable sinner

senses.definition: (as a personality trait) Negative minded, unpleasant to be around.
senses.example: My miserable roommate complained about everything and made every dinner unbearable.

senses.definition: A miserable person; a wretch.
senses.example: That miserable old man yelled at every child who walked past his porch.

senses.definition: A state of misery or melancholy.
senses.example: Her diary recorded the long, quiet miserable that followed her father's death.

core.definition: Very unhappy, uncomfortable, or unwell; feeling or causing misery. Also used for bad weather.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, MIZ. The word has three syllables in fast speech, because the middle 'uh' often disappears, so it sounds like 'MIZ-ruh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes strong unhappiness, discomfort, or bad conditions. In casual speech it can be used with humor, as in 'I feel miserable today.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use miserable often in everyday talk about feeling sick ('I feel miserable with this cold'), bad weather ('It's miserable outside'), or a bad day. It can be strong, so it is less polite for describing someone else. A natural reply to 'I feel miserable' is 'Aw, I'm sorry, get some rest.'

distinctions.note: Unhappy is milder and more general. Miserable is stronger and suggests deep discomfort or distress.
Sad describes an emotion. Miserable can describe both emotion and physical discomfort or bad conditions.

examples.everyday: I feel miserable with this sore throat, so I'm staying home today.
examples.professional: The meeting was miserable because every decision got delayed by the same two people.
examples.analytical: Augustine's description of the miserable soul shows how sin turns desire away from its true good.

nuance.analogy: Miserable is like a rainy day that never ends: it wears down your mood and comfort together.
nuance.etymology: From Latin miserabilis, from miser 'wretched, unhappy'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on MIZ.
Saying 'miserable' as four clear syllables in fast speech; the middle vowel is often lost.

miserable.etymology: Middle French *miserable*, from Old French, from Latin *miserabilis*, equivalent to *miser* + *able*.

conversation.text: I was miserable with the flu all weekend.
It's miserable outside: cold, wet and windy.
She was miserable at her old job, so she quit.

senses.definition: Lack of trust or confidence; distrust, untrust.
To have no confidence in (something or someone).
senses.example: Many voters mistrust the polling firms after the last election missed badly.

senses.definition: To be wary, suspicious or doubtful of (something or someone).
senses.example: I mistrust online reviews that appear too perfect or were posted all at once.

senses.definition: To suspect, to imagine or suppose (something) to be the case.
senses.example: I mistrust that the server crashed because of the recent update, but we should check.

senses.definition: To be suspicious.
senses.example: Older people in the village mistrust easily, especially toward strangers from the city.

core.definition: A lack of trust or confidence in a person, group, or idea; a feeling that someone may be dishonest or unreliable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TRUST, with a short u sound. Keep the r light and American, and avoid stretching the vowel into 'trust-ah'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a lack of confidence that can be justified or unfair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mistrust for a general, sometimes deep, lack of faith in institutions, people, or motives, especially in news or politics. In everyday talk people often say 'I don't trust him' or 'I'm suspicious of him', which sound more casual. Mistrust sounds more serious and is often used about groups or public attitudes.

distinctions.note: Distrust and mistrust are very close, but mistrust is more common for a general or lingering feeling, while distrust often describes a stronger, more active doubt.
Suspicion is a belief that someone has done wrong, while mistrust is a more general lack of confidence.

examples.everyday: After the rumors, a lot of my neighbors have real mistrust of the new developer.
examples.professional: Low engagement in the survey reflected a mistrust of the data pipeline among the business teams.
examples.analytical: Mistrust of institutions often grows when the reasons for official decisions are hidden from the public.

nuance.analogy: Mistrust is like a fence built between two yards; each side can see the other, but neither will open the gate.
nuance.etymology: From mis- and trust, from Middle English and Old Norse roots meaning confidence.
common_mistakes: Using 'mistrust of' with a verb directly instead of a noun, as in 'I mistrust him for' rather than 'I mistrust him because'.
Stressing the first syllable.

senses.definition: An alcoholic drink made from one or more kinds of liquor mixed with other ingredients.
senses.example: I like gin and tonic as a mixed drink, but I really prefer beer.

core.definition: An alcoholic drink made by mixing one or more kinds of liquor with other ingredients such as juice, soda or tonic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word drink. The t in mixed is quick and often almost silent before the d, and the r in drink is clear in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common, polite way to order an alcoholic drink that is not beer or wine.
nuance.usage_note: In American bars and restaurants, ordering a mixed drink means asking for a cocktail or a liquor-based drink such as a vodka soda. Bartenders often ask 'What kind of mixed drink would you like?' A natural reply names the liquor and the mixer, for example 'A gin and tonic, please.'

distinctions.note: Cocktail is a broader and sometimes more elaborate word for a mixed drink, often with garnishes or specialty recipes.
A shot is a small serving of straight liquor, usually drunk without mixing.

examples.everyday: Could I get a mixed drink, maybe a vodka soda with lime?
examples.professional: The conference dinner offered a full bar, but most guests ordered a simple mixed drink.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of taste have long asked whether a mixed drink is more than the sum of its ingredients.

nuance.analogy: A mixed drink is like a band: each liquor and mixer plays its part, but the sound is the whole group together.
nuance.etymology: Mixed from mix; drink from Old English drincan.
common_mistakes: Using mixed drink for any beverage that has more than one ingredient, such as a fruit smoothie, which Americans would not call a mixed drink.
Pronouncing mixed as mix-ed with an extra syllable.

senses.definition: Synonym of trailer park.
senses.example: They rented a small lot in a mobile home park near the highway.

core.definition: An area of land with rows of mobile homes, where families rent space and connect their homes to utilities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'MO' in 'mobile' and on 'PARK,' with 'home' lighter in the middle. The 'r' in 'park' is strong, and the vowel is the 'ah' of 'father.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on speaker. Some people find the term plain and practical; others think it carries a low-income stereotype.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'mobile home park' as a standard term, and it is used in real estate, local government, and news. 'Trailer park' is more casual and sometimes carries a negative stereotype, so use it carefully with neighbors or in polite conversation. In the industry, many communities now call themselves 'manufactured housing communities.'

distinctions.note: 'Trailer park' is the casual, older term and can sound dismissive; 'mobile home park' is the standard, more neutral term.
An 'RV park' is for recreational vehicles, which people visit on trips; a 'mobile home park' houses people as permanent residents.

collocations: live in a mobile home park
lot in a mobile home park

examples.everyday: My cousin rents a lot in a mobile home park on the edge of town, and the neighbors are very friendly.
examples.professional: The county zoning board approved an expansion of the mobile home park, which will add twenty new lots.
examples.analytical: Housing scholars argue that the mobile home park is a form of affordable housing that also raises questions about land ownership and tenant protection.

nuance.analogy: Like a row of parked cars that people actually live in, each on its own small plot of rented ground.
nuance.etymology: 'Mobile' from Latin 'mobilis,' movable; 'home' from Old English 'hām'; 'park' from Old French 'parc,' enclosed land.
common_mistakes: Saying 'mobile home park' with equal stress on every word. The compound is usually stressed on 'MO' and 'PARK.'
Using 'mobile home park' for a camping area. Campgrounds and RV parks are for travelers, not long-term residents.

senses.definition: Splitting a model itself across several devices because it is too large for one.
senses.example: Our team used model parallelism to train the language model across eight GPUs.

core.definition: A technique for splitting a single large model across several devices, such as GPUs, because it is too big to fit on one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAIR in 'parallelism', with a secondary stress on the first word. The 'al' in 'parallel' is a reduced vowel and the word ends in '-lel-iz-um', not '-lay-lism'. The middle 'l' is a clear l, and the final syllable is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers training large language models use this term in design reviews and technical documentation. It usually appears alongside 'data parallelism' and 'pipeline parallelism' in discussions of distributed training. In casual talk, people might say 'splitting the model across GPUs' instead.

distinctions.note: Data parallelism copies the whole model to each device and splits the training data, while model parallelism splits the model itself.
Pipeline parallelism assigns consecutive layers to different devices and passes data through them in stages, which is one form of model parallelism.

collocations: combine model parallelism with data parallelism

examples.everyday: My friend who trains AI models said they had to use model parallelism because the model was too big to fit on one graphics card.
examples.professional: We will use model parallelism across eight GPUs, but the communication overhead will slow each training step unless we tune the batch size.
examples.analytical: Model parallelism trades memory constraints for communication costs, so its scalability depends on how the network architecture partitions its computations.

nuance.analogy: It is like splitting a large orchestra score so each section plays its own part on a different stage, then coordinating the timing between them.
nuance.etymology: 'Model' comes from Latin modulus, a measure; 'parallel' comes from Greek parallēlos, alongside one another.
common_mistakes: Confusing model parallelism with data parallelism; the first splits the model, the second splits the data.
Stressing the wrong syllable in 'parallelism'; the main stress is on PAIR, not the final syllable.

conversation.text: Model parallelism splits the model itself across devices when it's too big for one.
Tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism are both forms of model parallelism.
Model parallelism adds communication overhead, so we use it only for the biggest models.

senses.definition: Of or relating to monergism.
senses.example: Her seminary paper argued for a monergistic view of salvation, in which God alone effects regeneration.

core.definition: Describing a view of salvation in which God alone, without human cooperation, produces regeneration and faith in a person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'jis,' the third syllable. The first syllables have weak 'er' sounds, so don't stress 'MAH' or add extra vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in theological discussion. It describes a position, so the tone depends on whether the speaker agrees with it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monergistic almost exclusively in theology and seminary contexts. It usually modifies words like 'view,' 'regeneration,' or 'doctrine.' In everyday talk, people simply say that God alone does the saving work.

distinctions.note: Synergistic describes a view where God and humans cooperate, while monergistic describes a view where God alone acts.
Calvinistic is broader and describes a whole theological system, while monergistic is specific to the role of God in regeneration.

examples.everyday: My pastor's sermon was really monergistic, saying that God does the whole work of salvation.
examples.professional: The monergistic framing of the document helped the committee explain why our grace-based policies had no conditions.
examples.analytical: A monergistic account of regeneration takes the Holy Spirit's action as the sole cause of the new birth, which raises difficult questions about human responsibility.

nuance.analogy: A monergistic view is like a painter who creates the whole painting alone, with the canvas merely receiving the paint.
nuance.etymology: From monergism plus the suffix -istic, from Greek monos 'alone' and ergon 'work.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the third (MAH-ner-JIS-tik).
Using monergistic as a general word for 'only one person doing something' outside theology.

senses.definition: A patch which alters the behavior of a program by forcibly overriding aspects of the original code at runtime.
To alter the behavior of a program by forcibly overriding aspects of the original code at runtime.
senses.example: The developer monkey patched the login function at runtime to fix the bug before the release.

core.definition: A change that alters a program's behavior at runtime by overriding parts of its original code, without editing the source.

pronunciation.tip: Give MUNG-kee secondary stress and PACH primary stress. The word monkey is usually reduced to MUNG-ki in fast speech, and the ng is a single sound with no hard g.

nuance.connotation: Mixed: programmers use it casually, but it can imply a quick, fragile fix.
nuance.usage_note: American developers use monkey patch in code reviews, Slack and documentation. It is informal and often carries a hint of risk, so teams may say 'we monkey patched it' to admit a temporary workaround. It is not a term outsiders usually need.

distinctions.note: A hotfix is an official, tested emergency release; a monkey patch is a runtime change that may bypass normal review.
Refactoring restructures code cleanly without changing behavior; a monkey patch overrides code from outside.

examples.everyday: My phone app kept crashing, so the developer said they'd monkey patch it until the update.
examples.professional: We can't wait for the vendor release, so let's monkey patch the library in staging and open a ticket.
examples.analytical: Monkey patching offers flexibility in dynamic languages, but it makes program behavior depend on load order and hides dependencies.

nuance.analogy: Like taping a cable over a broken part of a machine, a monkey patch works now but may cause trouble later.
common_mistakes: Writing it as one word in formal documents; use monkey patch or monkey-patch.
Using it for any bug fix; it specifically means overriding code at runtime.

monkey-patch.etymology: Apparently from earlier *guerrilla patch* (“code that sneakily changes other code”), understood as gorilla patch.

senses.definition: Containing holes by having been eaten by moth larvae.
Old and in poor condition; worn-out.
Antiquated; having been in use a long time.
senses.example: Her moth-eaten theories about the economy were decades out of date.

core.definition: Full of holes because moth larvae have eaten the fabric, or old, worn out, and in poor condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first word, MOTH, and then on the second part of the phrase, EE, with the final syllable reduced to a weak 'uhn'. Non-native speakers often stress the wrong syllable or pronounce the 'th' as a 't'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting something shabby, outdated, or falling apart.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say moth-eaten for old clothes, blankets, or a worn-out couch, and sometimes for an outdated idea or old policy. It is informal and vivid, so it can sound a bit harsh if used about a person's feelings or a friend's sweater. It is common in casual description and in writing that wants a sharp image.

distinctions.note: Worn out is a general term for used up, while moth-eaten specifically suggests holes and decay.
Outdated is neutral about condition, while moth-eaten adds the image of something shabby and falling apart.

examples.everyday: Grandma finally threw out her moth-eaten wool blanket after forty years.
examples.professional: The old reporting dashboard looks moth-eaten, so we should rebuild it before the audit.
examples.analytical: The author dismisses the moth-eaten doctrines of his predecessors as relics that no longer serve the argument.

nuance.analogy: Moth-eaten is like a sweater with lace-like holes: once solid, now riddled with gaps.
nuance.etymology: Compound of moth and eaten, from Old English etan, to eat.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphen when writing it.
Stressing MOTH-eaten as one unit without the reduced final syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Moth-eaten is not a biblical phrase, but the image appears in Scripture. James 5:2 (RSV) says riches have rotted and garments are moth-eaten, a warning against hoarding wealth. The phrase illustrates how worldly possessions decay.

senses.definition: (dated) A film or movie.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A film or movie; an older, more formal term for a motion picture shown on a screen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word on PIK, and pronounce -ture as chur, not as a long oo sound. Keep the middle vowel of moving short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly old-fashioned; it can sound nostalgic or precise, but may seem stiff in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, people say movie or film, not moving picture. The phrase survives in film history, museum labels, older writing, or when someone wants a deliberately period-style tone. In casual speech it sounds dated or like a joke.

distinctions.note: Movie is the everyday American word for a film shown in theaters or on streaming services.
Film is common in professional and critical talk, as in film studies or a film festival; moving picture is largely historical.

collocations: the history of the moving picture

examples.everyday: My grandmother still calls every movie a moving picture, which always makes us laugh.
examples.professional: Our archive team catalogs early moving pictures from the 1910s for the film preservation project.
examples.analytical: The early moving picture borrowed its conventions from the stage, which is why its staging looks so theatrical to modern viewers.

nuance.analogy: A moving picture is an old-fashioned name for a movie, like calling a car a horseless carriage.
nuance.etymology: Moving from move (Latin movere) and picture from Latin pictura, 'painting'; the phrase arose with early film technology.
common_mistakes: Using moving picture in everyday conversation where movie is expected; it sounds old-fashioned.
Pronouncing picture as PIK-tyoor; in American speech it is PIK-chur.

senses.definition: Anything that mutes or deadens sound.
A warm piece of clothing for the hands.
A kiln or furnace, often electric, with no direct flames (a muffle furnace)
The bare end of the nose between the nostrils, especially in ruminants.
A machine with two pulleys to hoist load by spinning wheels, polyspast, block and tackle.
To wrap (a person, face etc.) in fabric or another covering, for warmth or protection; often with up.
To wrap up or cover (a source of noise) in order to deaden the sound.
senses.example: to muffle the strings of a drum, or that part of an oar which rests in the rowlock

senses.definition: To mute or deaden (a sound etc.).
(dated) To speak indistinctly, or without clear articulation.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To prevent seeing, or hearing, or speaking, by wraps bound about the head; to blindfold; to deafen.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To make a sound quieter or less clear, or to wrap something to reduce noise or protect it from cold.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable a syllabic l with no separate vowel. The word is two syllables, not 'muf-fuhl' with a clear vowel in the second.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes making sound quieter, and it can be positive when people want quiet.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'muffle the sound' or 'muffle the TV' when they want quiet in a house or office. In cold weather, 'muffle up' or 'be muffled up' means to wrap warmly with a scarf and hat. The noun 'muffler' is more common in American English for a car part, so be careful when you hear the word in a car shop.

distinctions.note: Mute can mean to turn off sound completely, while muffle means to reduce or soften it without stopping it.
Dampen usually refers to reducing energy, enthusiasm, or moisture; muffle is specifically about sound or being covered for warmth.

examples.everyday: Can you close the door so the TV noise is muffled a bit while I'm on the phone?
examples.professional: We added foam panels to the conference room so that the conversation was muffled for people in the hallway.
examples.analytical: The author argues that institutional language muffles dissent by making disagreement sound technical rather than moral.

nuance.analogy: Muffling sound is like putting a thick blanket over a ringing alarm clock: you can still hear it, but it is no longer piercing.
nuance.etymology: From Old French mouffler, to cover the face or wrap up.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'muffle' with 'muffler,' which is the car part.
Using 'muffle' for turning sound off completely, which is closer to 'mute.'

muffle.etymology: From Middle English *muflen* (“to muffle”), aphetic alteration of Anglo-Norman *amoufler*, from Old French *enmoufler* (“to wrap up, muffle”), from *moufle* (“mitten”), from Medieval Latin *muffula* (“a muff”), of origin (—first recorded in the Capitulary…

senses.definition: A large cup for beverages, usually having a handle and used without a saucer.
The face.
The mouth.
senses.example: Shut your mug!

senses.definition: A gullible or easily cheated person.
senses.example: He's a gullible mug – he believed her again.

senses.definition: A criminal.
A mug shot.
Motherfucker (usually in similes, e.g. "like a mug" or "as a mug")
To assault for the purpose of robbery.
To exaggerate a facial expression for communicative emphasis; to make a face, to pose, as for photographs or in a performance, in an exaggerated or affected manner.
senses.example: The children weren't interested in sitting still for a serious photo; they mugged for the camera.

senses.definition: To photograph for identification; to take a mug shot of.
Uninteresting or unpleasant.

core.definition: A large cup, usually with a handle, for hot or cold drinks such as coffee or tea.

pronunciation.tip: One short vowel, the 'uh' sound of 'cup', followed by a hard g at the end. Don't stretch the vowel into 'moog' or drop the g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the cup; the senses for face, mouth or robbery are informal or negative.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, a mug is the everyday cup with a handle, often ceramic and taller than a teacup, used for coffee at home or at work. Diners and offices serve coffee in mugs, and you can ask for a refill in your mug. Mug also means face in informal slang, and to mug someone means to rob them, so be careful with those senses.

distinctions.note: Cup is the general word and often refers to a smaller vessel; a mug is larger, sturdier, and has a handle with no saucer.
A tumbler is a straight-sided glass or cup without a handle, usually for cold drinks or cocktails.

examples.everyday: Could I get a refill in my mug, please?
examples.professional: Please rinse your coffee mug before you leave the break room so the sink stays clear.
examples.analytical: The mug, unlike the cup, is defined by its height and handle, which make it practical for holding hot liquid without a saucer.

nuance.analogy: A mug is a cup built for everyday work, like a sturdy work boot compared with a dress shoe.
common_mistakes: Ordering a cup when you want a mug; a cup is usually smaller and may be served with a saucer.
Using mug for the face in formal writing; use face there instead.

senses.definition: To think deeply about something; to ponder, deliberate or ruminate.
senses.example: I have been mulling over this math problem for weeks.

core.definition: To think deeply about something for a while before deciding or responding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'OH' in over, while mull is weaker. In speech the two words link smoothly, so 'mull over' sounds like 'mul-LOH-ver'. The final 'er' is a rhotic American r, not a separate 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful, unhurried reflection before a choice or a conclusion.
nuance.usage_note: This is one of the most common phrasal verbs in American speech and writing. You can say it when someone asks for a decision you are not ready to make, and a natural reply is 'Sure, take your time' or 'Let me think about it.' It works in both casual and business settings, though in very formal writing you might choose consider or deliberate.

distinctions.note: Think over is the simpler, more everyday phrase. Mull over sounds slightly more deliberate and is often used for weightier matters.
Ponder is more formal and reflective, and it is used more in writing. Mull over is a common spoken phrase with a practical feel.

collocations: mull over it for a while

examples.everyday: Can you give me a day to mull it over? I want to make sure we're making the right call.
examples.professional: The board will mull over the budget options before Thursday's vote, so please send your analysis by Wednesday.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long mulled over whether moral truths exist independently of the minds that perceive them.

nuance.analogy: Like turning a stone over in your hand to see every side before you put it in your pocket.
common_mistakes: Saying 'mull on it' instead of 'mull it over'; mull over is the normal American form.
Stressing 'mull' too strongly; in the phrase, 'over' carries the main stress.

senses.definition: To do as a requirement; indicates that the sentence subject is required as an imperative or directive to execute the sentence predicate, with failure to do so resulting in a failure or negative consequence.
senses.example: You must arrive in class on time.

senses.definition: To do with certainty; indicates that the speaker is certain that the subject will have executed the predicate.
senses.example: If it has rained all day, it must be very wet outside.

senses.definition: Used to indicate that something is very likely, probable, or certain to be true.
senses.example: The children must be asleep by now.

senses.definition: To make musty.
senses.example: Damp air in the basement had musted every box we stored there.

senses.definition: To become musty.
senses.example: Stored too long in the damp garage, the paperbacks began to must.

senses.definition: Something that is mandatory, required or recommended.
senses.example: If you're trekking all day, a map is a must.

senses.definition: The property of being stale or musty.
senses.example: The cellar had a faint must that clung to the wool coats.

senses.definition: Something that exhibits the property of being stale or musty.
senses.example: The musts in the cellar were mostly spoiled bags of flour.

senses.definition: Fruit juice that will ferment or has fermented, usually from grapes (in winemaking) or apples (in cidermaking).
senses.example: The guide then explained that the must drains from the cider press and runs into the vats where it will ferment.

core.definition: Used to say that something is necessary or required, or to show that you are strongly sure something is true.

pronunciation.tip: In fast speech it is reduced to a weak form like 'must' with a schwa, so 'you must go' sounds like 'yoo-mus-GO'. Stress it only for emphasis, and never add an s or a to after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to strong. It can sound bossy or pushy when telling someone what to do, so softer options like should or have to are often better in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use must for strong recommendations, like 'You must try this', and for logical conclusions, like 'That must be the mail'. For ordinary obligations, people usually say have to or need to. The negative mustn't is rare in speech, so people often say you can't or you don't have to.

distinctions.note: Must expresses the speaker's own sense of necessity, while have to usually describes an outside rule or situation.
Must is stronger than should and implies that there is little choice, while should is a softer suggestion or advice.

examples.everyday: You must try the peach pie here, because it's the best in town.
examples.professional: We must finalize the model validation report before the Thursday review.
examples.analytical: Any adequate account of freedom must explain how a choice can be both caused and genuinely one's own.

nuance.analogy: Must is like a red stop sign: it tells you there is no real choice to make.
nuance.etymology: Originally the past tense of an Old English verb meaning to be allowed or able; the present sense developed later.
common_mistakes: Adding -s or 'to' after must, as in 'He musts go' or 'You must to try'.
Using must for past obligation, as in 'I must go yesterday' instead of 'I had to go yesterday'.

must.etymology: From Middle English *moste* "must", literally, "had to", the past tense of Middle English *moten* (“to have to”), from Old English *mōste* (“had to”), 1st & 3rd person singular past tense of *mōtan* (“to be allowed, be able to, have the opportunity to, be…

senses.definition: A transcendental union of soul or mind with the divine reality or divinity.
senses.example: Her years of meditation led to a deep mysticism in which she felt united with God.

senses.definition: The beliefs, ideas, or thoughts of mystics.
senses.example: Scholars studied the mysticism of medieval Rhineland nuns and their visionary writings.

senses.definition: A doctrine of direct communication or spiritual intuition of divine truth.
senses.example: The seminary course compared Protestant mysticism with the Catholic traditions of contemplative prayer.

senses.definition: Obscure thoughts and speculations.
senses.example: His rambling speeches about cosmic energy were pure mysticism that no one could follow.

core.definition: The belief or practice of seeking direct experience of, or union with, God or ultimate reality beyond ordinary understanding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a short 'i' as in 'miss'. The middle syllable is reduced to 'tuh', and the ending is 'siz-um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or positive in religious studies; can sound vague, irrational, or suspicious in casual use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for religious traditions and also loosely for anything spiritual or mysterious. Scholars use it more precisely for direct experience of the divine. Among Christians, it can be seen as deeply devotional or as a risky departure from doctrine.

distinctions.note: Spirituality is broader and more common, covering any pursuit of meaning or the sacred.
Occultism deals with hidden or secret powers and practices, not necessarily union with God.
Rationalism relies on reason, while mysticism emphasizes experience beyond reason.

examples.everyday: My grandmother loved reading about mysticism and the lives of the saints.
examples.professional: The seminar on mysticism looks at Meister Eckhart, Teresa of Avila, and Gregory Palamas.
examples.analytical: Orthodox mysticism holds that union with God is participation in divine energies, not absorption into the divine essence.

nuance.analogy: Mysticism is like standing at the edge of the ocean and feeling its depth, rather than reading a map.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mystikos, 'secret, connected with mysteries', from mystes, 'initiate'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel like 'my' instead of 'miss'.
Using it to mean fake or supernatural tricks.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as 'mis-TIS-i-zum'.
nuance.biblical_note: The word is not biblical, but many point to experiences such as Paul's being caught up to the third heaven in 2 Corinthians 12:2-4. John 15:4 speaks of abiding in Christ, and 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of sharing the divine nature, a text important to Orthodox ideas of theosis.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy treats mystical experience as part of ordinary church life, rooted in prayer, sacraments, and theosis. Hesychasm and the teaching of Gregory Palamas on divine energies are central.
Catholicism honors mystics such as Teresa of Avila and John of the Cross, within doctrine and under church discernment. Mystical union is seen as a gift of grace, not a human achievement.

Protestants are divided: Luther and Calvin spoke of union with Christ, but many Protestants distrust mysticism that bypasses Scripture. Pietist, Quaker, Pentecostal, and some Reformed traditions give experience of God greater weight.

mysticism.etymology: From *mystic* + *-ism*, from Old French *mistique* (“mysterious, full of mystery”), from Latin *mysticus* (“mystical, mystic, of secret rites”), from Ancient Greek *μυστικός* (“secret, mystic”), from *μύστης* (“one who has been initiated, initiate”) from…

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or characteristic of sailing, sailors, or the sea.
senses.example: I was mostly unfamiliar with the nautical terms used in the sailing documentary.

senses.definition: A nautical person or writer; a sailor.
senses.example: The nautical in the bar spent the evening telling stories about storms at sea.

core.definition: Relating to ships, sailing, or the sea and the people who work on it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a short 'ih', as in 'kit', and in fast speech the t is a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. In decor and fashion, nautical suggests a fresh, seaside style.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nautical for sailing and the sea in general, as in 'nautical theme' for decorations or 'nautical miles' in navigation and aviation. For the military navy, say 'naval', and for shipping and sea trade, say 'maritime'. In everyday speech, people often say 'sailing' or 'boating' instead.

distinctions.note: Naval refers to a navy and its military ships; nautical refers to seafaring in general, including civilian sailing.
Maritime concerns the sea in relation to shipping, trade, or law; nautical concerns navigation and sailing.

examples.everyday: The restaurant had a nautical theme, with fishing nets and little anchors on the walls.
examples.professional: The navigation team needs the nautical charts updated before the cargo ship leaves the port.
examples.analytical: Melville's nautical language in Moby-Dick is not mere decoration; it structures the novel's moral vision.

nuance.analogy: Like a sailor's vocabulary, where every word is tied to wind, rope, and tide.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nauticus, from Greek nautikos, of sailors, from nautes, sailor, from naus, ship.
common_mistakes: Confusing nautical with naval; a navy is naval, but a sailing trip is nautical.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'nau-TI-cal'; the stress falls on the first syllable.

nautical.etymology: From Middle French *nautique* (“of or relating to sailors or navigation”) or its etymon, Classical Latin *nauticus* (“of or relating to ships, seafaring”), *al*.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of a nebbish.
senses.example: He wore a nebbishy cardigan and apologized to the waiter for everything.

core.definition: Timid, awkward and ineffectual, in a self-deprecating or endearing way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The sh is a clear shh sound, and the final -y is a light ee, not a long eye.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or affectionate; it teases someone who is timid, awkward and easily overlooked.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nebbishy in casual conversation, often humorously, about someone who seems meek or socially awkward, like a mild-mannered accountant. It can sound hurtful if said directly to a person, so it is best used about a third person or in self-deprecating humor. A natural reply is 'Ha, you're being too hard on yourself; you're not nebbishy at all.'

distinctions.note: Meek is a general term for quiet and gentle; nebbishy adds a sense of awkward, unassertive and easily overlooked.
Nerdy describes enthusiasm for technical or niche interests; nebbishy describes a timid, ineffectual manner regardless of interests.

examples.everyday: He's a sweet guy, a little nebbishy, but he's great with his nephews.
examples.professional: The new analyst seems nebbishy in meetings, but her written reports are sharp and decisive.
examples.analytical: Many comic films build their humor on the nebbishy, self-doubting hero who hesitates to act.

nuance.analogy: Like a wallflower with a lunch box: harmless, easy to overlook, and quietly endearing.
nuance.etymology: From Yiddish nebekh, meaning poor thing or unfortunate one.
common_mistakes: Using nebbishy as an insult to someone's face; in American speech it can hurt.
Treating it as a synonym for shy or nerdy; nebbishy also suggests ineffectual and awkward, a stronger judgment.

senses.definition: A statement Q in relation to statement P such that P implies Q.

core.definition: A condition Q that must hold whenever a statement P holds; if P is true, Q must also be true, so P implies Q.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DISH in condition, and the word necessary is stressed on its middle syllable -SAIR-, not on the first syllable. The -ary ending reduces to a short ee sound, and the r is clearly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is standard vocabulary in mathematics, logic and statistics, used in lectures, proofs and technical writing. In casual speech Americans would say it only when explaining a logical requirement, such as saying something is a necessary condition for a result.

distinctions.note: A necessary condition must hold for P to hold, but it may not be enough by itself; a sufficient condition guarantees P when it holds.
A necessary and sufficient condition is both required and enough, so it is an if-and-only-if relationship.

collocations: necessary condition for the theorem to hold

examples.everyday: Having a valid ticket is a necessary condition for getting into the concert, but it isn't the only thing you need.
examples.professional: Finite variance is a necessary condition for this estimator to be unbiased, so we should check it before running the model.
examples.analytical: If the argument is valid, then the premises are a necessary condition of the conclusion, since no valid argument can have true premises and a false conclusion.

nuance.analogy: A necessary condition is like oxygen for a fire: without it there is no fire, but oxygen alone does not start one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin necessarius, needful, and condicio, agreement or stipulation.
common_mistakes: Confusing necessary with sufficient, so that a required condition is treated as a guarantee
Stressing necessary on the first syllable as NESS-uh-ser-ee rather than the middle

senses.definition: Sinful, villainous, criminal, or wicked, especially when noteworthy or notorious for such characteristics.
senses.example: Aliens have a nefarious connotation in many science fiction books.

core.definition: Wicked, evil, or criminal, especially in a way that is well known or openly shameful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'fair', and the 'ious' ending is two syllables, 'ee-us', not 'shus'. The first vowel is a short, reduced 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes villainy or criminal intent, often with a slightly dramatic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nefarious' in news, fiction, and everyday talk about schemes or plots, often with a playful or dramatic tone. It is a bit formal, so 'shady' or 'sneaky' is more casual. You can say 'nefarious plan' or 'nefarious scheme' naturally in conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Evil' is a broad moral word, while 'nefarious' focuses on criminal or secretive wickedness.
