nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes one organism harming another.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parasitize mainly in biology, ecology and entomology. In casual talk people say 'freeload' or 'live off' someone. The verb is precise and sounds technical, so it fits academic writing better than conversation.

distinctions.note: Infect means to introduce a pathogen that causes disease; parasitize means to live on or in a host, which does not always cause illness.
Exploit is a general word for using something unfairly; parasitize specifically means living on a host organism.

examples.everyday: Those mosquitoes basically parasitize the birds in our backyard every summer.
examples.professional: The ad network parasitizes publishers' traffic without sharing any of the revenue.
examples.analytical: Wasps parasitize caterpillars by laying eggs inside them, and the larvae feed on the host from within.

nuance.analogy: Like a squatter in a house: they live inside, use what is there, and leave the owner worse off.
nuance.etymology: From parasite plus -ize, meaning to act upon in the manner of.
common_mistakes: Using parasite as a verb ('parasite the host'); the correct verb is parasitize.
Stressing the -ize syllable instead of the first syllable.

senses.definition: Originally, one's oath or word of honor, given as a condition of release from custody; now specifically, describing the release of a former prisoner under certain conditions, especially the promise of good behavior.
senses.example: He will be on parole for nearly two more years.

senses.definition: Conditional release of a prisoner (now especially before the end of a custodial sentence), or the term or state of such release; the system governing such releases.
senses.example: He was granted parole after serving eight years of his twelve-year sentence.

senses.definition: Language in use, as opposed to language as a system.
senses.example: Linguists distinguish parole from langue when they analyze how speakers actually talk.

senses.definition: The permission for a foreigner who does not meet the technical requirements for a visa to be allowed to enter the U.S. on humanitarian grounds.
senses.example: The officer granted him parole into the country because his family needed urgent medical care.

senses.definition: (historical) A word of honor, especially given by a prisoner of war, to not engage in combat if released.
senses.example: The captured lieutenant gave his parole and was allowed to live in town.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (rare) A watchword or code phrase; a password given only to officers, distinguished from the countersign, which is given to all guards.
senses.example: The sentry demanded the parole before letting anyone pass through the gate.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To be released on parole.
senses.example: After two years of good behavior, he was paroled and returned to his mother's house.

senses.definition: To conditionally release an incarcerated person before completion of their sentence, subject to ongoing legal custody or supervision and compliance with specified terms of release.
senses.example: The board decided to parole the inmate, pending weekly check-ins with a supervising officer.

core.definition: Conditional early release of a prisoner under supervision, based on promised good behavior; to release someone on such terms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable ROHL, with a rhotic r and a clear l at the end. Do not add a vowel before the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal and official contexts; it can carry a negative association with crime and supervision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parole in courts, news reports, and criminal justice discussions. It refers to a supervised early release, not to a full pardon. People say he is up for parole or he was paroled. Probation is the related term for someone who is supervised instead of imprisoned.

distinctions.note: Probation is a sentence served in the community instead of prison; parole is release from prison before the sentence ends.
A pardon forgives the crime and removes the legal consequences; parole is a conditional release that continues supervision.

examples.everyday: My cousin was released on parole last year and has to check in with his officer every week.
examples.professional: The case manager reminded the client that his parole conditions include regular drug testing.
examples.analytical: The debate over parole reform often turns on whether rehabilitation or public safety should guide the decision.

nuance.analogy: Parole is like a leash on a dog let out of the yard: free to move, but still watched and required to come back if the rules are broken.
nuance.etymology: From Old French parole, word, from Latin parabola, speech, from Greek parabole; the legal sense began with a prisoner's word of honor.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like the English word pa-ROLE with a long o and a hard second syllable in a different place; the stress is on the single syllable.
Confusing parole with probation, which is a different sentence.

parole.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *parole* (“word, formal promise”), from Old French *parole*, from Late Latin *parabola* (“speech”), from Ancient Greek *παραβολή*.

senses.definition: Able to be parsed.
senses.example: Well-formed XML is an example of parsable text.

core.definition: Able to be analyzed into its grammatical or structural parts, so that a program or person can interpret it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the -able ending is reduced to a schwa plus /bəl/, not a stressed 'ay' sound. The American pronunciation rhymes the ending with 'syllable' in weak syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Parsable is the standard American spelling in dictionaries and most technical writing, though parseable also appears in software documentation. In programming, you often hear that data or a file is parsable or not. It is mostly used in technical settings, not casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Readable means easy for a human to read, while parsable means its structure can be analyzed by a program or grammar.
Valid means it follows the rules, while parsable means the structure can be broken down; a file can be parsable yet contain wrong data.

examples.professional: Make sure the export produces parsable JSON before the data pipeline tries to ingest it.
examples.analytical: A grammar is only useful when every well-formed sentence it generates is also parsable under its rules.

nuance.analogy: Like a sentence diagram, where every word has a clear, labeled place in the structure.
nuance.etymology: From parse (to analyze grammatically) plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -able ending or pronouncing it with a long a sound.
Mixing up parsable and parseable; both appear, but parsable is the more standard American dictionary spelling.

senses.definition: Remaining correlation of two random variables in a stochastic process after intervening random variables have been accounted for.
senses.example: In the time series model, the partial autocorrelation at lag three was close to zero.

core.definition: The correlation between a time series and its own value at a given lag, after removing the effects of the shorter lags in between.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AW in autocorrelation, and PAHR is the stressed syllable of partial. Say the -tial as shul, not shee-al, and remember that CORrelate shifts to correLAtion in the noun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this almost only in statistics, econometrics and time-series forecasting. People usually say the full phrase in papers and class, and the abbreviation PACF in software and reports. Outside data work, nobody uses it in conversation.

distinctions.note: The ordinary autocorrelation function measures correlation at each lag without removing intermediate lags; the partial version controls for them.
Partial correlation relates two different variables while holding others fixed; partial autocorrelation applies the same idea to one series at different lags.

examples.everyday: My coworker kept talking about partial autocorrelation at lunch, and I just nodded along.
examples.professional: The PACF plot shows one significant spike at lag 1 and nothing after, so an AR(1) model should fit the weekly sales data.
examples.analytical: Partial autocorrelation isolates the direct dependence between observations k periods apart, removing the influence of every intermediate lag.

nuance.analogy: Like tracing a rumor back to its source: you count only the person who told you directly, not the whole chain of people who passed it along.
nuance.etymology: Partial from Late Latin partialis ('of a part'); autocorrelation from Greek autos ('self') plus correlation, a relation between paired values.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing partial as PAR-shee-al instead of PAHR-shuhl
Confusing it with partial correlation, which concerns different variables rather than different lags
Writing it as one word or with a hyphen; it is two words

senses.definition: The condition of being penitent; a feeling of regret or remorse for doing wrong or sinning.

core.definition: Deep sorrow and regret for having done wrong or sinned, often with a desire to make things right.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowels. The -ence ending is a weak 'uns', not 'ance' or 'ents'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or solemn. It describes sincere sorrow for wrongdoing and is often used in religious or moral contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use penitence in religious writing, moral discussion, and literature. In daily speech they would say regret, remorse, or sorrow. Penitence can sound solemn, so it fits a sermon, an essay, or a formal apology better than casual talk.

distinctions.note: Remorse is a general feeling of guilt and is common in everyday speech. Penitence is more formal and implies a moral or religious turning toward making amends.
Penitence is the inner feeling of sorrow, while penance is the outward act done to express it.

examples.everyday: He apologized with real penitence after he broke the vase, and he offered to pay for a new one.
examples.professional: Our postmortem did not blame anyone, but the team showed penitence for skipping the review step.
examples.analytical: Augustine treats penitence not merely as an emotion but as a turning of the will toward God, which is why sorrow alone is insufficient.

nuance.analogy: Penitence is like a heavy heart that turns around and walks back toward home: the sorrow is the feeling, and the return is the change.
nuance.etymology: From Latin paenitentia, 'repentance', from paenitere 'to repent'.
common_mistakes: Using penitence for the act of penance rather than the feeling of sorrow.
Confusing penitence with penitentiary, the word for a prison.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV Bible uses repentance rather than penitence for the Greek metanoia, meaning a change of mind and heart toward God. Key passages are Matthew 3:8, where John the Baptist calls for fruit that befits repentance; Luke 15:7, where heaven rejoices over a sinner who repents; and 2 Corinthians 7:10, where Paul says godly grief produces a repentance without regret.

traditions.view: Orthodox teach that penitence is a continual change of heart and mind, expressed in confession, prayer, fasting, and the life of the Church. Sorrow for sin is seen as part of the healing of the whole person.

Catholics teach that penitence includes contrition, the sorrow and resolve not to sin again, which is joined to confession and satisfaction in the sacrament of Penance. Contrition is considered essential to forgiveness.

Most Protestants teach that penitence is a sincere repentance that flows from faith and the grace of God, rather than a work that earns forgiveness. Lutherans and Reformed differ on how the law and the gospel relate to sorrow for sin.

penitence.etymology: First attested circa 13th century, from Middle English *penitence*, from Old French *penitence*, from Latin *paenitentia* (“repentance, penitence”), from *paenitēns* (“penitent”), present active participle of *paeniteō* (“regret, repent”).

senses.definition: One who perambulates.
senses.example: The retired professor was a tireless perambulator, walking the city's parks every morning.

senses.definition: A surveyor's instrument for measuring distances, consisting of a wheel that rolls over the ground, along with a clockwork apparatus and a dial plate upon which the distance traveled is shown by an index.
senses.example: The county surveyor used a perambulator to measure the distance along the old boundary road.

core.definition: A measuring wheel that rolls along the ground and records the distance covered, used by surveyors.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'RAM'. Pronounce the 'r' clearly, and keep the last syllable weak, like 'ter'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'perambulator' for a baby carriage is mainly British; Americans say 'stroller' or 'baby carriage'. In US surveying and engineering the instrument is more often called a measuring wheel or surveyor's wheel. The sense of a person who walks about is rare.

distinctions.note: A measuring wheel is the common American name for the same kind of instrument, the one a crew would use on a road or job site.
A stroller is the American word for a baby carriage; 'perambulator' or 'pram' sounds British.

collocations: measuring the distance with a perambulator

examples.everyday: My neighbor, a retired surveyor, still has an old perambulator in his garage.
examples.professional: Before GPS, the crew used a perambulator to measure the length of the road along the ground.
examples.analytical: The perambulator translated wheel turns into distance, so its accuracy depended on the wheel's circumference.

nuance.analogy: Like a bicycle odometer on a wheel, counting every turn to tell you how far you have gone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perambulare, 'to walk through'.
common_mistakes: Using 'perambulator' for a baby carriage in American English, where 'stroller' is standard.
Stressing 'lay' instead of 'RAM'.
Confusing the noun with the verb 'perambulate'.

senses.definition: Lasting or remaining active throughout the year, for multiple years, or all the time.
senses.example: a perennial stream

senses.definition: Continuing without cessation or intermission for several years, or for an undetermined or infinite period; never-ending or never failing; perpetual, unceasing.
senses.example: His artwork has a perennial beauty.

senses.definition: Appearing or recurring again and again; recurrent.
senses.example: a perennial candidate in elections

senses.definition: Of a plant: active throughout the year, or having a life cycle of more than two growing seasons.
(rare) Appearing again each year; annual.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A thing that lasts forever.
A person or thing (such as a problem) that appears or returns regularly.
A plant that is active throughout the year, or has a life cycle of more than two growing seasons.

core.definition: Lasting or recurring year after year, or happening again and again over a long time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REN, the second syllable. The final syllable is reduced to 'ul', so it sounds like 'REN-ee-ul', not 'per-EN-ee-al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive for a lasting plant or tradition and negative for a recurring problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'perennial' for flowers that return each year, and for recurring issues like 'a perennial problem' or 'a perennial favorite'. It is common in news, business and everyday talk. Saying 'perennial' about a person who keeps appearing, like 'perennial candidate', is a casual but widely understood usage.

distinctions.note: An annual plant lives only one growing season, while a perennial comes back year after year.
Recurrent is a neutral term for happening again, while perennial often implies a long-lasting, persistent quality.

examples.everyday: Tomatoes are annuals, but the peonies in my yard are perennial and come back every spring.
examples.professional: Budget overruns are a perennial problem on this team, so we need a better forecasting process.
examples.analytical: The question of free will is perennial, returning in every century under new vocabulary.

nuance.analogy: A perennial is like a loyal friend who shows up at every family gathering year after year.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perennis, 'lasting through the year', from per 'through' and annus 'year'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'annual' when talking about plants.
Stressing the first syllable as 'PER-en-ial'.

perennial.etymology: The adjective is borrowed from Latin *perennis* (“lasting through the whole year or for several years, perennial; continual, everlasting, perpetual”) + *-al*.

senses.definition: Liable to perish, especially naturally subject to quick decomposition or decay.
senses.example: perishable goods

senses.definition: That which perishes or is short-lived.
senses.example: Youth is a perishable, and my grandmother often reminded us of that.

senses.definition: Food that does not keep for long.
senses.example: Keep the fresh fish on ice, since seafood is highly perishable in warm weather.

core.definition: Likely to decay, spoil, or go bad quickly, especially food; also short-lived or not built to last.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PAIR. The -shuh-buhl ending is weak and quick, and the r should be clear, not swallowed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It describes a quality, often with a note of concern for spoiling or loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use perishable mainly in shopping, grocery, shipping, and business settings, such as perishable goods or perishable items. In a store, a clerk might say these are perishable, so keep them cold. The noun form is rare and mostly literary.

distinctions.note: Spoiled describes food that has already gone bad; perishable describes food that is likely to go bad soon.
Durable means strong and long-lasting, the opposite quality of perishable.
Fresh describes food in a good, recently harvested state; perishable describes the risk of spoilage.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the milk and the strawberries? They're both perishable, so put them in the cooler bag.
examples.professional: Our shipping contract has a strict cold-chain requirement for perishable products to avoid spoilage claims.
examples.analytical: The author compares human memory to perishable goods, which decay unless they are carefully preserved.

nuance.analogy: A perishable item is like a carton of milk in a warm kitchen: it is fine now, but it has a short window before it turns.
nuance.etymology: From perish plus the suffix -able, meaning able to be perished or liable to decay.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as pe-RISH-uh-bul.
Using perishable to describe people or ideas in everyday speech, where it sounds strange or overly technical.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind perishable is phthartos (subject to decay, corruptible), describing things and bodies that wear out and decay. Matthew 6:19 warns against storing up treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, so that treasure is safe in heaven. 1 Corinthians 15:53 says this perishable nature must put on the imperishable, linking the future resurrection to the transformation of the mortal body. 1 Peter 1:18 says believers were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.

senses.definition: Lively and often cheerful and enthusiastic.
senses.example: She answered with a perky smile and bounced off.

senses.definition: Standing upright; firm.
senses.example: The plant looks much perkier since I watered it.

senses.definition: Early-ripening.
senses.example: Growers planted the perky apple variety because it ripens weeks before the others.

core.definition: Lively, cheerful, and full of energy, especially in a bright or upbeat way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress and the American r are on PUR. The final -y is a long ee, like key, not a short ih sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive to mildly negative. It usually describes a pleasant, lively mood, but can sound a bit too cheerful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use perky to describe a cheerful, energetic person, voice, or look, often at a time when others are tired, like early in the morning. It is informal and friendly. Calling someone perky can be a compliment or a light tease, depending on the tone.

distinctions.note: Cheerful describes a good mood in general; perky adds an image of bouncy, lively energy.
Chipper is also informal and cheerful, but it is more often said about someone who seems bright and alert after a long night.

examples.everyday: My sister is so perky in the morning, but I need at least an hour before I can talk.
examples.professional: The new hire has a perky energy in meetings that helps the team stay positive during long sprints.
examples.analytical: The narrator's perky tone makes the story's dark turns more unsettling, since the reader keeps expecting a cheerful resolution.

nuance.analogy: Perky is like a plant that stands up straight after a rain: it looks bright and lively, with energy in its shape.
nuance.etymology: From perk, from Middle English perk meaning pert or jaunty, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Saying the word with a stressed PER sound like pear; the vowel is ER, as in her.
Using perky to describe someone who is angry or sharp; it means cheerful and lively, not irritable.

senses.definition: In AI: A measure of how well a language model predicts text; lower perplexity means better prediction.
The state or quality of being perplexed.
senses.example: She stared at the proof with growing perplexity, unable to see where the error was.

senses.definition: Something that perplexes.
A measure of the accuracy with which a probability distribution or model predicts a sample.

core.definition: In AI, a score measuring how well a language model predicts text; lower perplexity means the model predicts the next word more accurately.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PLEK, and the final syllable is a light tee. Americans reduce the middle vowel, so avoid saying the middle syllable clearly as sih-tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In AI it is a technical measure; in everyday speech it means confusion.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and AI teams, Americans say perplexity almost always in the technical sense of model evaluation. In everyday talk the word is formal, so people usually say confusion. Note that a lower perplexity score is better, which often surprises learners.

distinctions.note: Confusion is everyday and general; perplexity in the AI sense is a precise numerical metric and is not a state of mind.
Accuracy measures how often predictions are correct; perplexity measures how uncertain the model is about the next token, so lower is better.

examples.everyday: I felt a sense of perplexity when the instructions changed twice in one afternoon.
examples.professional: Our new model reduced validation perplexity from 42 to 31, so it predicts the held-out text much better.
examples.analytical: Perplexity is a useful metric, but it does not directly measure whether a model's outputs are factually correct or useful.

nuance.analogy: Perplexity is like a quiz score for a model: the less surprised it is by the correct next word, the lower the score.
nuance.etymology: From perplex, from Latin perplexus, entangled, with the -ity noun suffix.
common_mistakes: Assuming higher perplexity is better; in language models, lower perplexity means better prediction.
Using perplexity to mean complexity in everyday talk, where it sounds formal and sometimes odd.

perplexity.etymology: From Middle English *perplexite*, borrowed from Middle French *perplexité* or post-classical Latin *perplexitās*, from *perplexus* (“entangled”).

conversation.text: Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token; lower is better.
Perplexity numbers aren't directly comparable across models with different tokenizers.
She stared at the error message in perplexity; the code hadn't changed at all.

senses.definition: Of a person: having a pleasing appearance; attractive; handsome.
senses.example: The new sales manager was charming, personable, and handsome, and everyone on the team liked him immediately.

senses.definition: Of a person: having a pleasant manner; amiable, friendly.
Synonym of personal (“done in person, without an intermediary”).
senses.example: The principal wanted a personable visit with each family, not just another form letter.

senses.definition: Being a legal person and thus able to maintain a plea in court, or to hold some property or right.
senses.example: Under the law, the company is a personable entity that can sue and own property.

core.definition: Pleasant, friendly, and easy to talk to; having an agreeable, approachable manner.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. In fast speech the middle syllable is often nearly silent, so it sounds like 'PURS-nuh-buhl', and the final -able is a weak schwa, not 'ay-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone for being warm and easy to deal with, but it is more modest than 'charming' or 'brilliant'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for people who are easy to get along with, especially in job interviews, reference letters, and casual talk about coworkers or neighbors. It describes a person, not a thing. The older sense of 'good-looking' is rarely used today in everyday American English.

distinctions.note: Friendly describes warmth in general, while personable adds the idea of being pleasant to deal with in a professional or first-meeting setting.
Charming suggests a strong, delightful appeal that can seem polished, while personable is plainer and more practical.

examples.everyday: Our new neighbor is really personable, so we invited her over for dinner next week.
examples.professional: The hiring manager said Dana was personable and clear in the interview, which helped her stand out from the other candidates.
examples.analytical: A personable person, in Aristotle's terms, shows settled goodwill in ordinary conduct rather than a performance staged for others.

nuance.analogy: A personable person is like a porch light left on: easy to approach and welcoming.
nuance.etymology: From person, from Latin persona (mask, character), plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'per-SOH-nuh-bul'.
Confusing it with 'personal', which means private or individual.

personable.etymology: From Late Middle English *personable*, *personabil* (“having a pleasing appearance, handsome”), and then from both of the following:

senses.definition: Clearly expressed, easy to understand; lucid.
(Of a language or notation) the process of inference from premises to conclusion is explicitly laid out.
senses.example: The notation is perspicuous: every inference from premises to conclusion is written out explicitly.

senses.definition: (rare) That can be seen through clearly; that lets light through.
senses.example: Through the perspicuous glass of the lantern, we could see the candle flickering steadily.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Clearly expressed and easy to understand; lucid. Used mostly for writing, arguments, and explanations.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPIK. Don't stress the first syllable or pronounce it as 'pair'; the first vowel is reduced to a short 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises writing or speech that is clear and precise, and it is rarely used for people in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in academic, philosophical, legal, or technical writing, and in reviews of prose. In everyday speech they would say clear, easy to follow, or straightforward. Using it in casual conversation can sound showy.

distinctions.note: Clear is everyday and covers all kinds of clarity; perspicuous is more formal and specifically describes clarity of expression.
Lucid can describe a clear mind or a calm, sensible moment as well as writing, while perspicuous applies only to expression and explanation.
Perspicacious means having sharp insight into people or situations; perspicuous means clearly written or stated. The two are often confused.

examples.everyday: Her email was so perspicuous that I didn't have to ask a single follow-up question.
examples.professional: The design doc is perspicuous enough that a new engineer could implement the service without a meeting.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein sought a perspicuous notation in which the logical form of propositions would become visible.

nuance.analogy: A perspicuous text is like a clean window: you look straight through it and see the idea without noticing the glass.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perspicuus, 'transparent, clear,' from perspicere, 'to see through.'
common_mistakes: Confusing perspicuous (clear) with perspicacious (insightful about people).
Stressing the first syllable as in 'PER-spi-cuous'.

perspicuous.etymology: From Latin *perspicuus*, in turn from *perspiciō* (“see through”).

senses.definition: Relating to the sounds of spoken language.
Relating to phones (as opposed to phonemes).
senses.example: The linguistics class studied phonetic transcription of vowels in several dialects.

senses.definition: Relating to the spoken rather than written form of a word or name, as opposed to orthographic.
senses.example: All unfamiliar names have been transcribed in phonetic spelling.

senses.definition: In such writing systems as the Chinese writing system, the portion of a phono-semantic character that provides an indication of its pronunciation; contrasted with semantic (which is usually the radical).
senses.example: In this character, the right-hand phonetic component hints at how it is pronounced.

core.definition: Relating to the actual sounds of speech, or written to show how a word is pronounced.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NET. The 'e' is short, as in 'bet'. Between vowels the 't' is often flapped, so it sounds like a soft 'd' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical word with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'phonetic' in linguistics, speech therapy and education, and in everyday talk about spelling, as in 'phonetic spelling' for how a word sounds. It does not mean 'simple' or 'easy', though learners sometimes assume that. In English, 'phonetic' often contrasts with spelling, since English spelling is not very phonetic.

distinctions.note: 'Phonetic' refers to actual physical sounds, while 'phonemic' refers to the sound units that distinguish meaning in a language.
'Phonics' is a method of teaching reading by connecting letters to sounds, while 'phonetic' describes sounds themselves.

examples.everyday: The menu had a phonetic spelling of the Italian dish, so I could finally say it right.
examples.professional: Our speech recognition model uses a phonetic lexicon to match words to the sounds people actually make.
examples.analytical: Phonetic evidence suggests the two vowels were once distinct, though the spelling hides that change.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe that tells you how the dish actually sounds when it is cooked, rather than how it is named on the menu.
nuance.etymology: From Greek phōnētikos, 'of sound or voice', from phōnē.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'phonetic' with 'phonemic'. Phonetic refers to actual sounds, while phonemic refers to sound categories that matter in a language.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'FOH-ne-tik'.

senses.definition: In a photographic manner.
Using photography.

core.definition: In a way that resembles a photograph, with extreme accuracy and detail; or by means of photography.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GRAF, and the -ically ending is usually reduced to ik-lee, with the middle vowel almost vanishing. Keep the r in graf, and do not stress the final -ly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually praises accuracy or describes a technical process.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use photographically in casual speech. It appears most often in art criticism, technical writing, or descriptions of rendering and imaging, where it means in a way that looks like a photograph. In everyday talk, say the picture looks like a photo or use an adjective such as photo-realistic.

distinctions.note: Realistically means in a way that is true to life, while photographically specifically suggests the precision of a camera image.
Accurately describes correctness in general, but photographically stresses visual exactness, like a copy of a scene.

examples.everyday: The painting looks photographically real from across the room, which is why people keep stopping to stare at it.
examples.professional: The design team wants the product shots rendered photographically, with natural shadows and sharp edges.
examples.analytical: The painter aimed to render the scene photographically, so that the canvas could pass for a camera's record of the moment.

nuance.analogy: Working photographically is like tracing the world through a window pane with a steady hand: nothing is added, and nothing is left out.
nuance.etymology: From photographic plus the suffix -ally, the adverb form of -ical.
common_mistakes: Using photographically in casual conversation where photo-realistic or like a photo would sound more natural.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the GRAF syllable.

senses.definition: Any compound that is a product of photosynthesis.

core.definition: Any organic compound, such as a sugar or starch, that a plant makes through photosynthesis and uses for growth or storage.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SIN, and the th is voiceless as in thin. The last syllable -ate is a clear ayt, not the reduced it used in words such as adjectives.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise botanical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use photosynthate almost only in biology, botany, agriculture, and plant science. Everyday speakers would say sugar or food the plant made. In a classroom, you will see the term in discussions of how plants move sugars from leaves to fruit or roots.

distinctions.note: Photosynthesis is the whole process by which plants make food from light, while a photosynthate is one of the products of that process.
Sugar is a general word for sweet carbohydrates in food, while photosynthate refers to any plant product made by photosynthesis, including starch and other compounds.

examples.everyday: My kid asked why the tree stores so much energy, so I explained that its leaves make photosynthates from sunlight.
examples.professional: The agronomy report measured how much photosynthate the wheat plants moved into the grain during flowering.
examples.analytical: Photosynthates link the energy of sunlight to the growth of the whole plant, and their transport shapes crop yield.

nuance.analogy: Photosynthates are like a paycheck that the leaves earn from sunlight and then spend or save throughout the plant.
nuance.etymology: From photosynthesis plus the chemical suffix -ate.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as putting the main stress on the last syllable.
Using photosynthate as a general word for food, when it refers to a specific plant product.

senses.definition: A restaurant that bakes and sells pizzas.

core.definition: A restaurant that makes and sells pizza, often a casual place where you can eat in or take food out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, 'REE'. Say the 'tz' sound as a single 'ts' blend, similar to 'pizza', and the final syllable is 'uh', not 'ee-ah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and casual. It suggests an inexpensive, friendly, family-style restaurant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say pizzeria for a place that specializes in pizza, often a small local shop, and it is a normal everyday word. Larger chain restaurants are usually called pizza places or by the brand name. In casual talk people often just say 'pizza' or 'let's get pizza'.

distinctions.note: Pizza place is the more casual, everyday American phrase; pizzeria sounds slightly more traditional or Italian.
Restaurant is general; pizzeria names a specific type of restaurant.
Trattoria is an Italian family-style restaurant serving a wider menu; a pizzeria focuses on pizza.

examples.everyday: Let's grab dinner at that little pizzeria on Fifth Street; their garlic knots are great.
examples.professional: Our team lunch is at the pizzeria across from the office, so let's meet there at noon.
examples.analytical: The rise of the independent pizzeria in American cities reflects a shift toward local, craft-based dining.

nuance.analogy: A pizzeria is to pizza what a bakery is to bread: a shop built around one main product.
nuance.etymology: From Italian pizzeria, a pizza shop, from pizza.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the 'z' as a plain 'z' sound; in pizza and pizzeria it is a 'ts' sound.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'PIT-suh-ree-uh'.

conversation.text: The pizzeria down the street sells pizza by the slice.
We ordered two large pies from our favorite pizzeria.
That little pizzeria makes its own dough every morning.

senses.definition: One who furnishes, fits, and repairs pipes and other apparatus for the conveyance of water, gas, or drainage.
senses.example: Mario and Luigi's profession is plumbers.

senses.definition: A person who investigates or prevents leaks of information.
senses.example: The security team hired a plumber to find who was leaking confidential memos to reporters.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of plumbers and firemen.
A urologist.
senses.example: After his blood test, the doctor referred him to a plumber for an enlarged prostate.

senses.definition: (dated) One who works in or with lead.
senses.example: In the 1820 parish ledger, the plumber was paid for sheets of lead.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To botch or ruin.
senses.example: Between the rushed deadline and the bad merge, he plumbed the whole release.

senses.definition: (rare) To work as a plumber.
senses.example: After the factory closed, he plumbed for a few years before returning to teaching.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To work on (something) as a plumber.
senses.example: He plumbed the old Victorian houses on our street, replacing every cast-iron pipe.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To do, work, devise (something).
senses.example: She plumbed a clever workaround so the script ran without the missing library.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To equip (something) with plumbing.
senses.example: The contractor plumbed the new basement bathroom before the electricians arrived.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A worker who installs and repairs pipes, faucets, and drains in houses and buildings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the last syllable a weak, rhotic 'er' sound. Do not pronounce the 'b' from the root 'plumb.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it refers to a respected skilled trade, though calling someone a plumber in a joke can imply a rough, practical job.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'plumber' for any professional who fixes water pipes or drains, and calling one for an emergency at home is very normal. People also say 'plumber's helper' or 'plumbing company.' The phrase 'a plumber's crack' is a crude joke, so avoid repeating it in polite company.

distinctions.note: Plumber is the person; plumbing is the system of pipes or the trade.
An electrician works on wires and power; a plumber works on water, gas, and drainage.

examples.everyday: Our kitchen sink is leaking, so we need to call a plumber before the floor gets wet.
examples.professional: The property manager asked the plumber to inspect the building's water lines before the inspection.
examples.analytical: The plumber's trade depends on detailed knowledge of pressure, materials, and building codes, not only on manual skill.

nuance.analogy: A plumber is like a doctor for a house's circulatory system, diagnosing where the flow is blocked.
nuance.etymology: From Latin plumbarius, a worker in lead, from plumbum (lead), since early pipes were made of lead.
common_mistakes: Saying 'plum-ber' with a 'b' sound at the end.
Using 'plumber' for an electrical problem; Americans call that an electrician.

plumber.etymology: From Middle English *plumber*, from Old French *plummier* (French *plombier*); from Latin *plumbārius*, from *plumbum* (“lead or lead shot”).

conversation.text: We need to call a plumber; the water heater is leaking.
The plumber said he could come Tuesday morning.
Plumbers charge a lot for weekend visits.

senses.definition: (poetic) Too deep to be plumbed.
senses.example: The poet described the plumbless ocean trench, a dark depth no sounding line had ever measured.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: Too deep to be measured or reached, especially in a literary or figurative sense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the ending a short, unstressed 'lis.' The middle 'l' is clear, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests vast, mysterious depths.
nuance.usage_note: 'Plumbless' is rare in American speech and writing. It appears mostly in poetry, fiction, or deliberately elevated prose. Everyday speakers would say 'bottomless' or 'unfathomable' instead. Use it only when you want a literary effect.

distinctions.note: Bottomless is common and can be literal or figurative; plumbless is more literary and emphasizes that depth cannot be measured.
Unfathomable is widely used for things that cannot be understood; plumbless is closer to the literal idea of unmeasured depth.

examples.professional: The report describes the plumbless uncertainty in the market, which makes forecasting difficult.
examples.analytical: The poem speaks of a plumbless grief that resists any attempt at measurement or consolation.

nuance.analogy: A plumbless sea is like a well with no visible bottom, where your weighted line never reaches the floor.
nuance.etymology: From plumb (a weight used to measure depth) plus the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Using 'plumbless' in casual conversation, where 'bottomless' sounds more natural.
Pronouncing the 'b' in 'plumb' because of the spelling.

senses.definition: Exaggerated speech or gestures used for emphasis during a performance.
senses.example: The actor overdid his points, waving his arms and shouting every line.

core.definition: Reward units earned through purchases that can be redeemed for discounts, products or other benefits, such as in a store's loyalty program.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a diphthong: 'oy' is a single glide from 'aw' to 'ee', not two separate sounds. Keep the final 'nts' cluster clear, without adding a vowel before the 's'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: points signal savings and value. The word is neutral in most contexts, but in a non-shopping sense it can mean sharp remarks or matters, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say points for loyalty or rewards credits at stores, airlines and credit cards, for example 'Do you have any points on your card?' At the register, a cashier may ask 'Do you want to use your points?' A natural reply is 'Yes, please' or 'Not today, thanks.'

distinctions.note: Coupons give a fixed discount on a specific item, while points accumulate over time and are redeemed for rewards.
Miles are the points used by airline and travel programs; points is the general term for most reward programs.

examples.everyday: I'm buying this at the grocery store because I still have enough points to get a discount.
examples.professional: Our finance team reported that the points redemption rate rose after we changed the reward tiers.
examples.analytical: Loyalty points function as a deferred form of price reduction, so their value depends on how easily consumers can redeem them.

nuance.analogy: Points are like tokens in an arcade: you collect them slowly, and you spend them later on something you want.
nuance.etymology: Plural of point, from Latin punctum, 'a prick or dot'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I have many points' in a shopping context without specifying the program; say 'I have a lot of points' or 'I have enough points' instead.
Confusing points with coupons; points are earned over time, not a one-time discount.

conversation.text: You earn two points for every dollar you spend.
I used my points to get twenty dollars off.
Do my points expire at the end of the year?

senses.definition: Resembling a poltroon; cowardly.
senses.example: He felt poltroonish for hiding behind the door instead of defending his friend.

core.definition: Cowardly, timid, and lacking the courage to face danger, difficulty or responsibility.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TROON. The final -ish is short, and the vowel is like the i in 'sit.'

nuance.connotation: Negative and somewhat contemptuous. It is a bookish insult and usually describes behavior rather than a whole person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans recognize poltroonish but rarely use it in speech. You will find it in literary prose, essays and older writing. In everyday conversation say cowardly, or scared, which is softer. Use poltroonish only when you want a formal or literary tone.

distinctions.note: Cowardly is the everyday word; poltroonish is a bookish synonym with a more contemptuous flavor.
Timid describes shyness or nervousness, often mild, while poltroonish implies a moral failure to face danger.

examples.professional: Leadership's poltroonish decision to delay the announcement left the engineers exposed to angry customers.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the poltroonish temper of the age was less about fear of death than about fear of commitment.

nuance.analogy: A poltroonish person is like a swimmer who stays on the dock while everyone else is already in the lake.
nuance.etymology: From poltroon, from Italian poltrone 'coward,' plus the adjective suffix -ish.
common_mistakes: Spelling it with one o; the oo is required in poltroonish.
Using it for mild shyness; it implies cowardice, which can sound harsh in casual talk.

senses.definition: Of or relating to polyphony.
senses.example: a polyphonic ringtone

senses.definition: Able to play more than one musical note at the same time.
senses.example: The synthesizer's polyphonic mode lets it play several notes at the same time.

senses.definition: Capable of being read in more than one way.
senses.example: The novel's polyphonic ending can be read as either a tragedy or a quiet triumph.

senses.definition: Having two or more independent but harmonic melodies.

core.definition: Relating to polyphony: music made of two or more independent melodic lines sounding together.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on FAH, the third syllable, with a lighter stress on POL. Don't stress the -ic ending, and keep the first vowel short and open as in 'pop'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and specialized. It sounds precise and somewhat technical, and it is usually a term of praise when applied to writing or music.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in music theory, choral singing, musicology and literary criticism. In everyday talk people say 'layered' or 'many-voiced' instead. The second sense, able to play several notes at once, is most often heard in technical talk about synthesizers or old phone ringtones.

distinctions.note: Homophonic music has one main melody with chords beneath it; polyphonic music has several melodies that move independently.
Monophonic music has a single melodic line with no accompanying voices, which is the opposite texture.
Polyphony is the musical texture or style itself, while polyphonic is the adjective describing it.

examples.everyday: My old phone had a polyphonic ringtone, so it played little chords instead of a single beep.
examples.professional: The audio team wants the product demo to highlight the polyphonic sound of the new synthesizer.
examples.analytical: Bach's fugues are often cited as the high point of polyphonic writing, because each voice keeps its own melodic identity.

nuance.analogy: A polyphonic piece is like a lively conversation in which several people speak at once, yet each sentence stays clear.
nuance.etymology: From Greek polyphōnos, 'many-voiced', from poly- 'many' and phōnē 'voice, sound'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the last syllable or on the wrong vowel; the main stress is on FAH, the third syllable.
Using polyphonic to mean 'having many speakers' or 'multilingual'; it refers to independent melodic lines or to multiple readings.

senses.definition: Someone who exhibits ungracious behavior during a game, whether winning or losing.
Someone who cannot take a joke.

core.definition: A person who behaves badly or ungraciously during a game, whether winning or losing, or who cannot take a joke.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SPORT, while poor keeps a lighter secondary stress and is not reduced. Pronounce the r in both words and avoid stretching the vowel of poor into pool.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a poor sport is a mild criticism, but it can sting, especially among adults.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use poor sport in casual talk about games, sports, board games and family activities, often as a light criticism. It can hurt, so save it for friends and family rather than using it in front of a boss or colleague. A natural reply is Fair enough, or You're right, I was being a sore loser.

distinctions.note: A sore loser is bitter only after losing, while a poor sport can be ungracious whether winning or losing.
Good sport is the positive opposite, describing someone who accepts teasing or defeat cheerfully.

collocations: take it like a good sport

examples.everyday: Don't be a poor sport, it was just a board game and you can still win next time.
examples.professional: When the team lead overruled the vote, Marcus sulked through the rest of the sprint review, and people stopped calling him a good sport.
examples.analytical: To call someone a poor sport is to suggest that fair play is more than following the rules; it is a disposition of respect toward others.

nuance.analogy: A poor sport is like a bad dinner guest at a game night: the game is fine, but the attitude spoils it for everyone.
nuance.etymology: Sport comes from Middle English disport, from Anglo-French desport, meaning amusement or pleasure. The phrase pairs poor with that sense of play.
common_mistakes: Using poor sport for someone who is simply unlucky or quiet; it describes behavior during a game, not a person's skill.
Saying poor sports for the singular person; the phrase is usually singular in this sense: he is a poor sport.
Pronouncing sport with a long o; the vowel is the aw of thought, as in sport /spɔɹt/.

senses.definition: After death.

core.definition: After a person has died, especially used for an award, honor, pardon, or publication that is given or released after the death.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel in 'post' is the American 'ah' sound. The 'th' in the middle is pronounced 'ch', so say 'PAHST-chuh-muss-lee', not 'POST-hyoo-mus-lee' in the British way.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to respectful; it is often used when honoring someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mostly in news and ceremonies, such as 'He was awarded the medal posthumously.' In casual talk people say 'after he died' or 'after his death'. It applies to awards, publications, and recognitions, not ordinary events.

distinctions.note: Postmortem can mean an autopsy or, more broadly, after death, while posthumously focuses on recognition or publication after death.
After death is plain and everyday, while posthumously is more formal and usually used for honors and publications.

examples.everyday: My grandfather received a military medal posthumously, and the whole family cried at the ceremony.
examples.professional: The foundation will name its research award after him and honor him posthumously for his work on drought models.
examples.analytical: The novel was published posthumously, so its reception depended on readers who never met the author.

nuance.analogy: Like a letter delivered after the sender has left: the words arrive, but the author does not.
nuance.etymology: From posthumous (from Latin postumus, 'last, following') plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using it for any later action, as in 'I'll finish the report posthumously'; it refers only to after death.
Using a British 'yoo' vowel in the middle, saying 'POST-hyoo-mus' instead of 'PAHST-chuh-mus'.

senses.definition: Having its own source of power, or a named source.
senses.example: Our new solar-powered garden lights switch on automatically at dusk.

core.definition: Operated by a particular source of energy, such as electricity, batteries, or an engine.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on POW, and the word has only one syllable after it, with the -ed pronounced as a plain d.ɚd/ lacked stress, so the correct form is /ˈpaʊɚd/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it simply describes how something runs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use powered mostly in compound adjectives such as battery-powered, solar-powered, gas-powered, and human-powered. It describes what drives a machine or device. Battery-operated is also common for small devices, and electric is used for vehicles and appliances in general. Alone, powered sounds a bit more formal, as in 'a powered wheelchair.'

distinctions.note: Battery-operated is the everyday phrase for toys, clocks and small gadgets; powered is more general and can refer to engines or motors as well.
Electric describes something that runs on electricity in general; powered names the specific source of energy that drives it.
Motorized means equipped with a motor; powered can mean driven by a motor, but also by batteries, solar panels or water.

examples.everyday: Our garage door is battery-powered, so it still works during a power outage.
examples.professional: We chose a solar-powered sensor node for the remote monitoring network because it requires no field maintenance.
examples.analytical: A system powered by renewable energy raises questions about storage and intermittency that a grid-connected system can often avoid.

nuance.analogy: A powered bike is like a bicycle with a helper motor: the rider still steers, but the engine supplies much of the effort.
nuance.etymology: From the verb power, from Old French poeir, from Latin potere, 'to be able,' plus the -ed participle ending.
common_mistakes: Saying 'powered on' to describe the energy source; the usual phrase is 'powered by,' as in 'powered by solar energy.'
Pronouncing it as two syllables, 'POW-er-ed'; it is one syllable after the stress, 'POW-erd.'

senses.definition: In a practicable manner.

core.definition: In a way that can actually be done in real conditions; as far as is feasible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PRAK. The -ti- and -ca- syllables are weak, and the final -ably is a reduced 'uh-blee', not 'AY-blee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes what is achievable, usually in a formal or official tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use practicably mostly in formal writing, policy, and phrases like 'as soon as practicably possible'. In casual talk, people say 'as soon as possible' or 'as soon as we can'. It is correct but can sound bureaucratic in conversation.

distinctions.note: Practicably means feasibly, in a way that can be done; practically means almost, or in effect, and is far more common in everyday speech.
Possibly describes what might happen; practicably describes what can realistically be carried out given real conditions.

examples.everyday: I'll call you back as soon as practicably possible, probably after my meeting.
examples.professional: The team will deploy the security fix as soon as practicably possible after testing.
examples.analytical: Such a policy cannot practicably be enforced across every jurisdiction without enormous expense.

nuance.analogy: Practicably is like a route map that avoids roads that exist only on paper: it shows what you can really travel.
nuance.etymology: From practicable plus -ly; practicable is from Late Latin practicabilis, meaning able to be done.
common_mistakes: Confusing practicably with practically, which is far more common and means almost or in effect.
Using it casually where 'as soon as possible' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Characterized by exceptionally early development or maturity.
senses.example: The precocious plant was already blooming flowers by day 4.

senses.definition: Exhibiting advanced skills and aptitudes at an abnormally early age.
senses.example: The precocious child began reading the newspaper at age four.

core.definition: Developing or showing skills, maturity or knowledge unusually early, especially in a child.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the middle syllable, -KOH-. The final syllables are reduced to 'shus', so do not pronounce a full 'ee' ending.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive when describing a talented child, but it can sound slightly negative if it implies a child is acting too grown-up or showing off.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'precocious' for children who read early, play an instrument well or speak like adults. Parents and teachers say it warmly, but calling a child 'precocious' to mean 'bratty' can also happen. It is less common for adults; for them, 'early-developing' or 'advanced for his age' is more natural.

distinctions.note: 'Gifted' describes high ability in general, while 'precocious' focuses specifically on developing that ability unusually early.
'Talented' describes skill without any reference to age; 'precocious' always implies that the skill appeared earlier than expected.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's six-year-old is so precocious that she already reads chapter books.
examples.professional: The school placed the precocious student in the advanced math track after her diagnostic test results.
examples.analytical: Mill treats precocious intellectual development as a test case for whether education shapes talent or merely reveals it.

nuance.analogy: A plant that blooms in early March while everything else is still frozen: it is ready before its season.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praecox, 'ripening early', from prae 'before' and coquere 'to cook or ripen'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'precocious' with 'precious', which means valuable or dearly loved.
Stressing the final syllable as in 'pre-co-SHUS'; the stress is in the middle.

precocious.etymology: From Latin *praecox* (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from *praecoquō* (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from *prae* (“before”) + *coquō* (“to cook, boil, ripen”).

senses.definition: The quality of being premature.

core.definition: The quality of being too early or too hasty, happening before the right time or before something is ready.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -ture syllable, which sounds 'chur' as in 'nature'; the first syllable has light secondary stress. The -ness ending is weak, so say 'nus', not a strong 'ness'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it names a quality of being too early or hasty, which usually carries an implied criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'prematureness' in conversation; they say 'the decision was premature' or 'it's too early to say'. For babies born early, the standard medical term is 'prematurity', not 'prematureness'. The noun appears mainly in formal writing when someone wants to discuss timing as an abstract quality.

distinctions.note: Prematurity is the standard noun, especially for infants born early; prematureness is rarer and more abstract.
Haste is acting too quickly; prematureness describes a timing problem, which may or may not involve haste.
Precocity is unusually early development in a person, usually positive; prematureness usually describes something that happened too soon.

examples.professional: Several reviewers flagged the prematureness of the launch date, given the open questions about testing.
examples.analytical: The prematureness of the theological conclusion lies less in its content than in the thin evidence on which it rests.

nuance.analogy: Like picking an apple before it ripens: it is technically fruit, but it is not ready to eat.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praematurus 'too early, overripe', from prae 'before' plus maturus 'ripe'.
common_mistakes: Using 'prematureness' for infants, where 'prematurity' is the standard term.
Saying the -ture ending as 'TOOR' or 'tyoor' instead of 'chur'.

senses.definition: Of the nature of a presentiment; foreboding.
senses.example: She had a presentimental chill that the storm would ruin the wedding, and it did.

core.definition: Having a vague, uneasy feeling that something bad is about to happen; foreboding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEN, the fourth syllable, with reduced vowels in the earlier syllables. Keep the middle syllables short, so the word does not sound like a sequence of equally strong vowels.

nuance.connotation: Negative and somber, suggesting dread about the future.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use presentimental in speech; it appears mostly in older or literary writing. The more common American word is presentiment, or they might say 'a bad feeling' or 'a sense of dread.' Use presentimental only when you want a literary or philosophical tone.

distinctions.note: Presentiment is the noun for the uneasy feeling itself, while presentimental describes something that has that quality.
Foreboding is more common in everyday American English and describes the same dread; presentimental is more literary and rare.

examples.professional: The team's presentimental mood before the launch was unfounded, since the test results were actually strong.
examples.analytical: The novel's presentimental atmosphere makes the reader sense catastrophe long before any character names it.

nuance.analogy: Like the stillness in the air before a thunderstorm, when you feel the weather change before you see clouds.
nuance.etymology: From presentiment, from French pressentiment, from pressentir, 'to feel beforehand,' from Latin praesentire.
common_mistakes: Using presentimental as a common everyday word; Americans usually say foreboding or uneasy.
Confusing it with presentable or presentational; the meanings are unrelated.

senses.definition: At an earlier time; already.
senses.example: The discovery of a previously unknown species had taken place nearly two years previously.

senses.definition: Recapitulating the preceding episodes of a series.
senses.example: Previously on the show, the detective discovered the body in the lake.

core.definition: At an earlier time; before now.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PREE-. The middle syllables are quick and light, and the final '-ly' is a clear 'lee' sound, not 'lih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it reports an earlier time or action without emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use previously in writing, reports, emails and formal speech: 'as previously stated'. In casual conversation, 'before' or 'I've already' is more natural. TV recaps often begin with 'Previously, on...', which is a familiar American phrase.

distinctions.note: Before is simple and natural in speech; previously is more formal and fits written reports better.
Formerly refers to an earlier status or role ('formerly a teacher'); previously refers to an earlier time or action.

examples.everyday: I've previously eaten at that restaurant, and the pasta is great.
examples.professional: As previously discussed in the meeting, the vendor contract will be signed by Friday.
examples.analytical: Previously held views about free will were challenged by later neuroscience, which the author summarizes with care.

nuance.analogy: Like a receipt from an earlier purchase: the event has already happened and cannot be changed.
nuance.etymology: From previous, with the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using previously in casual speech where before is more natural.
Placing previously too far from the verb it modifies, which can make a sentence unclear.

senses.definition: Any function whose integral over a set gives the probability that a random variable has a value in that set.

core.definition: A nonnegative function whose integral over an interval gives the probability that a continuous random variable falls in that interval.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress in 'probability' falls on 'bil', and 'density' stresses its first syllable. The -ity ending is a light 'tee', and 'function' has a strong 'fungk' before the 'shun' ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in statistics, engineering, and data science courses and papers. Engineers and data scientists often write its abbreviation PDF, which they say letter by letter, and it must not be confused with the portable document format. For discrete outcomes Americans use probability mass function, so choose the term that fits the variable.

distinctions.note: A PDF applies to continuous variables and gives density rather than a probability at a single point; a mass function applies to discrete variables and gives exact probabilities.
A CDF gives the probability that a variable is less than or equal to a value, while a PDF is its rate of change, or density.
A distribution is the complete assignment of probabilities, and a PDF is one way to describe a continuous distribution.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked why the bell curve is called a probability density function, so I explained that it shows how likely different values are.
examples.professional: Before we fit the model, we need to check the probability density function of the sensor noise, since the errors are not symmetric.
examples.analytical: A probability density function must be nonnegative and integrate to one over the whole real line.

nuance.analogy: A probability density function is like a sand pile: the height at each point tells you how much sand is there, and the amount in any region comes from adding up the sand in that region.
nuance.etymology: Probability comes from Latin probabilitas, density from Latin densitas, meaning thickness, and function from Latin functio, meaning performance.
common_mistakes: Treating the value of a PDF at a point as a probability; the probability of any single exact value of a continuous variable is zero.
Stressing 'PRO' in probability or saying 'PRAH-buh-bil-ih-tee' with the wrong vowel in the middle; the stress belongs on 'BIL'.

senses.definition: Someone who returns home from traveling or exile or who is welcomed back after disgrace, especially having repented of former extravagant or immoral behavior.
senses.example: After ten years away, the prodigal son finally drove back home to ask his father's forgiveness.

senses.definition: A marine fish, the cobia (Rachycentron canadum).
senses.example: Charter captains off the Carolinas often catch a prodigal son while fishing for grouper.

core.definition: A person who returns home after wasteful, reckless living and is welcomed back with forgiveness, especially after repenting of past misconduct.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SON, the main word, with a lighter secondary stress on PROD. Say the flapped t-less 'prodigal' with a clear, reduced final syllable, so it sounds like 'prah-dih-gul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or sympathetic, since the phrase celebrates forgiveness and return, though the story begins with wasteful behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for anyone who comes back after a long absence or estrangement, often with a hint of warm forgiveness. It appears in sermons, family conversation, and news stories about reconciliation. A natural reply, when someone describes a returning relative, is 'Well, it's good to have him back.'

distinctions.note: A black sheep is a family member who is disgraced or disapproved of, but the phrase does not imply a return or forgiveness as the prodigal son does.
A prodigy is a person of exceptional talent, usually young, with no link to wrongdoing or repentance.

collocations: the parable of the prodigal son

examples.everyday: My cousin finally came back to town after five years, and Mom threw a party like he was the prodigal son.
examples.professional: Our former engineer rejoined the team last month, and the manager joked that he was the prodigal son of the data group.
examples.analytical: The parable of the prodigal son invites readers to examine how the father's unconditional welcome reframes the younger son's repentance.

nuance.analogy: Like a lost sheep found and brought back into the fold, the prodigal son's homecoming turns the story from loss to celebration.
nuance.etymology: From the Latin prodigus, meaning wasteful or lavish, from prodigere, to drive forth or squander.
common_mistakes: Saying 'prodigy son' when meaning someone who returns; 'prodigy' means a talented young person.
Stressing the first word too heavily, making the phrase sound like 'PRAH-dih-gul SON' with equal emphasis.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase comes from Jesus' parable in Luke 15:11-32, which the RSV calls the parable of the lost son, and the Greek word asōtōs (loosely, in a dissolute or wasteful way) describes the younger son's life in Luke 15:13. In Luke 15:20, the father runs to embrace the son before he can finish his speech, showing that the return is met with grace. In Luke 15:32, the father tells the older brother that it was right to rejoice because the son who was lost has been found. Note that the RSV does not use the word 'prodigal' in the text; the title is a later convention.

senses.definition: A declaration of faith.
senses.example: She died only a few years after her profession.

senses.definition: A promise or vow made on entering a religious order.
senses.example: She died only a few years after her profession.

senses.definition: The declaration of belief in the principles of a religion; hence, one's faith or religion.
Any declaration of belief, faith or one's opinion, whether genuine or (as now often implied) pretended.
senses.example: Despite his continued professions of innocence, the court eventually sentenced him to five years.

senses.definition: A professional occupation.
senses.example: My father was a barrister by profession.

senses.definition: An occupation, trade, craft, or activity in which one has a professed expertise in a particular area; a job, especially one requiring a high level of skill or training.
senses.example: My father was a barrister by profession.

senses.definition: The practitioners of such an occupation collectively.
senses.example: His conduct is against the established practices of the legal profession.

core.definition: A public declaration of one's religious faith, or a formal vow taken on entering a religious order.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FESH, and the final syllable is a weak 'uhn', so the word sounds like pruh-FESH-un rather than pro-FESS-ee-on. Keep the sh sound clean.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to solemn. In religious use it signals sincere, public commitment. In everyday talk the occupational sense is neutral and slightly formal.
nuance.usage_note: In religious contexts Americans speak of professing faith or taking religious vows. In ordinary speech, profession usually means one's line of work, but people more often say job, work, or what someone does. The occupational sense appears naturally in forms and formal writing, such as Profession: teacher.

distinctions.note: Occupation is the formal word for a job category in forms and statistics, while profession suggests specialized training and a recognized body of knowledge.
Vocation stresses a sense of calling, often religious, while profession emphasizes a public declaration or a formal line of work.

examples.everyday: At the Bible study, Maria shared how her profession of faith at sixteen changed the way she saw her family.
examples.professional: In the seminary course, we compared the profession of faith in Acts with the confessions of later centuries.
examples.analytical: A profession of faith is more than assent to propositions; it is a public act that binds the believer to a community.

nuance.analogy: Like signing a contract in front of witnesses, a profession makes a private conviction public and binding.
nuance.etymology: From Latin professio 'public declaration', from profiteri 'to declare publicly'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'my profession is teacher' in casual talk; Americans say 'I'm a teacher' or 'I teach'.
Confusing profession with confession, the English word for the Greek homologia, which is a separate term in Scripture translations.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek term behind profession is homologia, meaning confession or acknowledgment; the Revised Standard Version usually renders it confession rather than profession. Key passages: 1 Timothy 6:12 describes Timothy's good confession made before many witnesses; Hebrews 4:14 urges believers to hold fast their confession; Hebrews 10:23 calls them to hold fast the confession of their hope without wavering.

traditions.view: Religious profession is the public vow of poverty, chastity and obedience taken by members of religious institutes, first for a temporary period and later perpetually, usually after a novitiate.
Monastic profession includes tonsure and vows of obedience, celibacy and poverty, given in stages such as rassophore and stavrophore, and is understood as a lifelong commitment.

Most Protestant churches do not treat profession as monastic vows; a profession of faith is usually a public confession at baptism, confirmation or church membership. Some Anglican, Lutheran and ecumenical communities such as Taizé do take vows.

senses.definition: Capable of being programmed.
senses.example: The new thermostat is programmable, so it lowers the heat automatically at night.

senses.definition: A calculator that allows the user to write programs.
senses.example: In college he saved for months to buy a programmable that could store formulas.

core.definition: Able to be set up with a series of instructions so that a machine or device can perform specific tasks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PRO-, and the -ma- and -ble endings are both reduced. Say four syllables: PROH-gram-uh-bul, with the middle vowel short, like 'ram', not 'may'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and positive, suggesting flexibility and customization.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use programmable mostly for devices and systems: a programmable thermostat, a programmable logic controller or a programmable calculator. It is rarely used for people. In a store you might ask 'Is this thermostat programmable?' and a natural answer is 'Yes, you can set a different schedule for each day.'

distinctions.note: Programmed means already set with instructions; programmable means able to be set by the user or engineer.
Configurable means adjustable through preset options; programmable implies writing custom instructions or sequences.
Automatic runs by default without user input; programmable can be changed by the user to suit different needs.

examples.everyday: We bought a programmable thermostat so the heat turns down before we wake up.
examples.professional: The new sensor is programmable over the network, so we can change the thresholds without a site visit.
examples.analytical: A Turing machine is a programmable device in the broad sense that its behavior is fixed by a finite table of instructions.

nuance.analogy: A programmable device is like a blank music box cylinder: the mechanism stays the same, but the pins you set decide the tune.
nuance.etymology: From program plus the suffix -able, meaning 'able to be programmed.'
common_mistakes: Using programmable to describe people; say coachable or trainable instead.
Pronouncing the middle syllable -ma- as 'may'; it is a short a, as in 'cat'.

senses.definition: One who writes computer programs.
One who decides which programs will be shown on a television station, or which songs will be played on a radio station.
senses.example: The station's programmer decided to move the drama series to Thursday nights for better ratings.

senses.definition: A device that installs or controls a software program in some other machine.
senses.example: The technician used a programmer to load new firmware onto the thermostat before the store opened.

senses.definition: (rare) A short film feature as part of a longer film program.
senses.example: The theater's evening programmer opened with a six-minute short about local wildlife before the feature.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A person who writes computer programs or software code.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PRO-, and the final -er is a reduced, rhotic 'ur'. Pronounce the r clearly and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a skilled professional, though some tech workers prefer developer or engineer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use programmer broadly for people who write code, but job titles often say software engineer or developer. In tech job postings, developer is more common. In casual talk, 'I'm a programmer' is natural, and coder is an informal alternative.

distinctions.note: An engineer designs, tests and maintains whole systems; a programmer usually focuses more narrowly on writing code.
Developer is the common US job title for people who build software, often with a broader role than programmer.
Coder is informal and can sound slightly dismissive; programmer is the standard word.

examples.everyday: My brother is a programmer at a bank, so he's always debugging something late at night.
examples.professional: We need a second programmer on the payments team before the release next month.
examples.analytical: A good programmer must reason precisely about what a program actually does, not just what its author intended it to do.

nuance.analogy: A programmer is to software what a recipe writer is to a meal: they decide every step the machine will follow.
nuance.etymology: From program, with the agent suffix -er meaning 'one who does the action.'
common_mistakes: Spelling it programer with one m; the standard American spelling has a double m.
Using programmer for a TV schedule planner in tech settings, which causes confusion; say scheduler or programming director instead.

senses.definition: An eigenvector.

core.definition: In linear algebra, an eigenvector: a nonzero vector that a square matrix only scales, not turns, when multiplied by it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on VEK in vector, and the first word is lightly stressed. The final -or is an unstressed r-colored vowel, so say VEK-ter, not VEK-tor.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, but dated.
nuance.usage_note: Modern American mathematicians say eigenvector. Proper vector is a dated term found in older textbooks and translations of German works. Recognize it when you read older texts, but in your own writing and in meetings, use eigenvector.
