distinctions.note: The two terms have the same meaning, but eigenvector is the current standard and proper vector is dated.
A vector is any element of a vector space, while an eigenvector is a special vector that a matrix only scales, which is what gives it its name.

collocations: proper vector associated with an eigenvalue

examples.everyday: My old statistics textbook calls it a proper vector, so I had to look up the modern name.
examples.professional: In the meeting I'll say eigenvector, since proper vector sounds dated to the rest of the team.
examples.analytical: Each proper vector of the transition matrix spans an invariant direction, and the long-run behavior of the system follows from those directions.

nuance.analogy: A proper vector is an arrow the matrix can stretch or shrink but never turn, like a flag that only gets longer in a steady wind.
nuance.etymology: Translation of German Eigenvektor, from eigen (own) and Vektor (vector).
common_mistakes: Using proper vector in a modern paper or talk, where eigenvector is expected.
Mispronouncing vector as VEK-tor; the final syllable is an unstressed r-colored er.

senses.definition: Someone who protects or guards, by assignment or on their own initiative.
senses.example: She was hired as a protector for the senator during the campaign.

senses.definition: A headmate who primarily fronts, or otherwise protects the system, in situations where the system is at risk of psychological harm.
senses.example: In our system, Ivy usually fronts as the protector whenever stressful memories surface.

senses.definition: A device or mechanism which is designed to protect.
senses.example: Always wear a protector over the lens when welding to shield your eyes.

senses.definition: One who prevents interference. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: Judges serve as protectors of the election process, preventing any outside interference with ballot counts.

senses.definition: A state or other subject under international law, exercising a protectorate over another subject in international law.
senses.example: The treaty made the larger nation the protector of the smaller state's foreign affairs.

senses.definition: A cardinal, from one of the more considerable Roman Catholic nations, who looks after the interests of his people at Rome; also, a cardinal who has the same relation to a college, religious order, etc.
senses.example: The cardinal protector represented the Spanish crown's interests at the papal court in Rome.

core.definition: A person or thing that guards, defends or keeps something safe from harm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on TEK. The final -or is a reduced r-colored vowel, so say it as ter, not tor, and keep the r clearly audible.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests care, responsibility and safety, though a protector can also be overbearing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use protector for people who guard children, property or the environment, and for things like a screen protector or a shield. In casual speech a parent might be called a protector, and the word is warm and positive. In the Bible, God is often described as a protector.

distinctions.note: A guardian has legal responsibility for someone, usually a minor; a protector may have no legal role.
A defender is someone who fights against an attack; a protector is broader and may prevent harm rather than respond to it.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was always the protector of the family, making sure everyone got home safe.
examples.professional: The security team acts as the protector of customer data, so every access request is logged.
examples.analytical: The psalmist names the LORD as his protector, a shield who guards the one who trusts in him.

nuance.analogy: A protector is like a lighthouse that stays lit through the storm so ships can find their way to safe harbor.
nuance.etymology: From Latin protector, defender, from protegere, to cover in front.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as tor instead of ter.
Confusing protector with protection, the noun for the act or the thing that protects.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, magen (מָגֵן) means shield, and it is used of God as protector. Psalm 18:2 describes the LORD as a rock, fortress, deliverer and shield in whom the psalmist takes refuge. Genesis 15:1 has God tell Abram, I am your shield. Psalm 28:7 says the LORD is the psalmist's strength and shield, in whom his heart trusts.

protector.etymology: From Middle English *protectour*, from Anglo-Norman *protectour*, *protector* and its etymon Latin *prōtēctor*, from *prōtegō* (“shield, protect”).

senses.definition: Unwillingly, with protests.
senses.example: She accepted the extra shift protestingly, sighing loudly as she grabbed her coat.

core.definition: In a reluctant way, objecting or complaining while still going along with something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TES. The ending '-ingly' has a short 'ing' sound followed by a light 'lee,' so keep the final syllable short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests reluctance and complaint, often with a hint of irony or resignation.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word in American English, found mostly in novels, formal writing, or a descriptive passage. In everyday speech, Americans say 'reluctantly,' 'with a complaint,' or 'grumbling.' Use it for description rather than conversation, since it can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Reluctantly describes hesitation, while protestingly adds that the person verbally objects while complying.
Grudgingly suggests resentful acceptance, while protestingly emphasizes that the person says or shows an objection.

examples.everyday: My little brother put on his coat protestingly, complaining the whole way to the car.
examples.professional: The manager accepted the revised deadline protestingly, noting for the record that it was unrealistic.
examples.analytical: The narrator yields protestingly to the older man's authority, a surrender that reads as both submission and quiet resistance.

nuance.analogy: Going along protestingly is like taking a turn at the wheel while saying, 'I still think we should have gone the other way.'
nuance.etymology: From protest plus the adjective ending -ing and the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using protestingly to describe a public demonstration, when it means reluctant complaint in an ordinary act.
Confusing protestingly with protesting, which is the verb or adjective form and can describe active objection.

senses.definition: Possessing, exercising, or demonstrating great care and consideration for the future.
senses.example: She was provident with her savings, setting aside money each month for retirement and emergencies.

senses.definition: Showing care in the use of something (especially money or provisions), so as to avoid wasting it.
senses.example: My grandmother was provident with flour and sugar, never letting a single cup go to waste.

senses.definition: Providing (for someone’s needs).
senses.example: The provident uncle kept the family fed and clothed through two lean winters.

core.definition: Careful and wise in planning for the future, especially in saving money or resources.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced 'ih', and the ending '-ent' is a quick 'unt', not 'ent' as in 'bent'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises prudent planning and thrift.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use provident mainly in formal writing, older-style speech or religious contexts. In everyday talk, people more often say 'careful,' 'prudent' or 'thrifty.' Calling a neighbor provident would sound slightly formal but complimentary.

distinctions.note: Prudent emphasizes sound judgment in choices; provident emphasizes planning and saving for future needs.
Thrifty focuses on spending little; provident focuses on preparing for what lies ahead.

examples.everyday: My uncle has always been provident with money, so he never worried about a rainy day.
examples.professional: A provident capacity plan keeps the cluster from running out of memory during the quarterly peak.
examples.analytical: A provident ethic of stewardship, as the author argues, links present restraint to the good of future generations.

nuance.analogy: Like a squirrel storing nuts before winter: it looks ahead and saves for the cold months.
nuance.etymology: From Latin providens, present participle of providere, to foresee.
common_mistakes: Confusing provident with 'prudent' in every context; provident focuses on planning ahead.
Mispronouncing it as 'PROH-vih-dent'; the first syllable is PRAH.

senses.definition: The quality of being provincial; having provincial tastes, mentality, manners.
senses.example: The blacksmith's provincialism showed in his speech and manner

senses.definition: A word or locution characteristic of a region or district.
senses.example: Words like 'pop' for soda are a charming provincialism of the Midwest.

senses.definition: Synonym of regionalism: belief in the superiority of one's regional government; the belief that most or nearly all political power should be decentralized to provincial governments.
senses.example: The senator's provincialism led him to oppose every federal highway project.

core.definition: Narrowness of outlook or taste; the quality of being limited to one's local area and unaware of wider ideas or customs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, VIN. The middle vowels reduce to a weak uh, and the final -ism is a light, unstressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone provincial suggests they are unsophisticated or narrow-minded, though the word can be neutral when describing a local dialect or culture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in essays, reviews and political commentary, for example to criticize a city's insularity or a politician's narrow views. In casual speech people more often say narrow-minded or small-town. Saying someone has provincialism to their face can sound harsh, so it is better kept for describing ideas or attitudes in discussion.

distinctions.note: Parochialism refers to a narrow focus on one's own small community or interests, often church or neighborhood, while provincialism is broader and stresses a lack of worldliness or sophistication.
Regionalism can be a neutral or positive term for loyalty to a region or its cultural traits; provincialism implies that the same loyalty has become narrow or dismissive.

examples.everyday: My cousin from Ohio thinks New York is weird, and honestly, that kind of provincialism gets old fast.
examples.professional: Our product team needs to fight a bit of provincialism and look at how users in Asia and Europe actually use the app.
examples.analytical: Critics have long argued that the novel's provincialism lies not in its setting but in its refusal to imagine any perspective beyond the narrator's village.

nuance.analogy: Like a house with the blinds always down, provincialism keeps out the light of the wider world.
nuance.etymology: From Latin provincialis, relating to a province, a territory administered outside Rome.
common_mistakes: Using provincialism to mean simply living in a small town; it implies narrowness, not location.
Confusing the stress, saying PROV-in-shuh-liz-um instead of pruh-VIN-shuh-liz-um.

senses.definition: To inflate with air.
senses.example: We puffed up the balloons.

senses.definition: To fluff up, such as an animal raising its fur or feathers to appear larger or conserve body heat.
senses.example: Small birds puff up while sleeping to keep warm.

senses.definition: To swell due to injury or illness.
senses.example: My hand puffed up where the cat had scratched me.

senses.definition: To become proud. (Often written as puffed up with pride.)
senses.example: He puffed up with pride when his daughter received the scholarship.

senses.definition: To trump up.
senses.example: The angry landlord tried to puff up unpaid fees to justify the eviction.

core.definition: To swell or inflate, becoming larger and rounder, often from injury, illness, air or fluid.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'up', and 'puff' has a lighter secondary stress. The two words link together, so it sounds like 'puf-UP'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing swelling; negative when used figuratively for someone who becomes self-important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say a face or eye puffs up after a bee sting, crying or an allergic reaction, and they also use it for birds fluffing their feathers. Figuratively, someone who puffs up is acting proud or boastful. This phrasal verb is separable, so you can say 'puff it up' or 'puff up the pillow'. For a bruise, people often say swell up or get puffy.

distinctions.note: Swell up is more general and more medical; puff up suggests a softer, airier, or more visible expansion.
Blow up means to inflate with air, often a balloon; puff up can describe the body or a swelling as well.

collocations: puff up after a bee sting

examples.everyday: My eye puffed up after I got hit by the screen door, so I put ice on it.
examples.professional: The vendor's report tends to puff up the savings, so let's check the raw numbers before we present them.
examples.analytical: Pride can puff a person up until the swelling is mistaken for strength.

nuance.analogy: Like a balloon slowly filling with breath until it becomes round and tight.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English puffen, imitative of the sound of blowing, combined with the adverb up.
common_mistakes: Using puff up without a sense of swelling or pride, when the phrase needs a clear context.
Saying puff up it instead of puff it up, since the phrasal verb is separable.

senses.definition: The quality of being puny.

core.definition: The quality of being small, weak, or insignificant; weakness or feebleness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the first vowel as a long 'yoo'. The final -ness is a reduced 'nuhs'. In American speech the standard form is 'puniness', so the spelling 'punyness' is rare.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that seems small, feeble, or unimpressive, often in a way that disparages.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always write 'puniness,' not 'punyness,' and 'punyness' appears mostly in older or literary texts. In everyday speech you would say 'how small' or 'how weak' instead. 'Puniness' is useful in writing about physical frailty, weak arguments, or small resources.

distinctions.note: Weakness is the general term for lacking strength; puniness emphasizes smallness and insignificance as well as feebleness.
Frailty is fragility, often from age or illness; puniness implies a small, unimpressive quality.

examples.everyday: After the big storm, the puniness of our little garden shed made me worry about the roof.
examples.professional: The puniness of our Q3 sample size makes the result hard to trust for a company-wide decision.
examples.analytical: Many religious writers describe a sense of human puniness before the vastness of creation, not as despair but as humility.

nuance.analogy: Puniness is like a candle at noon: small, not wrong, but easy to overlook in bright light.
nuance.etymology: From 'puny' (from Middle French 'puisne', later-born) plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'punyness' in American writing; the standard form is 'puniness'.
Using it for a neutral small size; it implies weakness or insignificance, which can sound insulting.

senses.definition: To blame a particular named person.
senses.example: Don't put the blame on your brother for something you did yourself.

core.definition: To say that a specific person is responsible for a problem or mistake.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on ON at the end, and blame has a secondary stress. In American English the vowel in 'on' sounds like 'ahn', the same as 'got'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests assigning fault, often unfairly or defensively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in workplaces, families, and news reports when someone is being held responsible. It can sound accusatory, so use it with care. A natural reply is 'That's not fair, I didn't do it,' or 'Let's figure out what happened first.' Use 'blame' directly when you want a shorter, more natural sentence.

distinctions.note: 'Blame' is shorter and more natural, as in 'They blamed me'; 'put the blame on' is wordier and slightly more emphatic.
'Point the finger at' is informal and conversational, and it suggests accusing someone publicly.
'Take the blame' means accepting responsibility, the opposite of putting the blame on someone else.

collocations: put the blame on the vendor
put the blame on the new hire
put the blame on the weather
put the blame on someone else
didn't want to put the blame on her

examples.everyday: Don't put the blame on me just because you forgot to lock the door.
examples.professional: The postmortem should focus on the process gap rather than putting the blame on any single engineer.
examples.analytical: Historians who put the blame on a single leader often ignore the structural pressures that shaped the decision.

nuance.analogy: Like pinning a name tag on the person who spilled the coffee, whether or not they actually did it.
nuance.etymology: 'Blame' comes from Old French blasmer, to find fault with, from Late Latin blasphemare.
common_mistakes: Saying 'blame to someone' or 'put blame him'; use 'blame him' or 'put the blame on him'.
Dropping 'the' and saying 'put blame on' in formal writing.

senses.definition: A grammatical device to mark quoted speech, such as be like in "he was like, 'who are you?'".
A form of the complementizer related to the verb say, found in many languages of West Africa and South Asia.
senses.example: In that dialect, the quotative derives from the verb 'say' and introduces every reported utterance.

senses.definition: Serving to mark quoted speech.
senses.example: Linguists noticed that the quotative particle appears most often before direct speech in conversations.

core.definition: A word or phrase, such as 'be like' or 'go,' that introduces someone's quoted speech in conversation or narrative.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -TAY-, and the ending -ive is a short 'iv.' Avoid stressing the first syllable or pronouncing the t as a clear 'd' in careful speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in linguistics. In everyday speech the informal quotative 'be like' is often seen as youthful or casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quotative mainly in linguistics when describing how speakers report speech. In ordinary conversation, people use the informal forms 'be like' or 'go' without any special term, as in 'I was like, why would I say that?' Avoid these informal forms in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Quote is the everyday verb for repeating someone's exact words, while quotative is the grammatical term for words that introduce that repetition.
A complementizer introduces a subordinate clause like 'that' in 'I think that,' whereas a quotative introduces reported or direct speech.

examples.everyday: My daughter uses 'be like' as a quotative all the time: 'I was like, no way that happened.'
examples.professional: In the usability report, quotative 'like' appeared often in user interviews, so we coded those passages separately.
examples.analytical: Quotative markers such as 'go' and 'be like' show how speakers reenact voices rather than simply reporting them.

nuance.analogy: A quotative is like a stage direction that tells the audience a character is about to speak.
nuance.etymology: From quote with the suffix -ative; quote comes from Medieval Latin quotare, 'to mark with numbers.'
common_mistakes: Using quotative as a synonym for the verb quote in ordinary sentences.
Using informal 'be like' in formal writing where 'said' or 'stated' is appropriate.

senses.definition: Happening every day; daily.
Having the characteristics of something which can be seen, experienced, etc, every day or very commonly.
senses.example: Writing code was a quotidian part of her job, something she did every single day.

senses.definition: Something which is considered humdrum or dull.
senses.example: After the novelty wore off, the commute became quotidian and utterly dull.

senses.definition: Recurring every twenty-four hours or (more generally) daily (of symptoms, etc).
senses.example: The doctor noted quotidian fevers that spiked every afternoon at roughly the same hour.

senses.definition: Commonplace or mundane things regarded as a class.
senses.example: She wrote about the quotidian of small-town life: groceries, weather, and neighborly gossip.

senses.definition: (historical) A daily allowance formerly paid to certain members of the clergy.
senses.example: The cathedral canon received his quotidian, a small daily payment from the chapter funds.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (rare, historical) A fever which recurs every day; quotidian malaria.
senses.example: The physician diagnosed quotidian malaria, a fever that returned every single day.
senses.label: rare, historical

core.definition: Happening every day; ordinary, routine, or commonplace, often in a way that seems dull.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, TID. The final "-ian" is a reduced syllable pronounced "un," not "ee-an."

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting something routine that may be dull; it can also be neutral when describing ordinary life without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quotidian mainly in writing, essays, and literary criticism, not in casual conversation. Speakers who use it in everyday talk may sound pretentious, so "daily" or "everyday" is the natural choice. It works well when describing the ordinary details of life, such as chores or routines.

distinctions.note: Daily is the common everyday word, while quotidian is more literary and can carry a tone of dullness or routine.
Mundane stresses boredom and lack of interest; quotidian stresses ordinary, repeated occurrence and can be neutral.

examples.everyday: Honestly, my quotidian chores like folding laundry are the part of my day I least enjoy.
examples.professional: The team's quotidian reporting tasks can be automated so analysts focus on the harder questions.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard saw the quotidian as the very place where faith is tested, not a distraction from it.

nuance.analogy: Quotidian is like a well-worn pair of slippers: comfortable, always there, and so familiar that you stop noticing them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quotidianus, "daily," from quotidie, "every day," from quot, "how many" and dies, "day."
common_mistakes: Using quotidian as a noun in everyday speech; it is mainly an adjective.
Pronouncing the last syllable as "ee-an" instead of "un."

quotidian.etymology: From Anglo-Norman *cotidian*, *cotidien*, Middle French *cotidian*, *cotidien*, and their source, Latin *cottīdiānus*, *quōtīdiānus* (“happening every day”), from adverb *cottidie*, *quōtīdiē* (“every day, daily”), from an unattested adjective derived from…

senses.definition: Rabidness.

core.definition: The quality of being rabid, meaning extreme, angry, or fanatical intensity in beliefs or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: The stress shifts from RAB-id in the adjective to the middle syllable of the noun, BID. The final -ity is a short 'ih-tee', not 'ee-tee', and the first syllable is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always implies harshness, lack of control, or excess.
nuance.usage_note: Rabidity is rare in everyday American speech, and Americans usually say 'fanaticism', 'zeal', or simply describe someone as 'rabid'. You may encounter it in editorials, literary criticism, or formal essays. Because it always suggests a harsh and uncontrolled quality, do not use it to praise someone's enthusiasm.

distinctions.note: Fervor is intense feeling that can be positive, while rabidity always suggests a harsh, uncontrolled, and often hostile quality.
Zeal is eagerness and devotion that can be admirable, while rabidity signals extremism and loss of judgment.
Fanaticism is the everyday term for extreme devotion to a cause, which is more common in conversation than rabidity.

examples.professional: The rabidity of the online debate made it hard for the team to focus on the actual bug.
examples.analytical: The rabidity of sectarian polemic often obscures the very questions it claims to settle.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire that consumes everything in its path, leaving no room for careful thought.
nuance.etymology: From rabid plus the suffix -ity; rabid is from Latin rabidus, meaning raging or mad, from rabere, to rage.
common_mistakes: Confusing rabidity with rabies, which is the disease; both words share the same Latin root but mean different things.
Using rabidity as a positive word, such as praising someone's rabidity for a cause.

senses.definition: In a rakish manner.

core.definition: In a stylish, slightly reckless or disreputable way that looks dashing and a little daring.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, RAY. The -ish is short and unstressed, and the final -ly is a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive to mildly playful. It praises a dashing style but may hint at a bit of unreliability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rakishly in descriptions of people, clothing, or a grin, often in novels, reviews, and fashion writing. It is not common in casual speech, where people say 'a little devilish' or 'dashing.' A natural reaction to a rakishly dressed person is a compliment, such as 'You look great in that hat.'

distinctions.note: Dashingly emphasizes bold good looks and courage, while rakishly adds a hint of casual, slightly unconventional charm.
Stylishly is general and neutral, while rakishly suggests a carefree or mildly disreputable flair.

examples.everyday: He wore his baseball cap tilted rakishly, which made him look like he was up to something.
examples.professional: The brand's campaign shows its models posing rakishly against city backdrops, aimed at younger buyers.
examples.analytical: The novel's narrator speaks rakishly, and his charm works as both a rhetorical strategy and a warning about self-deception.

nuance.analogy: Like a hat worn a little off-center, which looks confident and slightly careless at the same time.
nuance.etymology: From rakish, from rake (a dissolute man), used since the 17th century.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'rakishingly', which is not a word.
Confusing it with 'racily', which often refers to bold or suggestive material.
Pronouncing the first syllable like 'rack' rather than 'rake'.

senses.definition: In a rambling manner.

core.definition: In a long, disorganized way that wanders from the main point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RAM, and the final -ly is a light 'lee.' The b and l blend quickly, and the -ing is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It describes speech or writing that lacks focus.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use ramblingly in conversation. They say 'in a rambling way' or 'she went on and on,' and ramblingly appears mainly in literary reviews and narrative writing. Use it only when you want a precise description of a manner of speaking or writing.

distinctions.note: Discursively is more academic and means moving through topics in a long, reasoned way, while ramblingly suggests a lack of organization.
Aimlessly refers to a lack of purpose in action, while ramblingly refers to speech or writing that wanders.

examples.professional: The vendor explained the pricing ramblingly, so nobody on the call was sure what we had agreed to.
examples.analytical: The author writes ramblingly on purpose, and the loose structure becomes part of the argument about memory.

nuance.analogy: Like a hiker who takes every side trail, so the route becomes long and hard to follow.
nuance.etymology: From rambling plus the suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'ramblinly,' dropping the g.
Shifting stress to the -ing syllable.
Using it in casual speech where 'in a rambling way' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Malware that holds the data of a computer user for ransom, usually requiring or claiming to require payment to restore access.
senses.example: Our hospital's network was shut down by ransomware demanding payment in bitcoin.

senses.definition: Software that is released as open source only in exchange for payment.
senses.example: The startup released its database tool as ransomware, sharing the source code only for a fee.

core.definition: Malicious software that locks or encrypts a victim's files or computer and demands payment to restore access.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'RAN', with a lighter secondary stress on 'ware'. The middle syllable reduces to a weak 'sum', not 'some', and the final syllable is 'wair' with a clear r.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious crime and a serious threat to organizations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ransomware in news, IT security, and everyday conversation about computer problems. It is usually uncountable, but people also say a ransomware attack or a ransomware infection. Companies often describe ransomware as a risk to back up against, and reporting it to authorities is common in the US.

distinctions.note: Malware is the broad category of malicious software, while ransomware is one type that demands payment.
Spyware secretly gathers information, while ransomware locks files and demands payment for their release.

examples.everyday: My sister's laptop got hit with ransomware, so now she's paying a service to recover her photos.
examples.professional: We need offline backups, because a ransomware attack can encrypt our shared drives within minutes.
examples.analytical: Ransomware changes the economics of cybercrime, because the criminal profits from the victim's dependence on the data rather than from its theft.

nuance.analogy: Like a thief who changes the locks on your house and then sells you the new key.
nuance.etymology: From ransom, from Old French rançon (from Latin redemptio, 'redemption'), plus -ware, as in software and malware.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'some' vowel, saying 'RAN-some-wair'.
Spelling it 'ransomeware', with an extra e.

senses.definition: The ability, or degree of ability, not only to read words at all but also to understand the meaning conveyed by collections of words (such as phrases, sentences, and documents).
senses.example: Her third-grade reading comprehension scores improved sharply after the summer tutoring program.

core.definition: The ability to understand the meaning of words, sentences and documents when reading them.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on REE-ding and HEN-shun. The middle syllables of comprehension are reduced, so the 'pre' sounds like 'prih', not 'prey'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; strong reading comprehension is seen as an important skill for school and work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reading comprehension in schools, testing (such as the SAT or state exams) and in discussions of learning. In casual speech, people often say 'understanding what you read' instead. A natural sentence is 'Her reading comprehension improved a lot this year.'

distinctions.note: Fluency means reading smoothly and accurately at a good speed; comprehension means understanding what the text means.
Literacy is the broad ability to read and write; reading comprehension is one specific part of it.
Comprehension alone can refer to understanding spoken or visual information; reading comprehension is limited to written text.

examples.everyday: My son's reading comprehension got a lot better after he started reading graphic novels.
examples.professional: We revised the onboarding materials to improve reading comprehension for non-native speakers.
examples.analytical: Reading comprehension depends not only on decoding words but also on prior knowledge and the ability to infer.

nuance.analogy: Like hearing a song's lyrics clearly: you can pronounce every word and still miss the story.
nuance.etymology: Reading comes from read; comprehension comes from Latin comprehendere, to grasp together.
common_mistakes: Using reading comprehension for understanding spoken language; for listening, say 'listening comprehension'.
Stressing the middle of the word as kahm-PREH-hen-shun; the main stress in comprehension is on HEN.

senses.definition: To modify core data from which other data is derived in such a way that the final meaning is unchanged.
senses.example: Before publishing the dataset, she rebased the raw values so the units matched the standard scale.

senses.definition: To change the base address of.
senses.example: The loader rebased the shared library into a new memory address after the program started.

senses.definition: To integrate changes by appending them to another commit or branch, rather than pulling or merging in changes from a branch.
senses.example: Before opening the pull request, I rebased my feature branch onto the latest main branch.

senses.definition: To replace the base of a denture.

core.definition: In version control, to move a branch's commits onto a different base commit, replaying them so the history reads as a straight line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BASE, the same syllable as in 'base'. Many engineers say RE-base, which is wrong, and the final s becomes /ɪz/ in 'rebases'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Git users say it as both verb and noun, as in 'let's rebase onto main' or 'do an interactive rebase'. Careful use matters: rebasing commits that others already pushed forces teammates to reconcile their histories. Outside software, the word is almost never used.

distinctions.note: A merge joins two branches with a new merge commit that keeps both histories; a rebase rewrites your commits on top of the target branch.
A reset moves a branch pointer, often to discard commits; a rebase replays existing commits onto a new base.

examples.everyday: I'm stuck in the middle of a rebase, so I can't look at the new file yet.
examples.professional: Can you rebase your feature branch onto main before we review the pull request?
examples.analytical: A rebase preserves the content of each commit while changing its parent, so the history looks linear but no longer shows when the work actually happened.

nuance.analogy: Like copying your notes from one folder onto a fresh page in a new order, so they read straight through.
nuance.etymology: From re- 'again' plus base, from Greek basis 'step, foundation'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (RE-base) instead of ree-BAYS.
Using rebase to mean pull or merge; a rebase replays commits and rewrites history.
Rebasing shared commits that others have already pulled, which causes confusion for teammates.

senses.definition: To construct again; to restore.
senses.example: Volunteers worked for years to reconstruct the church after the fire destroyed its roof.

senses.definition: To attempt to understand an event by recreating, imagining, or talking through the circumstances.
senses.example: Investigators reconstructed the crash by reviewing radar data and cockpit recordings.

core.definition: To build or rebuild something again, or to piece together the details of a past event from the available evidence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STRUKT, the final syllable, and the vowel is the short American 'uh' of 'struck'. The con- reduces to 'kun', and the final t is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe physical rebuilding (positive) or careful inference from evidence, and it is often neutral in academic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reconstruct in formal contexts: rebuilding a building after a disaster, or investigators and historians piecing together events. In casual speech they say 'rebuild' or 'put back together'. Saying 'reconstruct the night' is natural among friends, but it sounds like police or lawyer talk.

distinctions.note: Rebuild is the everyday word for building something again; reconstruct can also mean recreating a past event or structure from clues.
Restore aims to return something to its earlier state, often an object or painting; reconstruct often involves rebuilding from fragments or evidence.

examples.everyday: We tried to reconstruct the night, but none of us remembered when the party ended.
examples.professional: Before the audit, we need to reconstruct the timeline of the database changes from the logs.
examples.analytical: Historians reconstruct early Christian worship largely from sparse letters and later liturgical texts, so their conclusions remain tentative.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a shattered vase back together from its pieces, using photos to guide you.
nuance.etymology: From re- ('again') and construct, from Latin construere ('to heap together, build').
common_mistakes: Using reconstruct for simple repair of an everyday object; 'fix' or 'rebuild' is more natural.
Confusing it with construct: construct means build something new, while reconstruct means rebuild or recreate something that existed before.

senses.definition: One in charge of a refectory.

core.definition: A person in charge of a refectory, the dining hall of a monastery or college, including its meals and kitchen.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'TOR', so the word is not stressed on the first syllable. The final '-ian' is reduced to 'ee-uhn', and the middle syllables are quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and institutional. It describes a specific administrative role.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use refectorian in daily life. It appears in historical writing about monasteries and in some college or religious histories. In monastic contexts the officer is more often called the refectorer, so refectorian is the less common form.

distinctions.note: Steward is a general word for someone who manages property or provisions, while refectorian names the specific officer responsible for the dining hall.
Refectorer is the more common term in monastic writing, while refectorian is a less frequent variant used in some dictionaries and older texts.

examples.everyday: Ask the refectorian about breakfast, since she handles all the meals on this retreat.
examples.professional: The college refectorian reported that the dining hall needed a bigger budget for the winter term.
examples.analytical: In medieval monasteries the refectorian's office carried moral weight, since feeding the community was itself an act of charity.

nuance.analogy: Like a ship's cook who also keeps the galley orderly and the crew fed.
nuance.etymology: From refectory plus the suffix -ian, from Medieval Latin refectorium, from Latin reficere 'restore'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'REF-ek-tor-ee-un' instead of 'ref-ek-TOR-ee-un'.
Confusing the person (refectorian) with the place (refectory).
Using refectorian for a modern cafeteria manager, where food service director or manager is the normal American term.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, refines.
senses.example: The refiner at the edge of town processes crude oil into gasoline and diesel for the regional market.

core.definition: A person or company that purifies raw material, such as crude oil, sugar or metal ore, into a usable form.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FINE, the second syllable, and the final -er is weak, sounding like the er in water. Do not stress the first syllable, which is a weak ri.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a precise industry term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use refiner mainly in energy, food and metals industries, as in the oil refiner or a sugar refiner. In casual talk, people usually say refinery for the plant itself and use refiner for the company or person running it. You will hear this word most often in news about gas prices.

distinctions.note: A refiner is the person or company that runs the process, while a refinery is the physical plant where it happens.
A processor is any company that changes raw materials into products, while a refiner specifically removes impurities to improve purity.

examples.everyday: My uncle works for an oil refiner in Texas, so gas prices come up at every family dinner.
examples.professional: Independent refiners are pushing for a new supply contract with the pipeline operator.
examples.analytical: A refiner's profit depends on the spread between crude input costs and finished product prices, so its margin can swing sharply.

nuance.analogy: Like a sieve that lets the fine grain through and holds back the chaff.
nuance.etymology: From refine plus the agent suffix -er, 'one who does something'.
common_mistakes: Using refiner and refinery as if they meant the same thing
Stressing the first syllable, as in REF-in-er

senses.definition: A rebirth of a soul, in a physical life form, such as a body.
senses.example: He is believed to be the reincarnation of Jesus.

senses.definition: A fresh embodiment.
senses.example: Some readers see the young poet as a reincarnation of the nineteenth-century romantics.

senses.definition: A new, considerably improved, version.
senses.example: a reincarnation of an old video game

core.definition: The belief or process in which a soul is born again into a new physical body after death.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -NAY- syllable, and the -car- syllable keeps a weaker secondary stress. Many learners say the vowel in -car- as a full 'car' sound, but it should be a lighter 'kuh' or 'kahr' with the r pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing a belief; it can be positive for believers and negative or dismissive for critics, depending on the speaker's stance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reincarnation mainly when talking about religion, philosophy, or popular culture, such as Hinduism, Buddhism, or a movie plot about past lives. In casual talk it is often used jokingly, as in 'In my last reincarnation I was a cat.' Be careful not to confuse it with incarnation, which in Christian usage means God taking on human flesh in Jesus.

distinctions.note: Transmigration is a more technical term for the movement of a soul from one body to another, often used in philosophy or comparative religion, while reincarnation is the everyday word.
Incarnation refers in Christian theology to the Son of God taking on a human nature, and it is a one-time event, not a repeated cycle of rebirths.
Resurrection means being raised from the dead in the same bodily life, usually in Christian belief, whereas reincarnation means being born again into a new body.

examples.everyday: My coworker half-jokes that in his last reincarnation he was a cat who ran the whole house.
examples.professional: In our comparative religion course, we compared how Buddhist and Hindu teachings explain reincarnation with Christian beliefs about the afterlife.
examples.analytical: The Christian rejection of reincarnation rests on the conviction that each human person is created by God as a unique individual whose destiny is decided at death.

nuance.analogy: Reincarnation is like a song covered by new singers over the years; the melody continues, but each performance is a new body and voice.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin reincarnatio, from re- 'again' plus in- 'in' and caro, carnis 'flesh'.
common_mistakes: Confusing reincarnation with incarnation, which in Christian theology refers to God becoming human, not to a soul being reborn.
Stressing the -car- syllable too strongly, instead of putting the main stress on -NAY-.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible does not teach reincarnation, and no Hebrew or Greek word in Scripture means the repeated rebirth of souls in new bodies. Hebrews 9:27 says that humans die once and then face judgment, which Christians read as against the idea of repeated lives. In John 9:2-3, Jesus rejects the idea that a man was born blind because of his own sin or his parents' sin, but this does not address reincarnation directly. In Matthew 11:14 and 17:12-13, Jesus says John the Baptist came in the spirit of Elijah, a statement sometimes linked to reincarnation, but Christians read it as a comparison of mission and not as the same soul returning. The Greek word palingenesia, meaning regeneration or new birth, appears in Matthew 19:28 and Titus 3:5, but it refers to spiritual renewal or the coming age, not reincarnation.

senses.definition: Of or relating to relativism.
Of or relating to relativity.
At or near the speed of light.

core.definition: Relating to Einstein's theory of relativity, especially effects that occur at speeds close to the speed of light.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, -VIS-, not on REL- as the spelling suggests. The middle vowels are weak, so say them quickly: rel-uh-tih-VIS-tik.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In philosophical debates, calling a view relativistic can sound like a criticism.
nuance.usage_note: In physics, Americans use relativistic for anything involving Einstein's special or general relativity, especially at speeds near light. In philosophy and ethics it can mean relativism, the view that truth or morality depends on perspective, and that sense is often used critically. In casual talk people usually say 'really fast' or 'near the speed of light' rather than relativistic.

distinctions.note: Relative is the general word for depending on something else; relativistic is narrower and refers specifically to relativity theory or relativism.
A relativist is a person who holds the view; relativistic describes the theory or the viewpoint itself.

examples.everyday: My son loves those shows about black holes, and he keeps asking about relativistic effects like time slowing down.
examples.professional: The simulation drops the relativistic corrections, so the timestamps from the satellites drift by a few microseconds.
examples.analytical: A relativistic account of truth holds that a claim is true only within a framework, and that position must be argued rather than assumed.

nuance.analogy: Like a clock on a fast train: the faster it moves, the more slowly it ticks compared with the station clock.
nuance.etymology: From relativity, from relative, from Late Latin relativus, 'referring back'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as REL-uh-tiv-ISS-tik; the main stress is on -VIS-.
Using relativistic for ordinary situations where relative or 'it depends' would be more natural.

senses.definition: To say or write something with different wording.
senses.example: Make sure to rephrase your thesis in your conclusion.

core.definition: To say or write something again using different words, often to make it clearer or more polite.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, FRAYZ, and the prefix re- is pronounced 'ree' with a clear vowel. Avoid a weak first syllable, which can make the word sound like 'rih-FRAYZ'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite; it is a helpful request or action that signals a wish for clarity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rephrase constantly at work and in conversation, especially in the polite request Could you rephrase that? when someone did not understand. Casually, people might say Say that again or What do you mean? For a formal written restatement, use paraphrase instead.

distinctions.note: Paraphrase is a specific restatement of a passage in new words, often used in academic writing and citation, while rephrase is the everyday verb for changing wording.
Restate means to say again, often in a formal or summarizing way, while rephrase emphasizes changing the wording itself.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I didn't catch that, could you rephrase it so I can understand?
examples.professional: Can you rephrase the second bullet so the deadline is clearer to the client before we send the email?
examples.analytical: The author rephrases the premise in technical terms, which exposes a hidden assumption about causation.

nuance.analogy: Like translating a sentence into simpler English for a friend: the meaning stays, but the clothes change.
nuance.etymology: From re- again plus phrase, from Greek phrasis, speech or expression.
common_mistakes: Using rephrase when you mean paraphrase in a written citation or academic summary.
Saying rephrase it again, which is redundant, instead of simply rephrase it.

senses.definition: Something that restrains, ties, fastens or secures.
senses.example: Make sure all the restraints are tight.

senses.definition: Control or caution; reserve.
senses.example: Try to exercise restraint when talking to your boss.

core.definition: Self-control in speech or action, or a device or force that holds someone or something back.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on -STRAINT, and the final t is clear and crisp. Do not add an extra vowel before the t, and keep the first syllable short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means self-control, negative or neutral when it means a physical device or legal limit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans praise a person for showing restraint, meaning they did not overreact or overeat or spend too much. The word also appears in police and medical settings, as in physical restraints. In casual talk, you might say 'I showed a lot of restraint,' and a friend may laugh and agree.

distinctions.note: Self-control is a broad quality, while restraint often describes holding back in a particular moment, such as not speaking or not spending.
Restriction is an external rule or limit, while restraint usually comes from a person's own choice or a device used to hold someone.

examples.everyday: She showed real restraint and did not argue with the waiter.
examples.professional: I appreciate your restraint during the escalation; it kept the client calm.
examples.analytical: Virtue ethics treats restraint not as repression but as the disciplined ordering of desire toward the good.

nuance.analogy: Like a brake that lets a car descend a hill safely.
nuance.etymology: From Old French restrainte, from restreindre, to restrain.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun restraint with the verb restrain, which takes no noun ending.
Mispronouncing the final t as silent or adding an extra vowel.

restraint.etymology: From Middle English *restreynte*, from Old French *restreinte*; more at *restrain*.

core.definition: The name of Moses' father-in-law, a priest of Midian, in the book of Exodus.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable, ROO, and the second syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'ROO-ul'. Keep the r clear at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name without strong emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet the name Reuel in Bible study. In Exodus the same man is also called Jethro, so readers sometimes need to know that they are the same person.

examples.everyday: In Bible study we noticed that Reuel and Jethro seem to be the same man in Exodus.
examples.professional: In my sermon on Exodus 2, I explained that Reuel welcomed Moses into his household after his flight to Midian.
examples.analytical: The narrative's naming of Reuel as a priest of Midian shows that the Israelite story recognizes a wider religious context outside Israel.

nuance.analogy: Like a host whose name appears in two different places in the same story.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Re'uel, often understood as 'friend of God' or 'friend of El'.
common_mistakes: Assuming Reuel and Jethro are different people; in Exodus they appear to be the same figure under two names.
Saying 'REE-ool' instead of 'ROO-ul'.
nuance.biblical_note: Reuel (Re'u'el, רְעוּאֵל) is the name of the priest of Midian who was the father-in-law of Moses. Exodus 2:18 gives his name as Reuel when Moses comes to his household after fleeing Egypt. Numbers 10:29 mentions 'Hobab the son of Reuel the Midianite' as Moses' brother-in-law, showing the family connection. Exodus 3:1 and 18:1 call the same man Jethro, which many scholars take to be a second name or a title.

senses.definition: Prearranged and fixed so that the winner or outcome is decided in advance.
senses.example: There was a vicious rumor that the final was rigged, as the defense seemed useless.

senses.definition: Having the rigging up.
senses.example: We were ready to embark upon our journey now the vessel was rigged.

core.definition: Secretly arranged in advance so that the result is decided beforehand, usually dishonestly.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a hard g and a clear final d. Don't add a vowel between the g and the d, as in 'rig-ed.'

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it implies cheating or a fixed outcome.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the game is rigged' or 'the election was rigged' when they believe someone secretly controlled the result, often as a complaint. It can also be used as a joke about unfair luck, as in 'The coin flip is rigged against me.' 'Rigged' is the past participle of the verb 'rig,' so the sentence 'They rigged the vote' is the active form.

distinctions.note: 'Fixed' is informal and can mean dishonestly arranged, but 'rigged' more specifically suggests a setup built to produce a certain result.
'Crooked' describes a dishonest person or practice in general, while 'rigged' describes a specific contest, vote, or system that has been manipulated.
'Fraudulent' is formal and legal, used for deception with intent to gain, while 'rigged' is everyday speech about an unfair setup.

examples.everyday: Everyone said the raffle was rigged because my cousin won three times in a row.
examples.professional: The vendor says the selection was fair, but people on the team think the scoring rubric changed after the bids came in and that it was rigged.
examples.analytical: A rigged game is one in which the outcome is fixed in advance, so the apparent chance of winning hides a predetermined result.

nuance.analogy: A rigged game is like a deck of cards stacked so that one player always gets the best hand.
nuance.etymology: From 'rig' in the sense of manipulating something dishonestly, a usage of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'rigged' (dishonestly fixed) with 'rigid' (stiff and not flexible).
Using the base verb 'rig' in place of the past participle, as in 'The vote was rig' instead of 'The vote was rigged.'

senses.definition: A tumultuous disturbance of the public peace by a large group of people, often involving violence or damage to property.
senses.example: The protests began peacefully but turned into riots after several days.

senses.definition: A wide and unconstrained variety.
senses.example: In summer this flower garden is a riot of color.

senses.definition: A humorous or entertaining event or person.
senses.example: My little brother's impression of our grumpy neighbor was an absolute riot at dinner.

senses.definition: Wanton or unrestrained behavior or emotion.
senses.example: After the breakup, she let loose in a riot of tears and reckless spending.

senses.definition: To create or take part in a riot; to raise an uproar or sedition.
senses.example: The nuclear protesters rioted outside the military base.

senses.definition: To cause to riot; to throw into a tumult.
senses.example: The rumor of canceled bonuses rioted the entire office into shouting and slammed doors.

senses.definition: To annoy.
senses.example: Stop that infernal whistling, Martha, you are going to riot me senseless.

core.definition: A violent, disorderly disturbance of public peace by a large group of people, often with damage to property.

pronunciation.tip: Use one syllable stress on the first syllable. The American r is a true r, and the final t is often very soft or almost silent, so say it as RY-ut, not RY-oh-ut.

nuance.connotation: Negative. A riot suggests violence, damage, and danger; it is a strong word for public disorder.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use riot for serious public disorder, such as after a sports championship or a police incident, and news coverage uses it often. In casual speech, 'a riot' can also mean something very funny, as in 'the party was a riot,' and 'run riot' means to act without control. Do not use riot for a peaceful protest; Americans would say protest or demonstration.

distinctions.note: A protest is usually peaceful and organized to express a view, while a riot involves violence or serious damage.
An uprising is a rebellion against authority and can be organized, while a riot is more spontaneous disorder.
A mutiny is a rebellion by people in the military or on a ship against their commanders, not a crowd in a city.

examples.everyday: The city was calm after the riot ended, but the neighborhood still looked wrecked.
examples.professional: The insurance claim covers property damage caused by the riot last weekend.
examples.analytical: Scholars often ask whether a riot expresses political grievance or simply reflects the breakdown of social order.

nuance.analogy: A riot is like a spilled pot of boiling water in a crowded room: once it starts, it spreads quickly and is hard to contain.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French riote, 'dispute, quarrel,' from the verb rioter, 'to quarrel'; the verb's exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using riot for a peaceful protest, which sounds much more violent to Americans.
Using riot as a countable noun without an article in phrases like 'a riot' versus 'riot' as a mass noun.

riot.etymology: From Middle English *riot* (“debauched living, dissipation”), from Old French *riote* (“debate”), from *rioter* (“to quarrel”), perhaps related to *riboter* or from Latin *rugio* (“to roar”).

senses.definition: The overall process of identifying all the risks to and from an activity and assessing the potential impact of each risk.
senses.example: Before launching the pilot, the project team completed a full risk assessment of the data pipeline.

senses.definition: The determination of the potential impact of an individual risk by measuring or otherwise assessing both the likelihood that it will occur and the impact if it should occur, and then combining the result according to an agreed rule to give a single measure of potential impact.
senses.example: The risk assessment scored each failure by likelihood and impact, then combined them into one number.

core.definition: The process of identifying possible risks and judging how likely each one is and how much damage it could cause.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun the first word, RISK, carries the main stress, and assessment has its own weaker stress on SESS. Learners often stress assess as a verb or put the main stress on the second word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a careful, professional process rather than a judgment of blame.
nuance.usage_note: In American business, government, and data work, risk assessment is a standard phrase in meetings, reports, and compliance documents. It usually refers to a formal, documented process. In casual talk, Americans might say we need to think through the risks instead.

distinctions.note: Risk assessment identifies and measures risks, while risk management also includes deciding and carrying out actions to reduce them.
Risk analysis is a broader term that can include assessment, modeling, and interpretation, while risk assessment is more often the evaluation step itself.

examples.everyday: Before we start the home renovation, we should do a quick risk assessment of the electrical work.
examples.professional: Before we deploy the model to production, we need a full risk assessment covering bias, data drift, and customer impact.
examples.analytical: A proper risk assessment separates the likelihood of harm from its severity, since treating them as one number can hide what matters most.

nuance.analogy: A risk assessment is like a weather report for a project: it names the storms, estimates how likely they are, and says how bad they could get.
nuance.etymology: Risk comes from Italian risco or rischio, and assessment comes from Latin assidere, to sit beside, via Old French assesser, to set a tax.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second word, assessment, as the main stress of the phrase.
Using risk assessment as a verb phrase, as in we risk assessed the plan; say we did a risk assessment of the plan.

senses.definition: To become rounder or plumper.
senses.example: It was Bill all right, but he'd really rounded out since I'd last seen him.

senses.definition: To make more complete by adding details.
senses.example: Here are some actual figures to round out the basic report.

core.definition: To make something more complete or balanced by adding what it lacks.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on out, so say 'rownd OWT'. Keep the d crisp before out and do not link it into a new syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it means improving or completing something, often a team, skill set, or meal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use round out in meetings and job talk: 'We need someone to round out the sales team,' or 'She rounds out her résumé with volunteer work.' It sounds professional but not stiff. In casual speech people often say 'fill out' or 'finish off' instead.

distinctions.note: Round off usually means finishing something smoothly or changing a number to a whole value; round out means adding what is missing to make it fuller.
Fill out often means completing a form or gaining weight; round out is about balance and completeness.
Round up means gather people together or raise a number to the next whole number; it has a different meaning.

examples.everyday: A side salad would really round out this meal.
examples.professional: We're hiring one more analyst to round out the team before the spring launch.
examples.analytical: The second study rounds out the first by testing whether the effect holds across different populations.

nuance.analogy: Like adding the last pieces to a puzzle so the picture feels whole.
nuance.etymology: From round (verb, to make round) plus out (adverb).
common_mistakes: Confusing round out with round up, which means to gather or increase; the verbs are different.
Forgetting that the phrasal verb is separable, so 'round it out' and 'round out it' is wrong, but 'round your skills out' is correct.

senses.definition: To forage for, or (figuratively) to quickly prepare, something.
senses.example: I'll see if I can rustle up a meal before the guests start arriving in 30 minutes.

core.definition: To quickly gather or prepare something, especially food, from whatever is available nearby.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on UP, the particle, so it sounds like RUHS-uhl UHP and not RUHS-uhl up with equal emphasis. The final l of rustle is a syllabic l, with no separate vowel before it.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests resourcefulness and a friendly willingness to help, often in a home or group setting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rustle up mostly in casual talk about cooking, as in 'I can rustle up some lunch.' You can also use it for finding people or supplies quickly, as in 'Let's rustle up a few volunteers.' A natural reply is 'Thanks, that would be great' or simply 'Sounds good.' In formal writing, say prepare or arrange instead.

distinctions.note: Throw together suggests making something quickly and carelessly, often with no real plan, while rustle up suggests resourcefulness with what is on hand.
Whip up is more lively and often implies a little flair or speed, while rustle up is plainer and more casual.
Scrounge up means to find something hard to get, often by searching or begging, and it does not necessarily involve making or preparing anything.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about dinner, I'll rustle up something with what's left in the fridge.
examples.professional: I can rustle up three people from the analytics team to review the dashboard before Friday's client call.
examples.analytical: Critics rustled up enough counterexamples from the recent literature to force the author to narrow the thesis.

nuance.analogy: Like a cook opening the pantry and gathering enough ingredients to make a meal in minutes.
nuance.etymology: A phrasal verb from rustle, an imitative verb for a crackling or stirring sound, plus up.
common_mistakes: Using rustle up for buying a single finished item in a store; it implies gathering and preparing from what is at hand.
Saying rustle up in formal writing, where prepare or arrange is more appropriate.

senses.definition: A place of safety or refuge.
A protected zone in a country, especially one designated for members of an ethnic or religious minority.
senses.example: The displaced families fled to a safe haven in the northern province, where soldiers guarded the refugee camps.

senses.definition: An investment that would lose little of its value in the event of a stock market crash.
senses.example: During the market turmoil, my advisor moved most of my savings into a safe haven like Treasury bonds.

senses.definition: A financially secure offshore bank or country during times of extreme uncertainty, or when domestic banks are suspected of becoming insolvent.
senses.example: When rumors about the local banks spread, many depositors wired their money to Switzerland as a safe haven.

senses.definition: The hours of the day when it is permissible for broadcasting radio stations in the United States to broadcast profanity over radio waves without fear of retribution from the FCC.
senses.example: Late-night hosts counted on the safe haven between ten p.m. and six a.m. for uncensored language on the air.

core.definition: A place of safety or refuge from danger, harm or trouble.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on HAY, and the second syllable of haven is weak, so it sounds like vun. Don't pronounce it hay-ven with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests protection, security and relief from threat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use safe haven in news about war, disasters or immigration, as in a safe haven for refugees, and in finance, as in gold is a safe haven during market crashes. In casual talk people often say a safe place or refuge. In the US, safe haven laws let parents leave newborns at hospitals or fire stations without penalty.

distinctions.note: Refuge is a general word for shelter from danger; safe haven often refers to a protected place or zone in news or politics.
A shelter is a physical building or covering; a safe haven can be a place, a zone or an investment.

collocations: a safe haven during a crash
a safe haven in the storm

examples.everyday: The library downtown became a safe haven for me when the apartment was too loud.
examples.professional: Treasury bonds are often seen as a safe haven when stock prices become volatile.
examples.analytical: Calling a protected zone a safe haven can obscure the question of who has the power to enforce its boundaries.

nuance.analogy: Like a harbor in a storm: it does not stop the weather, but it keeps the ship from being wrecked.
nuance.etymology: Safe from Latin salvus, and haven from Old English hæfen, meaning harbor.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing haven as hay-ven with a long e at the end; say HAY-vun.
Thinking safe haven only means a physical place; in finance it refers to assets that keep their value in a crash.

senses.definition: The property of being, or tasting, salty.

core.definition: The quality of tasting of salt or being salty; the degree to which food or water tastes of salt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle -i- is a quick 'ee', not 'eye', and the -ness ending reduces to 'nuhs'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it usually describes an unpleasant excess of salt, though cooks can discuss it neutrally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use saltiness to describe the taste of food, the flavor of sea water or air, or, figuratively, earthy and slightly crude humor. In conversation people more often say too salty than too much saltiness. Cooks often talk about balancing saltiness with acid or sweetness.

distinctions.note: Salinity is the scientific measure of dissolved salt in water or soil; saltiness is how it tastes or feels to people.
Salty is the everyday adjective; saltiness is the noun for the quality.

examples.everyday: The soup is a little too much, but a squeeze of lemon will balance the saltiness.
examples.professional: The product team logged complaints about the saltiness of the new snack, so we are testing a lower-sodium version.
examples.analytical: Consumers often judge saltiness by perceived intensity, which depends as much on texture and aroma as on actual sodium content.

nuance.analogy: Saltiness is the volume knob of taste: a little turns the flavor up nicely, but too much becomes painful.
nuance.etymology: From salty, from Old English sealt (salt), plus the noun suffix -iness.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: SAWLT-ee-nuhs, not sal-TEE-nuhs.
Using saltiness in technical contexts where salinity is the correct term.
Using it for a person's personality; it usually refers to taste or earthy humor.

senses.definition: A setting that controls how random a model's output is: lower is more predictable, higher is more varied.
senses.example: Lowering the sampling temperature made the chatbot's answers far more consistent across repeated runs.

core.definition: In AI, a setting that controls how random a language model's output is: lower values give more predictable text, higher values more varied text.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrase, the main stress moves to temperature; the first word, sampling, gets a secondary stress. Say temp as TEM and the final syllable as a reduced r-colored vowel, not tuh or tyoor.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Developers and data scientists use sampling temperature when configuring models through APIs or libraries. In a meeting, Americans say 'let's lower the temperature' or 'set the temp to 0.2' informally. The term is technical, so explain it briefly when speaking with non-specialists.

distinctions.note: Top-p (nucleus sampling) limits choices to a cumulative probability mass, while temperature rescales the whole probability distribution.
Temperature alone is the physical measure of heat, while sampling temperature is a model setting for randomness.

examples.everyday: My chatbot sounds too random, so I'm going to turn the sampling temperature down.
examples.professional: For the extraction pipeline, we set the sampling temperature to zero so the outputs are reproducible across runs.
examples.analytical: Raising the sampling temperature flattens the softmax distribution, which increases entropy and diversity but also the chance of incoherent tokens.

nuance.analogy: Sampling temperature is like a dial on a radio: turned down, the station is clear and predictable; turned up, it gets noisy and surprising.
nuance.etymology: Sampling from sample (verb); temperature from Latin temperatura, a mixing or proper measure.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing temperature with four clear syllables instead of three, with the middle one reduced.
Confusing sampling temperature with the physical temperature of the server or room.

conversation.text: Sampling temperature divides the logits before the softmax; lower values sharpen the distribution and higher values flatten it.
Set the sampling temperature to zero for extraction tasks; we want consistency, not creativity.
Sampling temperature is like a creativity dial: low is predictable, high is more surprising and more error-prone.

senses.definition: The wood just under the bark of a stem or branch; it differs from the heartwood in color and in physiologic activity (flow of sap).
senses.example: A popular myth is that sapwood is not as strong as heartwood.

core.definition: The living, lighter-colored outer layer of wood just under the bark, which carries sap through the tree.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAP, with a secondary stress on WOOD. The vowel in 'wood' is short, like 'good' and 'book', not the long 'oo' of 'food'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical term used in forestry, lumber, and woodworking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sapwood' in woodworking, forestry, carpentry, and lumber grading. Buyers often reject boards with too much sapwood because it can rot or attract insects more easily than heartwood. In everyday conversation people usually say 'the pale part of the wood' or just 'wood'.

distinctions.note: Heartwood is the dead, darker inner core that gives strength; sapwood is the living, lighter outer wood that conducts sap.
Bark is the protective outer covering of the tree; sapwood lies just beneath it.

examples.everyday: This board has a lot of pale sapwood, so it won't be as sturdy as the darker ones.
examples.professional: Our quality inspection rejects boards with excessive sapwood because it is prone to decay and insect damage.
examples.analytical: The dendrochronologist counted growth rings in the sapwood to estimate the tree's age before it was felled.

nuance.analogy: Sapwood is like the plumbing under the walls of a house: it carries the water through, while the heartwood is the solid frame that holds the house up.
nuance.etymology: From 'sap' plus 'wood'; the word names the wood that conducts sap.
common_mistakes: Confusing sapwood with sap, which is the liquid rather than the tissue.
Pronouncing 'wood' with a long oo sound, as in 'food'.

senses.definition: Pleasantly satisfied or full, as with food; sated.
senses.example: After the huge Thanksgiving dinner, we felt satiated and happy to nap on the couch.

core.definition: Completely full or satisfied, especially after eating, or having a desire or need fully met.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle 'ti' sounds like 'sh', not 't'. The ending '-ated' is pronounced 'ay-tid', with the final syllable reduced to a short 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests a state of comfortable fullness, but it can also imply excess when used of appetites.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use satiated mostly in writing, academic discussion or careful speech, such as 'The guests were satiated after dinner.' In casual talk people say 'full', 'stuffed' or 'I'm good, thanks', so satiated would sound stiff in a restaurant. It is common in nutrition and psychology, where it describes the feeling of having eaten enough.

distinctions.note: Sated is shorter and more literary, while satiated is more formal and often used in academic or technical writing.
Full is everyday and can describe a stomach or a container, while satiated focuses on the satisfaction of a desire or appetite.

examples.everyday: We ate so much pizza that everyone was satiated and nobody wanted dessert.
examples.professional: The study measured how quickly participants felt satiated after a high-protein lunch.
examples.analytical: A person who is satiated may still desire more, so satiation does not automatically end wanting.

nuance.analogy: Think of a phone battery at one hundred percent: it has taken in all it can hold and needs nothing more for now.
nuance.etymology: From satiate (verb), from Latin satiare 'to fill', from satis 'enough'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'satiated' in casual talk when 'full' or 'stuffed' is more natural.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'tee' instead of 'shee'.

senses.definition: One who scans.
senses.example: As a proofreader, he was a careful scanner of every page in the manuscript.

senses.definition: A device which scans documents in order to convert them to a digital medium.
senses.example: He put the picture in the scanner, then e-mailed a copy of it to his family.

senses.definition: A device which scans barcodes or QR codes for the purpose of charging a customer, performing a price check or enquiry, printing a price label or sticker, checking an item in or out of the store or warehouse, or finding an item ordered through click and collect and its corresponding location; a pricing gun or HHT.
senses.example: The cashier used the scanner to check the price of each item in my cart.

senses.definition: A radio receiver which iterates through a sequence of frequencies to detect signal.
senses.example: The old radio scanner kept jumping between police channels until it found the signal.

senses.definition: A device which uses radiation (ultrasound, X-ray, etc.) to generate images of tissue or surfaces for diagnostic purposes.
senses.example: The radiologist ordered a CT scanner exam to check for a blood clot in my lung.

senses.definition: A device which uses optics to detect printed data (such as a barcode).
senses.example: The grocery's handheld scanner read the printed barcode on the cereal box instantly.

core.definition: A device that reads barcodes, QR codes or paper documents and converts them into digital information.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SKAN. The final -er is a reduced American 'er', not 'ahr'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a practical everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scanner for the barcode reader at a store checkout, the flatbed scanner at an office, and the handheld price-check device the staff uses on shelves. People say 'the scanner beeped' or 'the cashier scanned my items.' A handheld device used to print price labels is usually called a pricing gun.

distinctions.note: A copier makes a paper duplicate of a document; a scanner converts it into a digital file.
Reader is a general term; scanner usually refers to a device that captures an image or barcode in one pass.

examples.everyday: The cashier's scanner beeped twice, so I know the discount came through.
examples.professional: Can you scan the signed contract on the office scanner and send it as a PDF?
examples.analytical: A scanner converts analog documents into digital data, which raises questions about accuracy and metadata.

nuance.analogy: A scanner is like a camera that photographs paper and turns the picture into a computer file.
nuance.etymology: From scan, which comes from Latin scandere, to climb, a term later used for scanning verse.
common_mistakes: Using scanner for a camera; a scanner converts documents or codes into digital data.
Putting the stress on the second syllable, as in 'skan-AIR'.

conversation.text: The scanner isn't reading the coupon on my phone.
There's a price scanner in aisle five if you want to check a price.
The cashier passed each item over the scanner really fast.

senses.definition: In a schismatic way.

core.definition: In a way that splits a religious body or organization into opposing factions, breaking its unity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -MAT-, and the final -ly is a light 'lee'; in schism itself the stress is on the first syllable, but it moves in schismatic.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It describes a break in unity, usually judged as harmful by the group involved.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, formal adverb found mainly in church history, theology and academic writing, so Americans would seldom use it in conversation. In everyday speech, people say 'in a divisive way' or 'in a way that splits the group'. The noun schism and the adjective schismatic are much more common than the adverb.

distinctions.note: Heretically describes denying accepted doctrine; schismatically describes breaking fellowship or unity, which can happen even without a doctrinal dispute.
Divisively is general and can describe anything that splits people; schismatically is specific to a church or religious body.
